uni-bsc-phy-solid-state.title: B.Sc Physics · Solid State Physics
uni-bsc-phy-solid-state.description: Crystal structure, X-ray diffraction, lattice vibrations, free-electron and band theory, magnetism, dielectrics and superconductivity, with solved numericals and unit exams. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Physics (Hons) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Crystal structure and X-ray diffraction
courses.summary: How atoms arrange in crystals: lattice plus basis, Bravais lattices, Miller indices, packing, Bragg diffraction, reciprocal lattice and structure factor, with solved numericals.
outcomes: Distinguish lattice, basis and crystal structure and name the 14 Bravais lattices
Compute packing fraction and density of SC, BCC and FCC crystals
Find Miller indices of planes and interplanar spacing in cubic crystals
Apply Bragg's law to X-ray diffraction data
Use structure factor to predict allowed reflections in BCC and FCC

lessons.title: Lattice, basis, unit cells and packing

scenes.text: At a Pune market, a vendor stacks oranges in a neat pyramid. Each layer sits in the hollows of the one below.
Meera wonders how much of the pyramid is fruit and how much is air. The same question about atoms gives us packing fraction.

steps.title: Crystal = lattice + basis
steps.body:
- A **lattice** is an infinite array of points, each with identical surroundings: R = n₁a₁ + n₂a₂ + n₃a₃.
- A **basis** is the group of atoms attached to every lattice point.
- A **primitive cell** contains exactly one lattice point; a **conventional unit cell** may contain more (BCC has 2, FCC has 4).
- In 3D there are **7 crystal systems** and **14 Bravais lattices**.

steps.title: Cubic cells at a glance
steps.body:
| Cell | Atoms/cell | Coordination no. | a in terms of r | Packing fraction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SC | 1 | 6 | a = 2r | π/6 ≈ 0.52 |
| BCC | 2 | 8 | a = 4r/√3 | √3π/8 ≈ 0.68 |
| FCC | 4 | 12 | a = 2√2 r | √2π/6 ≈ 0.74 |

HCP also reaches 0.74 with coordination number 12.

steps.title: Solved: density of copper
steps.body:
Copper is FCC with a = 3.61 Å and M = 63.5 g/mol.

- ρ = nM/(N_A a³)
- a³ = (3.61 × 10⁻⁸ cm)³ = 4.705 × 10⁻²³ cm³
- N_A a³ = 6.022 × 10²³ × 4.705 × 10⁻²³ = 28.33 cm³/mol
- ρ = 4 × 63.5 / 28.33 = **8.97 g/cm³** (measured: 8.96 g/cm³)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting corner atoms as whole atoms: each corner is shared by 8 cells (1/8), each face by 2 (1/2).
- Using a = 2r for BCC or FCC: atoms touch along the body diagonal in BCC and along the face diagonal in FCC.
- Forgetting to convert Å to cm when the density is wanted in g/cm³.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Iron is BCC at room temperature and FCC above about 912 °C. This change in packing is the basis of steel heat treatment in every Indian steel plant.

activity.prompt: Sodium is BCC with lattice constant a = 4.29 Å. Find the atomic radius r = √3a/4, in Å (two decimals).

quiz.q: The number of atoms per conventional unit cell of an FCC lattice is:
quiz.why: FCC has 8 corners × 1/8 + 6 faces × 1/2 = 1 + 3 = 4 atoms per cell.

quiz.q: The coordination number of a BCC lattice is:
quiz.why: In BCC the body-centre atom touches the 8 corner atoms, so the coordination number is 8.

quiz.q: How many Bravais lattices exist in three dimensions?
quiz.why: Combining the 7 crystal systems with the possible centrings gives 14 distinct Bravais lattices.

scenes.text: Rahul cuts a cube of jaggery along different directions in the lab and sees shiny flat faces appear.
Each family of parallel atomic planes has a label of three integers. These are the Miller indices.

steps.title: Finding Miller indices
steps.body:
1. Find intercepts of the plane on the axes in units of a, b, c.
2. Take reciprocals.
3. Clear fractions to the smallest integers (h k l).
4. A plane parallel to an axis has intercept ∞, so its index is 0. A negative intercept is written with a bar, e.g. (1̄00).

steps.title: Solved: intercepts 2a, 3b, ∞
steps.body:
- Intercepts: 2, 3, ∞
- Reciprocals: 1/2, 1/3, 0
- Multiply by 6: 3, 2, 0
- Miller indices: **(320)**

steps.title: Spacing in cubic crystals
steps.body:
For a cubic lattice of side a:

d_hkl = a / √(h² + k² + l²)

In a cubic crystal the direction [hkl] is perpendicular to the plane (hkl). This is not true in general for non-cubic crystals.

steps.title: Solved: d for (111) and (110)
steps.body:
a = 4.0 Å.

- d₁₁₁ = 4.0/√3 = **2.31 Å**
- d₁₁₀ = 4.0/√2 = **2.83 Å**
- d₁₀₀ = 4.0 Å

Higher indices mean more closely spaced planes.

steps.title: Exam habit
steps.body: Write intercepts, reciprocals and the final integers in three separate lines. Examiners award step marks for each line.

activity.prompt: A cubic crystal has a = 5.0 Å. Find the interplanar spacing d for the (200) planes, in Å.

quiz.q: A plane has intercepts a, ∞, ∞. Its Miller indices are:
quiz.why: The reciprocals of 1, ∞, ∞ are 1, 0, 0, so the plane is (100).

quiz.q: In a cubic crystal, d_hkl equals:
quiz.why: For cubic lattices the spacing between (hkl) planes is a divided by the square root of h²+k²+l².

quiz.q: Intercepts a, 2b, 3c give Miller indices:
quiz.why: Reciprocals 1, 1/2, 1/3 multiplied by 6 give 6, 3, 2, so the plane is (632).

scenes.text: In the university XRD lab, Anjali loads a powder of sodium chloride and watches peaks appear on the screen as the detector swings.
Each peak is a family of planes reflecting X-rays in phase. Bragg's law tells her the spacing.

steps.title: Bragg's law
steps.body:
Rays reflected from adjacent planes differ in path by 2d sinθ. They add constructively when:

**2d sinθ = nλ**

θ is the glancing angle (between ray and plane), n is the order. X-rays are used because λ ≈ 1 Å is comparable to atomic spacing. Cu Kα has λ = 1.54 Å.

steps.title: Solved: glancing angle
steps.body:
Cu Kα (λ = 1.54 Å) falls on (111) planes with d = 2.31 Å. First order:

- sinθ = λ/2d = 1.54/4.62 = 0.333
- θ = **19.5°**
- The detector angle 2θ is 39.0°.

steps.title: Solved: maximum order
steps.body: d = 2.0 Å, λ = 1.54 Å. Since sinθ ≤ 1, n ≤ 2d/λ = 4.0/1.54 = 2.6. So only **n = 1 and 2** are possible.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Laue method**: fixed crystal, white X-rays; gives symmetry.
- **Rotating crystal method**: monochromatic X-rays, crystal rotated.
- **Powder (Debye–Scherrer) method**: monochromatic X-rays, random grains; rings at each allowed 2θ. Used daily in materials labs.

steps.title: Watch the angle
steps.body: θ in Bragg's law is measured from the plane, not from the normal. Diffractometers record 2θ; halve it before using the formula.

activity.prompt: X-rays of wavelength 1.54 Å give a first-order Bragg peak at θ = 30°. Find the interplanar spacing d in Å.

quiz.q: Bragg's law is:
quiz.why: The path difference between rays reflected from adjacent planes is 2d sinθ, and constructive interference needs it to equal nλ.

quiz.q: X-rays are used for crystal diffraction because:
options: their wavelength is comparable to atomic spacing
quiz.why: Diffraction is strong only when the wavelength is similar to the spacing of the scatterers, and X-ray wavelengths are about 1 Å, like interatomic distances.

quiz.q: A diffractometer shows a peak at 2θ = 40°. The Bragg angle is:
quiz.why: The detector records twice the glancing angle, so θ = 40°/2 = 20°.

scenes.text: Anjali's tungsten (BCC) pattern has no (100) peak, though the planes clearly exist.
Her teacher explains: the body-centre atoms reflect exactly out of phase. The structure factor predicts which peaks vanish.

steps.title: Reciprocal lattice
steps.body:
Reciprocal vectors: b₁ = 2π(a₂ × a₃)/[a₁·(a₂ × a₃)], and cyclically.

- aᵢ·bⱼ = 2πδᵢⱼ
- Each reciprocal vector G = hb₁ + kb₂ + lb₃ is normal to the (hkl) planes, with |G| = 2π/d_hkl.
- Laue condition: Δk = G, which is equivalent to Bragg's law.
- Reciprocal of SC is SC; of BCC is FCC; of FCC is BCC.

steps.title: Structure factor
steps.body:
S_hkl = Σ fⱼ exp[2πi(h xⱼ + k yⱼ + l zⱼ)] over atoms in the cell. Intensity ∝ |S|².

- **BCC** (atoms at 000 and ½½½): S = f[1 + (−1)^(h+k+l)]. Reflection only if **h+k+l is even**.
- **FCC**: S = 4f if h, k, l are **all even or all odd**; otherwise 0.

steps.title: Solved: first lines of BCC and FCC
steps.body:
Order by h²+k²+l²:

- BCC allowed: (110) 2, (200) 4, (211) 6, (220) 8 → ratio 2:4:6:8
- FCC allowed: (111) 3, (200) 4, (220) 8, (311) 11 → ratio 3:4:8:11

So the ratio of sin²θ values identifies the lattice from a powder pattern.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: If your sin²θ ratios start 1:2:3:4:5:6:8 (no 7), the lattice is simple cubic.

steps.title: In industry
steps.body: Pharmaceutical companies use powder XRD to tell polymorphs of the same drug apart, because different crystal forms dissolve at different rates.

activity.prompt: For a BCC crystal, how many of these reflections are allowed: (100), (110), (111), (200), (210), (211)? Enter the count.

quiz.q: In BCC, the (100) reflection is absent because:
quiz.why: For BCC, S = f[1 + (−1)^(h+k+l)], which is zero when h+k+l is odd, as for (100).

quiz.q: The reciprocal lattice of an FCC lattice is:
quiz.why: The reciprocal of FCC is BCC and the reciprocal of BCC is FCC.

quiz.q: Which reflection is allowed in FCC?
quiz.why: FCC allows only reflections whose indices are all odd or all even, and (111) is all odd.

questions.q: The packing fraction of an FCC lattice is about:
questions.why: FCC packs √2π/6 ≈ 0.74 of space, the maximum for equal spheres.

questions.q: Atoms per unit cell in BCC:
questions.why: BCC has 8 × 1/8 corner atoms plus 1 body-centre atom, giving 2.

questions.q: In BCC, the atomic radius r and lattice constant a are related by:
questions.why: In BCC atoms touch along the body diagonal √3a, which equals 4r.

questions.q: Intercepts 3a, 2b, c give Miller indices:
questions.why: Reciprocals 1/3, 1/2, 1 multiplied by 6 give 2, 3, 6.

questions.q: For a = 3.0 Å, d₁₁₁ is about:
First-order Bragg reflection with λ = 1.54 Å and d = 1.54 Å occurs at θ =
questions.why: sinθ = λ/2d = 0.5, so θ = 30°.

questions.q: In the powder method, the sample is:
questions.why: The powder method uses many randomly oriented grains so every set of planes finds some grains at the Bragg angle.

questions.q: The magnitude of the reciprocal lattice vector G_hkl is:
questions.why: Each G_hkl is normal to the (hkl) planes with length 2π divided by their spacing.

questions.q: A powder pattern has sin²θ ratios 3:4:8:11. The lattice is:
questions.why: FCC's first allowed reflections (111), (200), (220), (311) have h²+k²+l² = 3, 4, 8, 11.

questions.q: The coordination number of an FCC lattice is:
questions.why: Each FCC atom touches 4 neighbours in its own plane, 4 above and 4 below, which makes 12.

questions.q: Aluminium is FCC with a = 4.05 Å and M = 27 g/mol. Its density is about:
With d = 2.0 Å and λ = 1.54 Å, the highest possible order of Bragg reflection is:
questions.why: n ≤ 2d/λ = 2.6, and n must be a whole number, so the highest order is 2.

questions.q: The Laue condition Δk = G is equivalent to:
questions.why: Taking magnitudes in Δk = G, with |G| = 2πn/d, gives 2d sinθ = nλ, which is Bragg's law.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Lattice vibrations and thermal properties
courses.summary: Atoms in a crystal vibrate as coupled oscillators. This unit derives dispersion relations for monatomic and diatomic chains, introduces phonons, and explains specific heat from Dulong–Petit to the Einstein and Debye models.
outcomes: Derive the dispersion relation of a monatomic linear chain
Explain acoustic and optical branches of a diatomic chain
Describe phonons as quanta of lattice vibration
Compare the Dulong–Petit, Einstein and Debye models of specific heat
Use the Debye T³ law in numericals

scenes.text: Kabir strings beads on springs in the hostel corridor and flicks one end. A ripple runs down the chain.
Short ripples move slower than he expects. A crystal behaves the same way, and the rule is the dispersion relation.

steps.title: Equation of motion
steps.body:
Atoms of mass m, spacing a, nearest-neighbour spring constant K:

m ü_n = K(u_{n+1} + u_{n−1} − 2u_n)

Try u_n = A exp[i(kna − ωt)]. This gives

**ω = 2√(K/m) |sin(ka/2)|**

steps.title: What the curve says
steps.body:
- For small k (long waves), ω ≈ a√(K/m)·k: a linear sound wave with speed v_s = a√(K/m).
- ω is periodic in k; all distinct modes lie in the **first Brillouin zone**, −π/a ≤ k ≤ π/a.
- At k = ±π/a, ω_max = 2√(K/m) and the group velocity dω/dk = 0: a standing wave.
- The chain acts as a **low-pass filter**: no wave propagates above ω_max.

steps.title: Solved: cut-off frequency
steps.body:
K = 10 N/m, m = 1.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg.

- K/m = 1.0 × 10²⁷ s⁻²
- √(K/m) = 3.16 × 10¹³ rad/s
- ω_max = 2 × 3.16 × 10¹³ = **6.32 × 10¹³ rad/s** (about 10 THz, in the infrared)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing sin(ka) instead of sin(ka/2).
- Treating k outside the first Brillouin zone as new modes: k and k + 2π/a describe the same atomic motion.

steps.title: Counting modes
steps.body: A chain of N atoms with periodic boundary conditions has exactly N allowed k values in the first zone, so N modes per branch.

activity.prompt: For a monatomic chain with K = 16 N/m and m = 4.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, find ω_max = 2√(K/m) in units of 10¹³ rad/s.

quiz.q: The dispersion relation of a monatomic chain is:
quiz.why: Substituting a travelling wave into m ü_n = K(u_{n+1} + u_{n−1} − 2u_n) gives ω = 2√(K/m)|sin(ka/2)|.

quiz.q: At the edge of the first Brillouin zone, the group velocity is:
quiz.why: The slope dω/dk = a√(K/m) cos(ka/2) vanishes at k = π/a, so the wave is standing.

quiz.q: The first Brillouin zone of a chain with spacing a extends over:
quiz.why: All physically distinct wave vectors lie between −π/a and π/a, which is the first Brillouin zone.

lessons.title: Diatomic chain: acoustic and optical branches

scenes.text: A spectroscopy group shines infrared light on a NaCl crystal and finds a sharp absorption band.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ move against each other at that frequency. That is an optical phonon.

steps.title: Two masses per cell
steps.body:
Alternate masses m and M (M > m), spring K, cell length 2a. Solving gives two branches:

ω² = K(1/m + 1/M) ± K√[(1/m + 1/M)² − 4 sin²(ka)/(mM)]

- Minus sign: **acoustic branch**, ω → 0 as k → 0.
- Plus sign: **optical branch**, ω(0) = √[2K(1/m + 1/M)].

steps.title: The gap
steps.body:
At the zone edge k = π/2a:

- acoustic top: ω = √(2K/M)
- optical bottom: ω = √(2K/m)

No vibration exists between these two frequencies. If m = M, the gap closes and we get back the monatomic chain.

steps.title: Solved: frequencies at the zone edge
Why 'optical'?
steps.body: In the optical mode at k ≈ 0, neighbouring ions move in opposite directions. In ionic crystals this makes an oscillating dipole that couples strongly to infrared light.

steps.title: Counting branches
steps.body: A 3D crystal with p atoms per primitive cell has 3 acoustic and 3p − 3 optical branches.

activity.prompt: A diatomic chain has K = 18 N/m, m = 1.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and M = 2.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Find the optical frequency at k = 0, ω = √[2K(1/m + 1/M)], in units of 10¹³ rad/s (two decimals).

quiz.q: In the acoustic branch near k = 0, neighbouring atoms move:
quiz.why: Long-wavelength acoustic modes move all atoms in a cell together, like a sound wave.

quiz.q: The frequency gap of a diatomic chain disappears when:
quiz.why: The gap lies between √(2K/M) and √(2K/m), which coincide when the two masses are equal.

quiz.q: A 3D crystal with 2 atoms per primitive cell has how many optical branches?
quiz.why: With p = 2 there are 3p = 6 branches in total, 3 acoustic and 3p − 3 = 3 optical.

scenes.text: In 1907 data showed diamond's heat capacity at room temperature was far below the classical 3R.
Einstein quantised the vibrations of each atom and explained the drop. The quanta are now called phonons.

steps.title: Phonons
steps.body: Each normal mode of frequency ω is a quantum oscillator with energy (n + ½)ħω. The quantum ħω is a **phonon**. Phonons carry crystal momentum ħk, obey Bose–Einstein statistics and are not conserved in number.

steps.title: Dulong–Petit and its failure
steps.body: Classically each atom has 3 oscillators with mean energy k_BT each, so molar C_V = 3R ≈ **24.9 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**. This works at high T, but experiment shows C_V → 0 as T → 0.

steps.title: Einstein model
steps.body:
All 3N oscillators have the same frequency ω_E. With θ_E = ħω_E/k_B and x = θ_E/T:

C_V = 3R x² eˣ/(eˣ − 1)²

- T ≫ θ_E: C_V → 3R.
- T ≪ θ_E: C_V ∝ x² e^(−x), which falls exponentially, faster than experiment shows.

steps.title: Limits of the model
steps.body: Real crystals have a spread of phonon frequencies. Low-frequency acoustic modes are still excited at low T, so the true C_V falls as T³, not exponentially.

activity.prompt: Using Dulong–Petit, find the heat needed to raise 2 mol of a solid by 10 K (C_V = 3R, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), in J.

quiz.q: The Dulong–Petit value of molar heat capacity is about:
quiz.why: Classical equipartition gives 3 oscillators per atom, each worth R per mole, so C_V = 3R ≈ 24.9 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

quiz.q: At very low temperature, the Einstein model predicts C_V falls:
quiz.why: With a single frequency, excitation needs ħω_E, so C_V varies as x²e^(−x), which drops exponentially.

quiz.q: Phonons obey:
quiz.why: Phonons are quanta of harmonic oscillators, any number can occupy a mode, so they are bosons.

lessons.title: Debye model and the T³ law

scenes.text: At a low-temperature lab in Mumbai, students measure the heat capacity of a copper sample below 20 K.
Plotted against T³ the points lie on a straight line. Debye's model predicts exactly that.

steps.title: Debye's assumptions
steps.body:
- Treat the crystal as an elastic continuum: ω = v_s k.
- Density of states g(ω) ∝ ω².
- Cut off at ω_D so the total number of modes is 3N.
- Debye temperature θ_D = ħω_D/k_B.

steps.title: Results
steps.body:
- High T (T ≫ θ_D): C_V → 3R.
- Low T (T ≪ θ_D): **C_V = (12π⁴/5) R (T/θ_D)³ ≈ 1944 (T/θ_D)³ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**.

Typical θ_D: Pb ≈ 105 K, Cu ≈ 343 K, diamond ≈ 2230 K. A high θ_D means stiff bonds and light atoms.

steps.title: Scaling trick
steps.body: If T doubles at low temperature, C_V rises by 2³ = 8. Use ratios to avoid long arithmetic.

steps.title: Diamond heat spreaders
steps.body: Because θ_D of diamond is so high, its phonons carry heat very efficiently. Synthetic diamond is used to cool high-power laser diodes.

activity.prompt: A solid has θ_D = 400 K. Using C_V = 1944 (T/θ_D)³ J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find C_V at T = 20 K (three decimals).

quiz.q: In the Debye model, the phonon density of states is proportional to:
quiz.why: For a continuum with linear dispersion, the number of modes in a shell of k-space grows as k², so g(ω) ∝ ω².

quiz.q: At low T, C_V of an insulator varies as:
quiz.why: Debye's model gives C_V ∝ (T/θ_D)³ at low temperature, which matches experiment.

quiz.q: If C_V = 0.1 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 5 K (low-T region), at 10 K it is about:
quiz.why: Doubling T multiplies C_V by 2³ = 8, giving 0.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.q: The maximum frequency of a monatomic chain is:
questions.why: At k = π/a, sin(ka/2) = 1, so ω_max = 2√(K/m).

questions.q: For small k, a monatomic chain carries waves with speed:
questions.why: For small k, ω ≈ a√(K/m) k, so the phase and group speed is a√(K/m).

questions.q: A crystal acts as a low-pass filter for elastic waves because:
options: waves above ω_max do not propagate
questions.why: The dispersion relation has no real k above ω_max, so higher frequencies are not transmitted.

questions.q: At k = 0 the optical branch frequency is:
questions.why: Setting k = 0 in the plus branch gives ω² = 2K(1/m + 1/M).

questions.q: Infrared absorption in ionic crystals is due to:
questions.why: Optical modes make oppositely charged ions move against each other, producing a dipole that absorbs IR light.

questions.q: A crystal with p atoms per primitive cell has how many acoustic branches?
questions.why: There are always 3 acoustic branches in 3D, one longitudinal and two transverse, whatever p is.

questions.q: The Dulong–Petit law holds best at:
questions.why: Equipartition is valid when k_BT is much larger than the phonon energies, which means high temperature.

questions.q: The Einstein model fails at low temperature because:
questions.why: A single frequency cannot represent the low-frequency acoustic modes that remain excited at low T.

questions.q: For θ_E = 300 K, the Einstein frequency ω_E is about:
A material with a very high Debye temperature has:
questions.why: θ_D grows with sound speed, which is large when bonds are stiff and atoms are light, as in diamond.

questions.q: θ_D = 200 K. Low-T C_V at 4 K is about:
The number of modes in the Debye model is fixed at 3N by:
questions.why: Debye chose ω_D so that integrating g(ω) up to it gives exactly 3N modes.

questions.q: Diatomic chain: K = 8 N/m, M = 4 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Top of the acoustic branch √(2K/M) is:
questions.why: 2K/M = 16/(4 × 10⁻²⁶) = 4 × 10²⁶, whose square root is 2 × 10¹³ rad/s.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Free electrons, band theory and the Hall effect
courses.summary: From Drude's classical electron gas to Sommerfeld's quantum free-electron model, then to energy bands in a periodic potential, the difference between metals, semiconductors and insulators, and the Hall effect.
outcomes: Derive σ = ne²τ/m and estimate relaxation time and drift velocity
Calculate Fermi energy and Fermi velocity of a metal
Explain the origin of energy bands with the Kronig–Penney model
Classify solids as metals, semiconductors and insulators using band gaps
Use the Hall effect to find carrier type and density

scenes.text: Ishaan flips the switch and the hostel bulb lights instantly, yet his professor says the electrons in the wire crawl at a fraction of a millimetre per second.
The signal moves fast; the electrons drift slowly. The Drude model makes both facts fit.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body:
- Valence electrons form a classical gas moving between collisions with ions.
- Mean time between collisions: relaxation time τ.
- In a field E, the drift velocity is v_d = −eEτ/m.
- Current density J = −nev_d = (ne²τ/m)E, so **σ = ne²τ/m** (Ohm's law).

steps.title: Solved: drift velocity
steps.body:
2 A flows in a copper wire of cross-section 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m².

- v_d = I/(neA) = 2/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁶)
- = 2/1.36 × 10⁴ = **1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s**, about 0.15 mm/s

steps.title: Where Drude fails
steps.body:
- It predicts an electronic heat capacity of (3/2)R per mole, which is not observed.
- It cannot explain positive Hall coefficients in some metals such as Zn.
- It gives the wrong temperature dependence of resistivity.

The Wiedemann–Franz law (κ/σT constant) comes out right, partly by luck.

steps.title: Units check
steps.body: σ = ne²τ/m: (m⁻³)(C²)(s)/(kg) = S/m. Always check units in derivations.

activity.prompt: A copper wire (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) of cross-section 2 mm² carries 3 A. Find the drift velocity in units of 10⁻⁴ m/s (two decimals).

quiz.q: In the Drude model, conductivity is:
quiz.why: Drift velocity eEτ/m times charge density ne gives J = (ne²τ/m)E.

quiz.q: Drift velocity in a household wire is typically about:
quiz.why: With n ≈ 10²⁹ m⁻³, ordinary currents need only v_d of order 10⁻⁴ m/s.

quiz.q: A major failure of the Drude model is:
quiz.why: Drude predicts a large (3/2)R electronic heat capacity, but metals show only about 1% of that.

scenes.text: In a hostel where each room takes only two students, latecomers must go to higher floors even if they would like the ground floor.
Electrons obey the same rule, the Pauli principle. The top filled 'floor' at 0 K is the Fermi energy.

steps.title: Electrons in a box
steps.body:
Free electrons in a cube of side L with periodic boundary conditions have E = ħ²k²/2m. Each k-state holds 2 electrons (spin).

Filling a sphere of radius k_F with N electrons gives

- k_F = (3π²n)^(1/3)
- **E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3)**
- v_F = ħk_F/m, T_F = E_F/k_B

steps.title: Fermi–Dirac distribution
steps.body:
f(E) = 1/[exp((E − E_F)/k_BT) + 1].

At room temperature k_BT ≈ 0.025 eV ≪ E_F, so only electrons within about k_BT of E_F can be excited. This explains why the electronic heat capacity is small: C_el = (π²/2) R (T/T_F).

steps.title: Density of states
steps.body: In 3D, g(E) ∝ √E. At T = 0 every state below E_F is full and every state above it is empty.

steps.title: Common slip
steps.body: Use n in m⁻³, not cm⁻³. For copper, 8.5 × 10²² cm⁻³ = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.

activity.prompt: For copper, k_F = 1.36 × 10¹⁰ m⁻¹. Find the Fermi velocity v_F = ħk_F/m in units of 10⁶ m/s (two decimals; ħ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg).

quiz.q: The Fermi energy depends on electron density n as:
quiz.why: E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3), so it scales as n to the power 2/3.

quiz.q: At T = 0 K, the Fermi–Dirac function for E < E_F is:
quiz.why: At absolute zero all states below the Fermi energy are fully occupied, so f = 1.

quiz.q: The electronic heat capacity of metals is small because:
options: only electrons near E_F can be excited
quiz.why: The Pauli principle blocks most electrons; only a fraction of about T/T_F near E_F can absorb thermal energy.

scenes.text: Graphite in a pencil conducts; diamond in a ring does not. Both are pure carbon.
The arrangement changes the band structure. Whether a band is full or partly full decides if a solid conducts.

steps.title: Bloch's theorem
steps.body:
In a periodic potential V(x + a) = V(x), electron wavefunctions take the form

ψ_k(x) = u_k(x) e^(ikx), with u_k(x + a) = u_k(x).

The electron is spread through the crystal, modulated by the lattice.

steps.title: Kronig–Penney result
steps.body:
For a lattice of square barriers (strength P):

P (sin αa)/(αa) + cos αa = cos ka, with α² = 2mE/ħ².

The right side lies between −1 and +1. Energies where the left side goes outside that range are forbidden. This gives **allowed bands separated by gaps**. Gaps open at k = nπ/a, at the Brillouin-zone edges. As P → 0 we get free electrons; as P → ∞ we get discrete atomic levels.

steps.title: Effective mass
steps.body: m* = ħ²/(d²E/dk²). Near the bottom of a band m* > 0; near the top m* < 0, and the electron behaves like a positive **hole**.

steps.title: Metals, semiconductors, insulators
steps.body:
- **Metal**: partly filled band, or overlapping bands (Cu, Na, Mg).
- **Semiconductor**: full valence band, small gap (Si 1.12 eV, Ge 0.66 eV, GaAs 1.42 eV at 300 K).
- **Insulator**: large gap (diamond ≈ 5.5 eV).

steps.title: Solved: absorption edge of silicon
steps.body:
Photons are absorbed across the gap when hc/λ ≥ E_g.

- λ (nm) ≈ 1240/E_g (eV)
- Si: 1240/1.12 = **1107 nm**

So silicon absorbs visible light but is transparent beyond about 1.1 μm.

activity.prompt: GaAs has a band gap of 1.42 eV. Using λ (nm) = 1240/E_g (eV), find its absorption-edge wavelength in nm.

quiz.q: Energy gaps in the Kronig–Penney model appear at:
quiz.why: At k = nπ/a waves are Bragg-reflected by the lattice and standing waves split in energy, opening gaps.

quiz.q: Near the top of a band, the effective mass is:
quiz.why: The E–k curve bends downward near a band top, so d²E/dk² < 0 and m* is negative.

quiz.q: A solid with a completely full valence band and a 6 eV gap is:
quiz.why: A full band carries no current, and 6 eV is far too large for thermal excitation, so it is an insulator.

scenes.text: Two unlabelled silicon wafers sit in a drawer. One is n-type, one p-type. Shreya puts each in a magnet and passes a current.
The sign of the sideways voltage tells her which is which. That sideways voltage is the Hall voltage.

steps.title: Carriers in semiconductors
steps.body:
- Intrinsic: n = p = nᵢ, with nᵢ ∝ T^(3/2) exp(−E_g/2k_BT). The Fermi level is near mid-gap.
- n-type (P, As donors): electrons are majority carriers.
- p-type (B, Al acceptors): holes are majority carriers.
- Conductivity: σ = e(nμ_e + pμ_h).
- Mass-action law: np = nᵢ².

steps.title: Hall effect
steps.body:
Current I along x, field B along z. The Lorentz force pushes carriers to one side until the Hall field balances it.

- R_H = 1/(qn): negative for electrons, positive for holes
- **V_H = IB/(nqt)**, t = thickness along B
- Mobility μ = |R_H| σ

steps.title: Solved: Hall voltage in copper
steps.body:
I = 5 A, B = 1 T, t = 0.1 mm, n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.

- net = 8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁴ = 1.36 × 10⁶
- V_H = 5 × 1/1.36 × 10⁶ = **3.7 μV**

In a semiconductor with n ~ 10²¹ m⁻³ the same setup gives volts, which is why Hall sensors use semiconductors.

steps.title: Solved: carrier density from R_H
steps.body:
A sample has R_H = −6.25 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C.

- Negative: electrons are majority carriers (n-type)
- n = 1/(e|R_H|) = 1/(1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6.25 × 10⁻⁴) = **1.0 × 10²² m⁻³**

steps.title: Hall sensors
steps.body: Hall-effect sensors measure wheel speed in ABS brakes, detect lid closure in laptops and phones, and measure current without contact.

activity.prompt: A semiconductor strip 1 mm thick carries 10 mA in a 0.5 T field. Its carrier density is 1.0 × 10²¹ m⁻³. Find the Hall voltage V_H = IB/(net) in mV (two decimals).

quiz.q: A positive Hall coefficient indicates:
quiz.why: R_H = 1/(qn) is positive when the charge q of the majority carriers is positive, which means holes.

quiz.q: The mass-action law in a semiconductor is:
quiz.why: In thermal equilibrium the product of electron and hole densities equals nᵢ², whatever the doping.

quiz.q: Hall sensors use semiconductors rather than metals because:
options: low carrier density gives a large V_H
quiz.why: V_H = IB/(nqt) is inversely proportional to n, so the low n of semiconductors gives a much larger, measurable voltage.

questions.q: In the Drude model, resistivity ρ equals:
questions.why: Resistivity is the reciprocal of σ = ne²τ/m.

questions.q: Copper's Fermi energy is about:
questions.why: With n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3) ≈ 7 eV.

questions.q: The Fermi wave vector is k_F =
questions.why: Filling a sphere in k-space with 2 electrons per state gives k_F³ = 3π²n.

questions.q: At T > 0, the probability of occupation at E = E_F is:
questions.why: At E = E_F the exponential is 1, so f = 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2.

questions.q: Bloch functions have the form:
questions.why: Bloch's theorem says the wavefunction is a plane wave times a function with the lattice period.

questions.q: In the Kronig–Penney model as P → ∞, the bands become:
questions.why: Infinitely strong barriers isolate each well, so electrons occupy separate atomic-like levels.

questions.q: Which has the smallest band gap at 300 K?
questions.why: Ge has a gap of about 0.66 eV, smaller than Si (1.12 eV), GaAs (1.42 eV) and diamond (about 5.5 eV).

questions.q: Effective mass is defined as:
questions.why: m* = ħ²/(d²E/dk²) makes an electron in a band respond to forces like a free particle of that mass.

questions.q: Silicon doped with phosphorus is:
questions.why: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons and donates one extra electron, giving an n-type semiconductor.

questions.q: For R_H = −1.25 × 10⁻³ m³/C, the electron density is about:
Hall mobility is obtained from:
questions.why: Since σ = neμ and R_H = 1/(ne), multiplying |R_H| by σ gives μ.

questions.q: Electronic heat capacity of a free-electron metal varies with T as:
questions.why: Only a fraction T/T_F of electrons is excited, each gaining about k_BT, so C_el ∝ T.

questions.q: Doubling the electron density n changes E_F by a factor of:
questions.why: E_F ∝ n^(2/3), so doubling n multiplies E_F by 2^(2/3) ≈ 1.59.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Magnetic and dielectric properties
courses.summary: How solids respond to magnetic and electric fields: dia-, para- and ferromagnetism with the Langevin, Curie and Weiss theories, domains and hysteresis, then dielectric polarisation, local field, the Clausius–Mossotti relation and ferroelectrics.
outcomes: Classify materials by magnetic susceptibility and explain each type
Use Langevin theory and the Curie and Curie–Weiss laws
Explain domains, hysteresis and soft versus hard magnets
Relate polarisation, susceptibility and dielectric constant
Apply the Clausius–Mossotti relation and describe ferro- and piezoelectricity

scenes.text: In a famous experiment a live frog was levitated in a 16 T magnet. Water in its body is weakly diamagnetic.
Back in the lab, Riya sees liquid oxygen cling to a magnet's poles instead. That is paramagnetism.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Magnetisation M = χH, B = μ₀(H + M) = μ₀(1 + χ)H.
- **Diamagnetic**: χ small and negative (about −10⁻⁵), temperature independent. Present in all materials (Cu, Bi, water).
- **Paramagnetic**: χ small and positive (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³), decreases with T (Al, O₂, CuSO₄).
- **Ferromagnetic**: χ large and positive, spontaneous magnetisation below T_C (Fe, Co, Ni).

steps.title: Langevin theory of paramagnetism
steps.body:
Permanent moments μ in a field B at temperature T align partially. Mean moment = μL(x), x = μB/k_BT, L(x) = coth x − 1/x.

For small x, L(x) ≈ x/3, giving

**χ = μ₀nμ²/(3k_BT) = C/T** (Curie law).

steps.title: Origin of diamagnetism
steps.body: An applied field changes the orbital motion of electrons (Lenz's law), inducing a moment opposite to B. Langevin's result: χ = −μ₀nZe²⟨r²⟩/(6m).

steps.title: Common slip
steps.body: The Curie law applies only when μB ≪ k_BT. In very strong fields at low T, magnetisation saturates at nμ.

activity.prompt: A paramagnetic salt obeys the Curie law with χ = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ at 300 K. Find χ at 200 K, in units of 10⁻⁴.

quiz.q: Diamagnetic susceptibility is:
quiz.why: Induced orbital moments oppose the field, giving a small negative χ of about −10⁻⁵.

quiz.q: The Curie law states that:
quiz.why: Thermal agitation disorders the moments, so χ = C/T falls as temperature rises.

quiz.q: Diamagnetism is present in:
quiz.why: Every electron orbit responds to an applied field by Lenz's law, so all materials have a diamagnetic contribution.

scenes.text: At a substation near Nagpur, an engineer explains why transformer cores use thin silicon-steel sheets.
Each cycle of AC drags the iron round its hysteresis loop. A thin loop wastes less energy as heat.

steps.title: Weiss molecular field
steps.body:
Weiss assumed each moment feels an internal field B_m = λM, proportional to magnetisation. This produces spontaneous magnetisation below the **Curie temperature T_C**. Above T_C:

**χ = C/(T − T_C)** (Curie–Weiss law).

T_C: Fe ≈ 1043 K, Ni ≈ 627 K, Co ≈ 1388 K. Heisenberg later showed λ comes from quantum exchange interaction.

steps.title: Domains
steps.body: An unmagnetised piece of iron contains many **domains**, each fully magnetised but pointing in different directions. Domains reduce magnetostatic energy. Domain walls (Bloch walls) separate them. Applying H first moves walls, then rotates domains.

steps.title: Hysteresis loop
steps.body:
- **Retentivity (remanence) B_r**: B left at H = 0.
- **Coercivity H_c**: reverse H needed to bring B to 0.
- Energy lost per cycle per unit volume = area of the B–H loop.
- **Soft magnets** (Si-steel, ferrites): thin loop, low H_c; used in transformers.
- **Hard magnets** (NdFeB, alnico): wide loop, high H_c; used in permanent magnets.

steps.title: Solved: hysteresis loss
steps.body:
A transformer core of volume 0.01 m³ has a loop area of 250 J/m³ and runs at 50 Hz.

- Loss per cycle = 250 × 0.01 = 2.5 J
- Power loss = 2.5 × 50 = **125 W**

steps.title: Other ordered magnets
steps.body: Antiferromagnets (MnO) have opposed equal moments and lose order above the Néel temperature. Ferrimagnets (magnetite, ferrites) have opposed unequal moments and a net magnetisation.

activity.prompt: An iron core has volume 2 × 10⁻³ m³ and B–H loop area 400 J/m³. Find the hysteresis power loss at 50 Hz, in W.

quiz.q: Above the Curie temperature, a ferromagnet becomes:
quiz.why: Thermal energy destroys spontaneous order above T_C, and χ then follows the Curie–Weiss law of a paramagnet.

quiz.q: Transformer cores should have:
options: low coercivity and a thin loop
quiz.why: Loss per cycle equals loop area, so soft materials with a thin loop and low H_c waste least energy.

quiz.q: The physical origin of Weiss's molecular field is:
quiz.why: Heisenberg showed the strong alignment comes from quantum exchange between electron spins, much stronger than dipole forces.

story.title: The capacitor in a phone charger

scenes.text: Aditya opens a dead phone charger and finds tiny ceramic capacitors marked in microfarads.
A ceramic with a huge dielectric constant lets a small chip store a lot of charge. Polarisation is the reason.

steps.title: Key relations
steps.body:
- Polarisation P = dipole moment per unit volume.
- D = ε₀E + P = ε₀ε_rE.
- P = ε₀χ_eE with χ_e = ε_r − 1.
- A capacitor filled with a dielectric has C = ε_rC₀.

steps.title: Mechanisms of polarisation
steps.body:
- **Electronic**: electron cloud shifts relative to nucleus; present in all materials; fast (up to optical frequencies).
- **Ionic**: ions shift in ionic crystals; up to infrared frequencies.
- **Orientational**: permanent dipoles align (water); temperature dependent, ∝ 1/T; drops out at microwave frequencies.
- **Space-charge**: charges pile up at interfaces; lowest frequencies.

steps.title: Solved: polarisation
steps.body:
A dielectric with ε_r = 4 is in a field E = 1.0 × 10⁵ V/m.

- P = ε₀(ε_r − 1)E = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 3 × 10⁵
- P = **2.66 × 10⁻⁶ C/m²**

steps.title: Frequency rule
steps.body: As frequency rises, mechanisms drop out one by one: space-charge, then orientational, then ionic. At optical frequencies only electronic polarisation remains, so ε_r = n², the refractive index squared.

steps.title: Dielectric breakdown
steps.body: Every dielectric fails above a maximum field (dielectric strength). Air breaks down at about 3 MV/m, which is why high-voltage lines need large spacing.

activity.prompt: A dielectric with ε_r = 5 sits in a field of 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m. Find P = ε₀(ε_r − 1)E in units of 10⁻⁷ C/m² (two decimals).

quiz.q: Electric susceptibility χ_e is related to ε_r by:
quiz.why: From D = ε₀E + P = ε₀ε_rE and P = ε₀χ_eE, it follows that χ_e = ε_r − 1.

quiz.q: Which polarisation depends strongly on temperature?
quiz.why: Permanent dipoles are disordered by thermal motion, so orientational polarisation falls as 1/T.

quiz.q: At optical frequencies, ε_r of a non-magnetic material equals:
quiz.why: Only electronic polarisation follows optical fields, and Maxwell's relation gives ε_r = n².

scenes.text: Click a kitchen gas lighter and a spark jumps with no battery inside.
A tiny crystal is squeezed and produces thousands of volts. That is piezoelectricity, a cousin of ferroelectricity.

steps.title: Local (Lorentz) field
steps.body:
An atom inside a dielectric feels the applied field plus the field of all other dipoles. For cubic symmetry:

E_loc = E + P/(3ε₀)

Each atom gets a dipole p = αE_loc, where α is polarisability.

steps.title: Clausius–Mossotti relation
steps.body:
Combining P = NαE_loc with the local field gives

**(ε_r − 1)/(ε_r + 2) = Nα/(3ε₀)**

It links the macroscopic ε_r to the microscopic α. Replacing ε_r with n² gives the Lorentz–Lorenz formula.

steps.title: Ferroelectrics and piezoelectrics
steps.body:
- **Ferroelectrics** (BaTiO₃, PZT) have spontaneous polarisation that can be reversed by a field; they show P–E hysteresis and a Curie temperature (BaTiO₃ ≈ 120 °C). Above T_C, ε_r follows a Curie–Weiss law.
- **Piezoelectrics** (quartz, PZT) produce charge when stressed and deform in a field. All ferroelectrics are piezoelectric, but not all piezoelectrics (e.g. quartz) are ferroelectric.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body: PZT transducers create ultrasound for medical scans; quartz crystals keep time in watches at 32,768 Hz; BaTiO₃ is the workhorse of multilayer ceramic capacitors.

activity.prompt: A cubic solid has ε_r = 7. Compute (ε_r − 1)/(ε_r + 2) from the Clausius–Mossotti relation (three decimals).

quiz.q: The Lorentz local field in a cubic dielectric is:
quiz.why: Summing the fields of surrounding dipoles in a cubic lattice adds P/(3ε₀) to the applied field.

quiz.q: Which material is piezoelectric but not ferroelectric?
quiz.why: Quartz lacks a centre of symmetry so it is piezoelectric, but it has no reversible spontaneous polarisation.

quiz.q: The Clausius–Mossotti relation connects ε_r with:
options: molecular polarisability α and number density N
quiz.why: (ε_r − 1)/(ε_r + 2) = Nα/(3ε₀) relates the bulk dielectric constant to atomic polarisability and density.

questions.q: Which is paramagnetic?
questions.why: Aluminium has a small positive susceptibility, while Bi, Cu and water are diamagnetic.

questions.q: In Langevin theory, for small x, L(x) ≈
questions.why: Expanding coth x − 1/x for small x gives x/3, which leads to the Curie law.

questions.q: A Curie-law salt has χ = 5 × 10⁻⁴ at 100 K. At 250 K, χ =
The Curie–Weiss law is:
questions.why: With the Weiss molecular field, the paramagnetic susceptibility above T_C becomes C/(T − T_C).

questions.q: Energy lost per hysteresis cycle per unit volume equals:
options: the area of the B–H loop
questions.why: Work done per cycle on unit volume is ∮H dB, which is the area enclosed by the loop.

questions.q: Permanent magnets should have:
questions.why: A permanent magnet must keep its magnetisation and resist demagnetisation, so both B_r and H_c must be high.

questions.q: Ferrites are:
questions.why: Ferrites have antiparallel sublattices of unequal moments, giving a net moment: ferrimagnetism.

questions.q: A core of 5 × 10⁻³ m³ with loop area 300 J/m³ at 50 Hz loses:
questions.why: 300 × 5 × 10⁻³ = 1.5 J per cycle, times 50 cycles per second gives 75 W.

questions.q: For ε_r = 3 in a field of 10⁶ V/m, P is about:
Which polarisation survives at optical frequencies?
questions.why: Only light electrons can follow fields oscillating at about 10¹⁵ Hz.

questions.q: BaTiO₃ above its Curie temperature behaves as:
options: a paraelectric with ε_r following a Curie–Weiss law
questions.why: Above T_C the spontaneous polarisation vanishes, and ε_r falls as C/(T − T_C), like a paramagnet's χ.

questions.q: For n = 10²⁸ m⁻³ moments of 2 μ_B at 300 K, the Curie-law χ is about:
questions.why: χ ∝ μ², so doubling μ multiplies the 1 μ_B value of 8.7 × 10⁻⁵ by 4, giving about 3.5 × 10⁻⁴.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Superconductivity
courses.summary: Zero resistance and perfect diamagnetism: critical temperature and field, Meissner effect, type I and type II superconductors, London penetration depth, isotope effect, BCS theory, Josephson effects and applications from MRI to maglev.
outcomes: State the defining properties of superconductors and use H_c(T)
Explain the Meissner effect and distinguish type I and type II
Calculate the London penetration depth
Describe Cooper pairs, the BCS energy gap and the isotope effect
Use the Josephson frequency relation and list applications

scenes.text: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cools mercury with liquid helium. Near 4.2 K its resistance suddenly drops below anything he can measure.
Currents set up in superconducting rings have circulated for years without measurable decay.

steps.title: Basic facts
steps.body:
- Below a **critical temperature T_c** the DC resistance becomes zero.
- Examples: Hg 4.2 K, Pb 7.2 K, Nb 9.2 K, NbTi ≈ 9.5 K, YBa₂Cu₃O₇ ≈ 92 K.
- Good normal conductors (Cu, Ag, Au) do not superconduct at ordinary pressure.

steps.title: Critical field
steps.body:
A magnetic field above H_c destroys superconductivity. Empirically

**H_c(T) = H_c(0)[1 − (T/T_c)²]**

A current large enough to create H_c at the surface also destroys it (Silsbee rule), which sets the critical current.

steps.title: Solved: temperature for a given field
steps.body:
Find T at which B_c = 0.040 T for the same Pb.

- 1 − (T/T_c)² = 0.5 → T/T_c = 0.707
- T = 0.707 × 7.2 = **5.1 K**

steps.title: Other changes at T_c
steps.body: Specific heat jumps at T_c and then falls exponentially below it, a sign of an energy gap. Entropy drops because electrons become more ordered.

activity.prompt: A superconductor has T_c = 4.0 K and B_c(0) = 0.040 T. Find B_c at 2.0 K, in T.

quiz.q: Superconductivity was discovered in mercury by:
quiz.why: Kamerlingh Onnes found mercury's resistance vanish near 4.2 K in 1911, after liquefying helium.

quiz.q: The empirical critical field law is:
quiz.why: Experiments fit H_c(T) = H_c(0)[1 − (T/T_c)²], which is zero at T_c.

quiz.q: Which does NOT superconduct at ordinary pressure?
quiz.why: Copper is an excellent normal conductor but has never been found to superconduct at ambient pressure.

lessons.title: Meissner effect, types I and II, London equations

scenes.text: At a science fair in IISc Bengaluru, a small magnet hovers above a black YBCO disc soaked in liquid nitrogen.
The disc expels the magnet's field. This is more than perfect conduction: it is the Meissner effect.

steps.title: Meissner effect (1933)
steps.body: When cooled below T_c in a field, a superconductor **expels** the magnetic field: B = 0 inside. So χ = −1, a perfect diamagnet. A merely perfect conductor would trap the field, not expel it, so superconductivity is a new thermodynamic state.

steps.title: Type I and type II
steps.body:
- **Type I** (Pb, Hg, Sn): complete expulsion up to H_c, then normal. Low H_c.
- **Type II** (Nb, NbTi, Nb₃Sn, YBCO): full expulsion below H_c1; between H_c1 and H_c2 a **mixed (vortex) state** lets in quantised flux tubes; normal above H_c2. H_c2 can exceed 10 T, so type II materials are used in magnets.

steps.title: London equations
steps.body:
London's second equation gives ∇²B = B/λ_L², so field decays inside as B(x) = B₀e^(−x/λ_L), with

**λ_L = √(m/(μ₀n_se²))**

Typical λ_L ≈ 50 nm.

steps.title: Flux quantum
steps.body: Each vortex carries one flux quantum Φ₀ = h/2e = 2.07 × 10⁻¹⁵ Wb. The 2e is evidence that carriers are pairs of electrons.

activity.prompt: If n_s is 4.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ (four times the solved example), find λ_L in nm. Remember λ_L ∝ 1/√n_s.

quiz.q: Inside a superconductor in the Meissner state, the susceptibility is:
quiz.why: B = μ₀(1 + χ)H = 0 inside, which requires χ = −1, a perfect diamagnet.

quiz.q: Superconducting magnets for MRI use:
options: type II materials such as NbTi
quiz.why: Type II superconductors stay superconducting up to very high H_c2, so they can carry large currents in strong fields.

quiz.q: The London penetration depth varies with superelectron density as:
quiz.why: λ_L = √(m/(μ₀n_se²)), so it is inversely proportional to the square root of n_s.

scenes.text: In 1950, two groups found that mercury made from heavier isotopes became superconducting at a slightly lower temperature.
The lattice was involved. Seven years later Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer explained how phonons glue electrons into pairs.

steps.title: Isotope effect
steps.body: T_c M^α = constant, with α ≈ ½ for many simple metals. So T_c ∝ M^(−1/2), like phonon frequencies (ω ∝ 1/√M). This points to electron–phonon interaction.

steps.title: Cooper pairs and BCS
steps.body:
- An electron distorts the lattice; a second electron is attracted to the distortion.
- Electrons of opposite momentum and spin form a **Cooper pair** (charge 2e, a boson-like object).
- Pairs condense into one coherent state with an **energy gap** 2Δ at the Fermi level.
- BCS result: **2Δ(0) = 3.52 k_BT_c**.
- Coherence length ξ is the size of a pair, about 100 nm–1 μm in classic metals.

steps.title: Limits of BCS
steps.body: BCS works well for conventional superconductors. Cuprate high-T_c superconductors (T_c up to about 133 K at ambient pressure) are not fully explained by simple phonon-mediated BCS theory.

activity.prompt: Aluminium has T_c = 1.2 K. Use 2Δ = 3.52 k_BT_c to find the gap in meV (three decimals).

quiz.q: The isotope effect shows T_c ∝
quiz.why: Heavier isotopes vibrate more slowly, and T_c falls as M^(−1/2), pointing to phonon involvement.

quiz.q: A Cooper pair has total charge:
quiz.why: A Cooper pair is two electrons bound together, so its charge is 2e.

quiz.q: BCS theory predicts 2Δ(0) equals about:
quiz.why: The weak-coupling BCS result is Δ(0) = 1.76 k_BT_c, so the full gap 2Δ is 3.52 k_BT_c.

scenes.text: The magnetic field of the human brain is about a billion times weaker than Earth's.
SQUID sensors built from Josephson junctions can still detect it. That is magnetoencephalography.

steps.title: Josephson junction
steps.body:
Two superconductors separated by a thin insulator (about 1–2 nm). Cooper pairs tunnel through.

- **DC Josephson effect**: a supercurrent I = I_c sin δ flows with zero voltage, δ being the phase difference.
- **AC Josephson effect**: a DC voltage V makes the current oscillate at **f = 2eV/h**, about 483.6 GHz per mV.

steps.title: Solved: Josephson frequency
steps.body:
V = 10 μV.

- f = 2eV/h = 2 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁵/6.626 × 10⁻³⁴
- f = **4.84 GHz**

This exact relation is used in voltage standards: frequency can be measured very precisely, so voltage can too.

steps.title: SQUIDs
steps.body: A ring with one or two Josephson junctions. Its current varies periodically with the flux through the ring, with period Φ₀ = h/2e. It can detect a small fraction of Φ₀, roughly 10⁻¹⁴ T in practice.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
- MRI scanners: NbTi coils at 4.2 K giving 1.5–3 T.
- Particle accelerators: LHC magnets of 8.3 T.
- Maglev trains (Japan's SCMaglev uses superconducting magnets).
- Fault-current limiters and power cables.
- Superconducting qubits in quantum computers.

quiz.q: SQUIDs are mainly used to measure:
quiz.why: Their response repeats every flux quantum, which makes them the most sensitive magnetometers available.

questions.why: The defining property is zero DC resistance below the critical temperature.

Which is a type II superconductor?

questions.q: Between H_c1 and H_c2, a type II superconductor is in:
questions.why: Flux penetrates as quantised vortices while the rest of the material stays superconducting.

questions.q: London penetration depth is of order:
questions.why: For n_s ≈ 10²⁸ m⁻³, λ_L = √(m/μ₀n_se²) ≈ 50 nm.

For T_c = 10 K, the BCS gap 2Δ is about:
