uni-bsc-phy-stat-mech.title: B.Sc Physics · Statistical Mechanics
uni-bsc-phy-stat-mech.description: Microstates and entropy, phase space and ensembles, Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics and the partition function, the classical ideal gas, and Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac statistics with blackbody radiation, Bose–Einstein condensation and the electron gas, with solved numericals and unit exams. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Physics (Hons) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Microstates, entropy, phase space and ensembles
courses.summary: The basic ideas of statistical physics: macrostates and microstates, thermodynamic probability, the postulate of equal a priori probability, Boltzmann's entropy S = k ln W, Stirling's approximation, phase space and its quantisation, ensembles, and counting for distinguishable particles, bosons and fermions.
outcomes: Count microstates for coins, spins and particles in cells
Relate entropy to thermodynamic probability and use Stirling's approximation
Describe phase space, phase cells of size h and the number of accessible states
Distinguish microcanonical, canonical and grand canonical ensembles
Count arrangements under MB, BE and FD rules

story.title: The coin toss in the canteen

scenes.text: Four friends toss coins to decide who pays for chai. Arjun notes that two heads and two tails turns up far more often than four heads.
There are six ways to get two heads but only one way to get four. Statistical mechanics is built on this counting.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Microstate**: a complete specification of every particle (e.g. HTHT).
- **Macrostate**: what we measure (e.g. 2 heads), regardless of which coins.
- **Thermodynamic probability W**: number of microstates in a macrostate.
- For N two-state objects with n in one state: W = N!/[n!(N − n)!].

steps.title: Solved: four coins
steps.body:
Total microstates = 2⁴ = 16. Macrostates (heads): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with W = 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

- P(2 heads) = 6/16 = **0.375**
- P(4 heads) = 1/16 = 0.0625

steps.title: Postulate of equal a priori probability
steps.body: An isolated system in equilibrium is equally likely to be in any of its accessible microstates. So the observed macrostate is the one with the largest W.

steps.title: Solved: sharpening of the peak
steps.body:
10 coins, 5 heads: W = 252, P = 252/1024 = 0.246.

For N = 10²³ coins, the relative width of the distribution is about 1/√N ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹². The most probable macrostate is essentially certain: this is why thermodynamics works.

steps.title: Checking your counts
steps.body: The W values of all macrostates must add up to the total number of microstates (2ᴺ for coins).

activity.prompt: Six coins are tossed. Find the probability of exactly 3 heads (three decimals).

quiz.q: For 4 coins, the macrostate with the most microstates is:
quiz.why: W = 4!/(2!2!) = 6 is the largest of 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

quiz.q: The postulate of equal a priori probability says that in equilibrium:
options: all accessible microstates are equally likely
quiz.why: Each accessible microstate of an isolated system is assumed equally probable; macrostates differ only in how many microstates they contain.

quiz.q: The relative fluctuation about the most probable state varies as:
quiz.why: The binomial standard deviation is √N/2, so relative to N it shrinks as 1/√N.

scenes.text: Ludwig Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna carries one short equation: S = k log W.
It links the heat-engine entropy of Carnot and Clausius to the counting of microstates.

steps.title: Boltzmann entropy
steps.body:
**S = k_B ln W**, k_B = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

- For two independent systems W = W₁W₂, so S = S₁ + S₂: entropy is additive because of the logarithm.
- Maximising W is the same as maximising S, giving the second law.

steps.title: Solved: spin entropy
steps.body:
N = 100 spins, each up or down with no field: W = 2¹⁰⁰.

- S = 100 k ln 2 = 100 × 1.381 × 10⁻²³ × 0.693
- S = **9.57 × 10⁻²² J/K**

For one mole: S = R ln 2 = 5.76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

steps.title: Stirling's approximation
steps.body:
For large N: **ln N! ≈ N ln N − N**.

Example: ln(100!) = 363.74 exactly; Stirling gives 100 ln 100 − 100 = 360.5, an error under 1% that vanishes for N ~ 10²³.

steps.title: Temperature from entropy
steps.body: 1/T = (∂S/∂E)_V,N. Two systems in thermal contact share energy until their ∂S/∂E are equal, which defines equal temperature. This is the statistical basis of the zeroth law.

steps.title: Third law
steps.body: At T = 0 a system in a unique ground state has W = 1, so S = 0. Glasses and some crystals with frozen disorder keep a residual entropy.

activity.prompt: A system has W = 10⁶ microstates. Find S = k_B ln W in units of 10⁻²² J/K (two decimals; ln 10⁶ = 13.816).

quiz.q: Entropy is additive because:
options: W multiplies and the logarithm turns products into sums
quiz.why: Independent systems have W = W₁W₂, and ln(W₁W₂) = ln W₁ + ln W₂.

quiz.q: Stirling's approximation is:
options: ln N! ≈ N ln N − N
quiz.why: For large N, the sum of ln k from 1 to N is well approximated by the integral, giving N ln N − N.

quiz.q: Statistically, temperature is defined by:
quiz.why: Equilibrium between systems maximises total entropy when ∂S/∂E is equal, and that common value is 1/T.

scenes.text: Plot a pendulum's position against its momentum and you get a closed ellipse, not a line.
Quantum mechanics divides this plane into cells of area h. Counting cells counts states.

steps.title: Phase space
steps.body: For N particles in 3D, phase space has 6N dimensions (3 position + 3 momentum each). One point = one microstate (classically). As the system evolves, the point traces a trajectory. **Liouville's theorem**: the density of points in phase space is conserved along the flow.

steps.title: Quantised cells
steps.body: Uncertainty Δx Δp ≳ h implies that each state occupies a cell of volume **h** per degree of freedom (h³ per particle in 3D). Number of states = phase volume/h^f.

steps.title: Solved: 1D harmonic oscillator
steps.body:
E = p²/2m + ½mω²x². The curve E = const is an ellipse with semi-axes √(2mE) and √(2E/mω²).

- Area = π × √(2mE) × √(2E/mω²) = 2πE/ω
- States with energy below E: (2πE/ω)/h = **E/ħω**

This matches the quantum level spacing ħω.

steps.title: Solved: free particle in a box
steps.body:
Number of states with momentum below p in volume V:

N(p) = V(4/3)πp³/h³

Differentiating gives the density of states g(E) dE = (2πV/h³)(2m)^(3/2) √E dE, which we use throughout this course.

steps.title: Units check
steps.body: Phase area (m × kg m/s) has units of J s, the same as h. Dividing by h gives a pure number of states.

activity.prompt: For a 1D harmonic oscillator, how many quantum states have energy less than E = 10ħω, using states = E/ħω?

quiz.q: The phase space of N particles in three dimensions has dimension:
quiz.why: Each particle needs three position and three momentum coordinates, giving 6N.

quiz.q: Each quantum state occupies a phase-space volume per degree of freedom of:
quiz.why: The uncertainty principle implies one state per cell of area h in each (x, p) plane.

quiz.q: Liouville's theorem states that:
options: phase-space density is conserved along trajectories
quiz.why: Hamiltonian flow is incompressible in phase space, so the density of representative points stays constant along the motion.

lessons.title: Ensembles and counting rules for MB, BE and FD

scenes.text: Two guests must be placed in three hotel rooms. If they are twins nobody can tell apart, the number of distinct arrangements changes.
If the rule is one guest per room, it changes again. These three rules are MB, BE and FD statistics.

steps.title: Ensembles
steps.body:
An ensemble is a large collection of imaginary copies of a system, each in a possible microstate.

- **Microcanonical**: fixed N, V, E (isolated).
- **Canonical**: fixed N, V, T (in contact with a heat bath).
- **Grand canonical**: fixed μ, V, T (exchanges energy and particles).

Ergodic hypothesis: time averages equal ensemble averages.

steps.title: Three counting rules
steps.body:
- **Maxwell–Boltzmann (MB)**: particles distinguishable, any number per state.
- **Bose–Einstein (BE)**: indistinguishable, any number per state (integer spin: photons, ⁴He).
- **Fermi–Dirac (FD)**: indistinguishable, at most one per state (half-integer spin: electrons, protons).

steps.title: Solved: 2 particles in 3 states
steps.body:
- MB: each particle has 3 choices → 3² = **9**
- BE: combinations with repetition C(3 + 2 − 1, 2) = **6**
- FD: choose 2 different states C(3, 2) = **3**

steps.title: General formulas
steps.body:
For n_i particles in a level with g_i states:

- MB: W = N! Π g_i^(n_i)/n_i!
- BE: W = Π (n_i + g_i − 1)!/[n_i!(g_i − 1)!]
- FD: W = Π g_i!/[n_i!(g_i − n_i)!]

When g_i ≫ n_i all three give the same result (after dividing MB by N!): the classical limit.

steps.title: Spin–statistics
steps.body: Relativistic quantum field theory links spin to statistics: integer spin → bosons, half-integer → fermions. Satyendra Nath Bose's 1924 paper from Dhaka, translated by Einstein, founded BE statistics.

activity.prompt: Two indistinguishable bosons are placed in 4 single-particle states. How many distinct arrangements are there? (Use C(g + n − 1, n).)

quiz.q: An ensemble with fixed N, V and T is:
quiz.why: A canonical ensemble describes systems in contact with a heat bath at temperature T, with N and V fixed.

quiz.q: Electrons obey:
quiz.why: Electrons have spin ½, so they are fermions and obey the Pauli exclusion principle.

quiz.q: Two fermions in three states can be arranged in how many ways?
quiz.why: Fermions cannot share a state, so we choose 2 of 3 states: C(3, 2) = 3.

questions.q: The total number of microstates for 5 coins is:
questions.why: Each coin has two outcomes, so 2⁵ = 32.

questions.q: For 8 coins, W for 4 heads is:
Boltzmann's entropy formula is:
questions.why: Boltzmann related entropy to the logarithm of the number of microstates.

questions.q: The molar entropy of a paramagnet with two equally likely spin states is:
questions.why: W = 2^(N_A) gives S = N_A k ln 2 = R ln 2 ≈ 5.76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.q: Using Stirling, ln(1000!) is about:
Phase space of a single particle moving in 1D is:
questions.why: One position and one momentum coordinate give a two-dimensional phase plane.

questions.q: The phase-space area enclosed by a 1D oscillator orbit of energy E is:
questions.why: The ellipse has semi-axes √(2mE) and √(2E/mω²), so area = π × their product = 2πE/ω.

questions.q: An isolated system with fixed E is described by the:
questions.why: The microcanonical ensemble has fixed energy, volume and particle number.

questions.q: Two distinguishable particles in 4 states (MB) can be arranged in:
questions.why: Each particle independently picks one of 4 states: 4² = 16.

questions.q: Three fermions in 5 states can be arranged in:
questions.why: Choose 3 different states out of 5: C(5, 3) = 10.

questions.q: The classical limit of quantum statistics applies when:
questions.why: When states greatly outnumber particles, multiple occupancy is rare and indistinguishability effects vanish.

questions.q: If W of a system doubles, its entropy increases by:
questions.why: ΔS = k ln(2W) − k ln W = k ln 2.

questions.q: Three bosons in 3 states can be arranged in:

courses.title: Unit 2 · Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics and the partition function
courses.summary: Deriving the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution with Lagrange multipliers, the Boltzmann factor, the partition function and how all thermodynamic quantities follow from it, the two-level system and paramagnetism, and the equipartition theorem with its successes and failures.
outcomes: Derive n_i = g_i e^(−α − βE_i) and identify β = 1/k_BT
Use the Boltzmann factor to compare level populations
Compute Z and obtain U, F, S and C_V from it
Analyse a two-level system and a spin-½ paramagnet
Apply equipartition to gases and solids and explain where it fails

scenes.text: Trekkers on the way to Kedarnath feel breathless: air at 3,500 m is noticeably thinner.
Molecules with higher gravitational energy are exponentially rarer. That exponential is the Boltzmann factor.

steps.title: The derivation in outline
steps.body:
Maximise ln W for distinguishable particles subject to fixed N = Σn_i and E = Σn_iE_i. With Lagrange multipliers α and β and Stirling's formula:

**n_i = g_i e^(−α) e^(−βE_i)**

Comparing with thermodynamics gives β = 1/k_BT.

steps.title: Boltzmann factor
steps.body:
The relative population of two levels:

n₂/n₁ = (g₂/g₁) exp[−(E₂ − E₁)/k_BT]

At 300 K, k_BT = 0.0259 eV ≈ 1/40 eV. Levels many k_BT above the ground state are almost empty.

steps.title: Solved: population ratio
steps.body:
Two non-degenerate levels 0.10 eV apart at 300 K.

- ΔE/k_BT = 0.10/0.02585 = 3.87
- n₂/n₁ = e^(−3.87) = **0.021**

steps.title: Solved: barometric formula
steps.body:
For air (m ≈ 29 u) at 290 K, n(h) = n₀ exp(−mgh/k_BT).

- Scale height H = k_BT/mg = (1.381 × 10⁻²³ × 290)/(4.82 × 10⁻²⁶ × 9.8) ≈ **8.5 km**
- At 3.5 km: n/n₀ = e^(−0.41) ≈ 0.66, about two-thirds of sea-level density

steps.title: Degeneracy matters
steps.body: Always include g_i. Hydrogen's n = 2 level has g = 8 (with spin) compared with g = 2 for n = 1; ignoring this gives the wrong ratio by a factor of 4.

activity.prompt: Two non-degenerate levels are 0.050 eV apart. Find n₂/n₁ at 300 K (k_BT = 0.02585 eV), to three decimals.

quiz.q: The Lagrange multiplier β in the MB derivation equals:
quiz.why: Matching the statistical entropy to thermodynamics shows β = 1/k_BT.

quiz.q: At room temperature k_BT is about:
Raising the temperature makes n₂/n₁ for E₂ > E₁:
quiz.why: As T → ∞, the exponential tends to 1, so the ratio tends to the ratio of degeneracies.

story.title: One function to rule them all

scenes.text: Priya's teacher says: find Z and you have the whole thermodynamics of the system.
Energy, free energy, entropy, pressure and heat capacity all come from derivatives of ln Z.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
Single-particle partition function:

**Z = Σ g_i e^(−E_i/k_BT)**

Probability of level i: P_i = g_i e^(−E_i/k_BT)/Z. Z counts the number of thermally accessible states.

steps.title: Thermodynamics from Z
steps.body:
For N distinguishable particles (Z_N = Zᴺ):

- U = Nk_BT² (∂ ln Z/∂T)
- F = −Nk_BT ln Z
- S = (U − F)/T
- P = Nk_BT (∂ ln Z/∂V)_T
- C_V = (∂U/∂T)_V

For indistinguishable gas particles, Z_N = Zᴺ/N!.

steps.title: Solved: harmonic oscillator
steps.body:
E_n = (n + ½)ħω.

- Z = e^(−x/2)/(1 − e^(−x)), x = ħω/k_BT
- U per oscillator = ħω/2 + ħω/(eˣ − 1)
- High T: U → k_BT; low T: U → ħω/2 (zero-point energy)

This is Einstein's model of solids from the Solid State course.

steps.title: Factorisation
steps.body: If E = E_trans + E_rot + E_vib, then Z = Z_trans Z_rot Z_vib, and ln Z is a sum. Each contribution can be treated separately.

activity.prompt: A system has non-degenerate levels at 0, ε and 2ε with ε = k_BT. Find Z = 1 + e⁻¹ + e⁻² to two decimals.

quiz.q: The Helmholtz free energy is related to Z by:
quiz.why: Combining U and S from Z gives F = U − TS = −Nk_BT ln Z.

quiz.q: At very low temperature, Z tends to:
options: the degeneracy of the ground state (with E₀ = 0)
quiz.why: All Boltzmann factors except the ground level vanish, leaving Z = g₀.

quiz.q: For a gas of identical particles, Z_N is:
quiz.why: Dividing by N! corrects for overcounting permutations of indistinguishable particles.

story.title: A bump in the heat capacity

scenes.text: Low-temperature physicists measuring a paramagnetic salt see a hump in its heat capacity near 1 K.
Schottky explained it: each ion has just two magnetic levels, and the hump appears when k_BT matches their gap.

steps.title: Two-level system
steps.body:
Levels 0 and ε.

- Z = 1 + e^(−ε/k_BT)
- Mean energy per particle: ⟨E⟩ = ε/(e^(ε/k_BT) + 1)
- At high T, both levels are nearly equally populated and ⟨E⟩ → ε/2 (never more).
- Heat capacity has a peak (**Schottky anomaly**) near k_BT ≈ 0.42ε.

steps.title: Spin-½ paramagnet
steps.body:
Moment μ in field B: energies ∓μB.

- Z = 2 cosh(μB/k_BT)
- Mean moment: ⟨μ⟩ = μ tanh(μB/k_BT)
- **M = Nμ tanh(μB/k_BT)**
- Weak field: M ≈ Nμ²B/k_BT, which is Curie's law

steps.title: Solved: degree of alignment
steps.body:
μ = 1 μ_B = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ J/T, B = 1 T, T = 1 K.

- x = μB/k_BT = 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴/1.381 × 10⁻²³ = 0.671
- tanh(0.671) = **0.586**, so M is 59% of saturation

At 300 K, x = 0.0022 and the alignment is only 0.22%.

steps.title: Negative temperature
steps.body: A two-level system can be prepared with more particles in the upper level. Then ∂S/∂E < 0, which formally means T < 0. Such states are 'hotter' than any positive temperature and are used in lasers (population inversion).

steps.title: Common slip
steps.body: Use tanh, not the Langevin function, for spin-½. Langevin's L(x) is for classical moments that can point in any direction.

activity.prompt: A spin-½ paramagnet has μB/k_BT = 1.0. Find M/(Nμ) = tanh(1.0) to three decimals.

quiz.q: The maximum mean energy of a two-level system (positive T) is:
quiz.why: As T → ∞ both levels are equally populated, giving ⟨E⟩ = ε/2.

quiz.q: The magnetisation of a spin-½ paramagnet is:
quiz.why: Averaging +μ and −μ with Boltzmann weights e^(±x) gives μ tanh x.

quiz.q: The Schottky anomaly is:
options: a peak in C_V of a system with a finite number of levels
quiz.why: With a bounded energy spectrum, C_V rises and then falls, producing a peak near k_BT ~ ε.

scenes.text: Hydrogen gas at room temperature has C_V ≈ (5/2)R, but cooled below about 80 K it drops to (3/2)R.
Rotations 'freeze out'. Classical equipartition cannot explain that, but quantum levels can.

steps.title: The theorem
steps.body: In classical equilibrium, every term in the energy that is **quadratic** in a coordinate or momentum contributes **½k_BT** to the mean energy (and ½k_B to C_V per particle).

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
| System | Quadratic terms | C_V (per mole) |
|---|---|---|
| Monatomic gas | 3 (translation) | 3R/2 |
| Diatomic, rigid | 3 + 2 (rotation) | 5R/2 |
| Diatomic, vibrating | 3 + 2 + 2 | 7R/2 |
| Solid (3D oscillators) | 6 | 3R (Dulong–Petit) |

steps.title: Solved: energy of a gas
steps.body:
1 mol of helium at 300 K:

- U = (3/2)RT = 1.5 × 8.314 × 300 = **3741 J**
- Mean KE per atom = (3/2)k_BT = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J = 0.039 eV

steps.title: Freezing out
steps.body:
Equipartition holds only when k_BT ≫ level spacing.

- Rotations of H₂: characteristic temperature ≈ 85 K
- Vibrations of N₂: ≈ 3400 K, frozen at room temperature

So N₂ at 300 K has C_V ≈ 5R/2, not 7R/2.

steps.title: Ultraviolet catastrophe
steps.body: Applying equipartition to the infinite number of electromagnetic modes in a cavity predicts infinite energy. Planck's quantisation (Unit 4) solved this.

activity.prompt: Using equipartition, find the internal energy of 2 mol of a rigid diatomic gas at 300 K (U = (5/2)nRT, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), in J (nearest 10 J).

quiz.q: Each quadratic term in the energy contributes on average:
quiz.why: Integrating a Gaussian Boltzmann weight over a quadratic term gives a mean of ½k_BT.

quiz.q: At room temperature, C_V of N₂ is about:
quiz.why: Translation and rotation are active, but vibration (θ ≈ 3400 K) is frozen, giving 5R/2.

quiz.q: Equipartition fails at low temperature because:
quiz.why: When k_BT is smaller than the level spacing, the degree of freedom cannot be excited and contributes nothing.

questions.q: The Boltzmann factor is:
questions.why: The probability of a state of energy E is proportional to e^(−E/k_BT).

questions.q: Two levels with g₁ = 1, g₂ = 3 are 0.0259 eV apart at 300 K. n₂/n₁ is about:
Internal energy from the partition function is:
questions.why: Differentiating ln Z with respect to β = 1/k_BT gives the mean energy, equivalent to k_BT² ∂ln Z/∂T.

questions.q: Z for a two-level system (0 and ε) at very high T approaches:
questions.why: Both Boltzmann factors approach 1, so Z → 2.

questions.q: The high-temperature mean energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator is:
questions.why: For k_BT ≫ ħω, U ≈ k_BT, matching equipartition for two quadratic terms.

questions.q: For a spin-½ paramagnet in a weak field, M is proportional to:
questions.why: tanh x ≈ x for small x, so M ≈ Nμ²B/k_BT: Curie's law.

questions.q: Scale height of an isothermal atmosphere is:
questions.why: n ∝ exp(−mgh/k_BT), so density falls by 1/e over a height k_BT/mg.

questions.q: C_V for one mole of a rigid diatomic ideal gas is:
questions.why: Three translational and two rotational quadratic terms give (5/2)R.

questions.q: The Dulong–Petit law follows from equipartition because each atom in a solid has:
questions.why: Each of 3 oscillation directions has kinetic and potential quadratic terms, giving 3k_BT per atom and 3R per mole.

questions.q: Population inversion in a two-level system corresponds formally to:
questions.why: With more particles in the upper level, ∂S/∂E < 0, so 1/T < 0.

questions.q: For levels 0, ε, 2ε with ε = k_BT, the probability of the ground state is about:
The two-level mean energy at k_BT = ε is:

courses.title: Unit 3 · The classical ideal gas
courses.summary: The Maxwell speed distribution and its characteristic speeds, the ideal gas from the translational partition function and the thermal de Broglie wavelength, the Gibbs paradox and the Sackur–Tetrode entropy, and the criterion that decides when classical statistics fails.
outcomes: Use the Maxwell speed distribution and compute v_p, v̄ and v_rms
Derive PV = Nk_BT and U = (3/2)Nk_BT from Z = V/λ³
Explain the Gibbs paradox and its resolution by N!
Calculate entropy of an ideal gas with the Sackur–Tetrode equation and entropy of mixing
Use nλ³ to decide whether a gas is classical or degenerate

story.title: Why the Moon has no air

scenes.text: Chandrayaan images show a Moon with no atmosphere. Its escape speed is only 2.4 km/s.
A small fraction of gas molecules in the tail of the Maxwell distribution are fast enough to escape, and over billions of years the gas leaks away.

steps.title: The distribution
steps.body:
Fraction of molecules with speed between v and v + dv:

f(v) dv = 4π (m/2πk_BT)^(3/2) v² exp(−mv²/2k_BT) dv

The v² factor comes from the volume of a spherical shell in velocity space; the exponential is the Boltzmann factor.

steps.title: Characteristic speeds
steps.body:
- Most probable: **v_p = √(2k_BT/m)**
- Mean: **v̄ = √(8k_BT/πm)**
- Root-mean-square: **v_rms = √(3k_BT/m)**

Ratio v_p : v̄ : v_rms = 1 : 1.128 : 1.225.

steps.title: Experimental test
steps.body: Molecular-beam experiments with rotating slotted discs (Stern; Miller and Kusch, 1955) confirmed the distribution. Effusing beams carry an extra factor of v, because faster molecules hit the hole more often.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.body: All speeds scale as √(T/m). Hydrogen (2 u) moves 4 times faster than oxygen (32 u) at the same temperature.

activity.prompt: Find v_rms = √(3k_BT/m) for oxygen (m = 32 u = 5.314 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) at 300 K, in m/s (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: The order of characteristic speeds is:
If the temperature is quadrupled, v_rms:
quiz.why: v_rms ∝ √T, so 4 times T gives 2 times v_rms.

quiz.q: The v² factor in the Maxwell distribution arises from:
options: the volume of a spherical shell in velocity space
quiz.why: Velocity vectors with speed between v and v + dv fill a shell of volume 4πv² dv.

lessons.title: Ideal gas from the partition function

scenes.text: School taught PV = nRT as an experimental law found by Boyle, Charles and Avogadro.
Statistical mechanics derives it in three lines from a single partition function.

steps.title: Translational partition function
steps.body:
Integrating e^(−p²/2mk_BT) over phase space and dividing by h³:

**Z = V/λ³**, with the thermal de Broglie wavelength

**λ = h/√(2πmk_BT)**

Z counts how many 'boxes' of size λ³ fit into the volume V.

steps.title: Results
steps.body:
With Z_N = Zᴺ/N!:

- F = −Nk_BT[ln(V/Nλ³) + 1]
- P = −(∂F/∂V)_T = **Nk_BT/V**, the ideal gas law
- U = (3/2)Nk_BT, C_V = (3/2)Nk_B
- μ = k_BT ln(nλ³)

steps.title: Scaling
steps.body: λ ∝ 1/√(mT). Lighter particles and lower temperatures give longer wavelengths and more quantum behaviour.

steps.title: Don't forget N!
steps.body: Without the 1/N! the free energy is not extensive: doubling the system does not double F. This is the Gibbs paradox (next lesson).

activity.prompt: Helium has λ ≈ 0.50 Å at 300 K. Using λ ∝ 1/√T, find λ at 3 K, in Å.

quiz.q: The thermal de Broglie wavelength is:
quiz.why: Gaussian integration over momentum in Z gives λ = h/√(2πmk_BT).

quiz.q: From F = −Nk_BT ln(V…) + …, the pressure is:
quiz.why: P = −∂F/∂V = Nk_BT/V because only the ln V term depends on volume.

quiz.q: Halving the mass of the gas particles at fixed T makes λ:
quiz.why: λ ∝ 1/√m, so halving m multiplies λ by √2.

lessons.title: Gibbs paradox and the Sackur–Tetrode equation

scenes.text: A box has argon on both sides of a partition, same pressure and temperature. Remove the partition: nothing changes.
Yet the classical formula said entropy went up. Gibbs saw that identical particles must not be counted as different.

steps.title: The paradox
steps.body:
Without 1/N!, S = Nk_B[ln(V/λ³) + 3/2]. Joining two identical halves (N, V each) gives

ΔS = 2Nk_B ln 2 > 0,

even though the state is unchanged. Gibbs' fix: divide by N! because permuting identical particles gives the same microstate.

steps.title: Sackur–Tetrode equation
steps.body:
With the N! correction:

**S = Nk_B [ln(V/Nλ³) + 5/2]**

Now S is extensive and joining identical gases gives ΔS = 0.

steps.title: Solved: entropy of helium
steps.body:
300 K, 1 atm: V/N = k_BT/P = 4.09 × 10⁻²⁶ m³; λ³ = (5.04 × 10⁻¹¹)³ = 1.28 × 10⁻³¹ m³.

- V/Nλ³ = 3.19 × 10⁵, ln = 12.67
- S/Nk_B = 12.67 + 2.5 = 15.17
- Molar S = 15.17 × 8.314 = **126 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**, matching calorimetric data

steps.title: Entropy of mixing
steps.body:
For two *different* gases, each expands into the full volume:

**ΔS_mix = −Nk_B Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ**

For 1 mol each of two gases: ΔS = 2R ln 2 = **11.5 J/K**. The jump from 11.5 J/K to 0 when the gases become identical has no smooth limit, showing identity is a quantum concept.

steps.title: Planck's constant from thermodynamics
steps.body: Sackur and Tetrode (1912) noticed that measured absolute entropies require the cell size to be exactly h. This was an early independent check of quantum theory.

activity.prompt: 1 mol of N₂ and 1 mol of O₂ at the same T and P are allowed to mix. Find ΔS_mix = 2R ln 2 in J/K (two decimals).

quiz.q: The Gibbs paradox is resolved by:
options: dividing the partition function by N!
quiz.why: Treating identical particles as indistinguishable removes the overcount of N! permutations.

quiz.q: Mixing two samples of the same gas at the same T and P gives ΔS:
quiz.why: With the N! correction the final state is identical to the initial one, so entropy does not change.

quiz.q: The Sackur–Tetrode equation contains Planck's constant through:
quiz.why: λ = h/√(2πmk_BT) appears in V/Nλ³, so absolute entropy depends on h.

story.title: Electrons are not a classical gas

scenes.text: Treat the conduction electrons in copper as an ideal gas, and you predict a large heat capacity. Experiment says otherwise.
Compare the electrons' thermal wavelength with their spacing: it is far larger. They overlap, and quantum statistics takes over.

steps.title: Degeneracy parameter
steps.body:
Compare λ with the mean interparticle spacing n^(−1/3).

- **nλ³ ≪ 1**: wave packets do not overlap; MB statistics is accurate (non-degenerate).
- **nλ³ ≳ 1**: quantum effects dominate (degenerate); use BE or FD statistics.

Equivalently, the average occupancy per state ⟨n⟩ ≈ nλ³ must be small.

steps.title: Solved: helium gas at room conditions
Solved: electrons in copper
steps.body:
m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, T = 300 K: λ = h/√(2πmk_BT) = 4.3 × 10⁻⁹ m.

- λ³ = 7.97 × 10⁻²⁶ m³
- nλ³ = 8.5 × 10²⁸ × 7.97 × 10⁻²⁶ ≈ **6800**
- Highly degenerate: Fermi–Dirac statistics required (Unit 5).

steps.title: Where quantum statistics is essential
steps.body:
- Electrons in metals and white dwarfs (FD)
- Neutrons in neutron stars (FD)
- Photons in a cavity and phonons in solids (BE)
- Liquid ⁴He below 2.17 K and ultracold atomic gases (BE)

steps.title: Quick test
steps.body: Lower T, higher density or lighter particles all push nλ³ up. Electrons are about 7000 times lighter than helium atoms, which is why they turn quantum so easily.

activity.prompt: Find the number density of an ideal gas at 300 K and 101325 Pa, n = P/k_BT, in units of 10²⁵ m⁻³ (two decimals).

quiz.q: Classical MB statistics is valid when:
quiz.why: A small nλ³ means wave packets rarely overlap, so occupancy per state is low and quantum effects are negligible.

quiz.q: Electrons in metals are degenerate mainly because:
options: their small mass gives a large thermal wavelength, and their density is high
quiz.why: λ ∝ 1/√m is large for electrons, and with n ≈ 10²⁹ m⁻³, nλ³ is in the thousands.

quiz.q: Which system needs Bose–Einstein statistics?
quiz.why: Photons are bosons, and their number in a cavity is not small per mode at relevant frequencies.

questions.q: The most probable speed is:
questions.why: Setting df/dv = 0 for v² e^(−mv²/2k_BT) gives v_p = √(2k_BT/m).

questions.q: v_rms of hydrogen (2 u) compared with oxygen (32 u) at the same T is:
For N₂ at 300 K, v̄ is about:
questions.why: v̄ = √(8k_BT/πm) ≈ 476 m/s, between v_p (422) and v_rms (517).

questions.q: The translational partition function of one particle is:
questions.why: Integrating over positions gives V and over momenta gives (2πmk_BT)^(3/2)/h³ = 1/λ³.

questions.q: Mean translational KE per molecule is:
questions.why: Three quadratic momentum terms each give ½k_BT.

questions.q: Without the 1/N! factor, the entropy of an ideal gas is:
questions.why: S would contain N ln V instead of N ln(V/N), so doubling the system would not double S.

questions.q: The Sackur–Tetrode equation is:
questions.why: Using Z_N = Zᴺ/N! and S = (U − F)/T gives this extensive result.

questions.q: Mixing 1 mol of A with 3 mol of B (ideal gases) gives ΔS of about:
The thermal de Broglie wavelength varies with temperature as:
questions.why: λ = h/√(2πmk_BT) is inversely proportional to √T.

questions.q: For helium gas at 300 K and 1 atm, nλ³ is about:
questions.why: n = 2.45 × 10²⁵ m⁻³ and λ³ ≈ 1.28 × 10⁻³¹ m³ give about 3 × 10⁻⁶, deep in the classical regime.

questions.q: The chemical potential of a classical ideal gas is:
questions.why: μ = k_BT ln(nλ³), and since nλ³ ≪ 1 for a classical gas, μ is large and negative.

questions.q: An effusing molecular beam has a speed distribution proportional to:
questions.why: The flux through a hole carries an extra factor v, turning v² into v³.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Bose–Einstein statistics: photons and condensates
courses.summary: The Bose–Einstein distribution, the photon gas and Planck's radiation law derived from it, the Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien laws as consequences, and Bose–Einstein condensation in an ideal Bose gas with its link to superfluid helium and ultracold atoms.
outcomes: Derive and interpret the Bose–Einstein occupancy
Derive Planck's law from photon statistics with μ = 0
Obtain the Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien displacement laws and use them
Calculate the BEC transition temperature and the condensate fraction
Relate BEC to liquid helium-4 and to laser-cooled atomic gases

scenes.text: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose, a lecturer at Dhaka University, mailed Einstein a short paper deriving Planck's law by a new way of counting photons.
Einstein translated it into German, had it published, and extended the idea to atoms. Particles that follow it are now called bosons.

steps.title: Derivation in outline
steps.body:
Maximise ln W_BE = Σ ln[(n_i + g_i − 1)!/(n_i!(g_i − 1)!)] with fixed N and E. The result for mean occupancy of a single state:

**⟨n⟩ = 1/[exp((E − μ)/k_BT) − 1]**

μ is the chemical potential. For bosons μ ≤ lowest energy level (otherwise ⟨n⟩ < 0).

steps.title: Comparing the statistics
steps.body:
⟨n⟩ = 1/[e^((E − μ)/k_BT) + a]

- a = −1: Bose–Einstein (can exceed 1)
- a = +1: Fermi–Dirac (between 0 and 1)
- a = 0: Maxwell–Boltzmann

When (E − μ) ≫ k_BT all three agree.

steps.title: Solved: photon occupancy
steps.body:
For photons μ = 0.

- At hν = k_BT: ⟨n⟩ = 1/(e − 1) = **0.58**
- At hν = 0.1k_BT: ⟨n⟩ = 1/(e^0.1 − 1) = 9.5 (many photons per mode)
- At hν = 10k_BT: ⟨n⟩ = 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ (MB-like)

steps.title: Why μ = 0 for photons and phonons
steps.body: Their number is not conserved: walls absorb and emit photons freely. Minimising F with respect to N then gives μ = ∂F/∂N = 0.

steps.title: Bunching
steps.body: BE statistics enhances the probability of bosons occupying the same state. This 'bunching' underlies laser action and the Hanbury Brown–Twiss effect.

activity.prompt: Find the mean photon occupancy ⟨n⟩ = 1/(e^x − 1) for a mode with hν = 2k_BT (x = 2), to three decimals.

quiz.q: The BE occupancy is:
quiz.why: Counting indistinguishable particles with no limit per state gives the −1 in the denominator.

quiz.q: For photons the chemical potential is:
quiz.why: Photon number is not conserved, so equilibrium requires ∂F/∂N = μ = 0.

quiz.q: The particles that obey BE statistics have:
quiz.why: By the spin–statistics theorem, integer-spin particles are bosons.

scenes.text: A potter in Khurja judges the kiln temperature by colour: dull red, then orange, then bright yellow-white.
The colour of glowing objects follows Planck's law, the first triumph of quantum statistics.

steps.title: Counting modes
steps.body:
In a cavity of volume V, the number of electromagnetic modes between ν and ν + dν (two polarisations) is

g(ν) dν = (8πV/c³) ν² dν

steps.title: Planck's law
steps.body:
Multiply modes by mean energy per mode hν⟨n⟩:

**u(ν) dν = (8πhν³/c³) · 1/(e^(hν/k_BT) − 1) dν**

- Low ν (hν ≪ k_BT): u ≈ 8πν²k_BT/c³, the classical Rayleigh–Jeans law
- High ν: u ≈ (8πhν³/c³)e^(−hν/k_BT), Wien's law; the UV catastrophe disappears

steps.title: Wien displacement
steps.body:
The wavelength of maximum emission obeys

**λ_max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K**

steps.title: Solved: three sources
steps.body:
- Sun (5778 K): λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³/5778 = **501 nm** (green-blue, visible)
- Human body (310 K): **9.35 μm**, far infrared, as used in thermal cameras
- Cosmic microwave background (2.725 K): **1.06 mm**, microwaves

steps.title: The best blackbody ever measured
steps.body: The COBE satellite (1990s) found the cosmic microwave background matches Planck's law to better than 1 part in 10⁴, at T = 2.725 K.

activity.prompt: An incandescent filament is at 3000 K. Find λ_max = 2.898 × 10⁻³/T in nm (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: At low frequencies Planck's law reduces to:
quiz.why: For hν ≪ k_BT, ⟨n⟩hν ≈ k_BT, giving the classical equipartition result.

quiz.q: Planck's law avoids the ultraviolet catastrophe because:
options: there are fewer modes at high frequency
quiz.why: When hν ≫ k_BT the occupancy falls as e^(−hν/k_BT), so high-frequency modes carry little energy.

quiz.q: If T doubles, λ_max:
quiz.why: λ_max T is constant, so λ_max is inversely proportional to T.

story.title: Solar panels on a hostel roof

scenes.text: Students in Jodhpur measure about 1000 W/m² of sunlight on a clear afternoon.
Working backwards with the Stefan–Boltzmann law gives the Sun's surface temperature: close to 5800 K.

steps.title: Integrating Planck's law
steps.body:
Total energy density:

u = ∫ u(ν) dν = aT⁴, a = 8π⁵k_B⁴/(15h³c³) = 7.57 × 10⁻¹⁶ J m⁻³ K⁻⁴

Power emitted per unit area of a blackbody:

**j = σT⁴**, σ = ac/4 = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴

steps.title: Solved: radiant exitance
steps.body:
A blackbody at 1000 K:

- j = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 10¹² = **5.67 × 10⁴ W/m²**

At 2000 K it is 2⁴ = 16 times larger.

steps.title: Other properties of the photon gas
steps.body:
- Pressure P = u/3 (radiation pressure)
- Entropy S = (4/3)aT³V
- Number density n ≈ 2.03 × 10⁷ T³ m⁻³
- In an adiabatic expansion VT³ = constant: the expanding universe cools as T ∝ 1/(scale factor).

steps.title: Real surfaces
steps.body: Real bodies emit j = εσT⁴ with emissivity ε < 1. Polished metals have ε ≈ 0.05; human skin ≈ 0.98, which is why thermal cameras read skin temperature well.

activity.prompt: Find the power radiated per square metre by a blackbody at 2000 K, j = σT⁴ (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴), in units of 10⁵ W/m² (two decimals).

quiz.q: If the temperature of a blackbody doubles, the radiated power:
quiz.why: j = σT⁴, so doubling T multiplies j by 2⁴ = 16.

quiz.q: Radiation pressure of isotropic blackbody radiation is:
quiz.why: For an ultra-relativistic gas, P = u/3, since photon momentum is E/c spread equally over three directions.

quiz.q: During adiabatic expansion of radiation:
quiz.why: Entropy S ∝ VT³ is constant in a reversible adiabatic process.

scenes.text: Cornell and Wieman cool rubidium atoms with lasers and magnetic traps to about 170 nanokelvin.
A sharp peak of atoms in the lowest state appears: the first Bose–Einstein condensate in a gas, seventy years after Bose and Einstein's prediction.

steps.title: The idea
steps.body:
For an ideal Bose gas with fixed N, μ rises towards zero as T falls. The number of particles in excited states has a maximum:

N_ex(max) = 2.612 V/λ³

Below a temperature T_c the excess particles must go into the ground state: a macroscopic **condensate**.

steps.title: Critical temperature
steps.body:
Setting nλ³ = 2.612:

**T_c = (2πħ²/mk_B)(n/2.612)^(2/3)**

Condensate fraction below T_c:

**N₀/N = 1 − (T/T_c)^(3/2)**

steps.title: Solved: liquid helium-4
steps.body:
ρ = 145 kg/m³, m = 6.65 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, n = 2.18 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.

- (n/2.612)^(2/3) = (8.35 × 10²⁷)^(2/3) = 4.12 × 10¹⁸
- 2πħ²/mk_B = 7.61 × 10⁻¹⁹ m² K
- T_c ≈ **3.1 K**

The observed superfluid transition is at 2.17 K; the difference comes from strong interactions in the liquid.

steps.title: Solved: condensate fraction
steps.body: At T = T_c/2: N₀/N = 1 − (0.5)^1.5 = 1 − 0.354 = **0.65**. About two-thirds of the atoms are in the single lowest state.

steps.title: Recognition
steps.body: Cornell, Wieman and Ketterle won the 2001 Nobel Prize for atomic BECs. Condensates are now used to study superfluidity, quantised vortices and precision atom interferometry.

activity.prompt: An ideal Bose gas is at T = 0.7 T_c. Find the condensate fraction N₀/N = 1 − (T/T_c)^(3/2) to two decimals. (0.7^1.5 ≈ 0.586)

quiz.q: BEC occurs when the degeneracy parameter nλ³ reaches about:
quiz.why: Excited states can hold at most 2.612V/λ³ bosons, so condensation starts when nλ³ = 2.612.

quiz.q: Below T_c, the condensate fraction is:
quiz.why: The excited states hold N(T/T_c)^(3/2), and the rest must be in the ground state.

quiz.q: Liquid ⁴He becomes superfluid at 2.17 K, not 3.1 K, because:
options: the formula is wrong for all gases
it is not ideal: atoms interact strongly
quiz.why: The ideal-gas estimate ignores the strong interactions in the liquid, which shift the transition.

questions.q: In BE statistics the occupancy of a state can be:
questions.why: Bosons have no exclusion principle, so many can share one state.

questions.q: For bosons, μ must be:
options: at or below the lowest energy level
questions.why: If μ exceeded a level energy, its occupancy 1/(e^((E−μ)/k_BT) − 1) would be negative.

questions.q: The mode density of a cavity varies with frequency as:
questions.why: The number of standing-wave modes in a 3D box grows as the area of a sphere in k-space, ∝ ν².

questions.q: Wien's constant λ_max T is about:
questions.why: Maximising Planck's law in wavelength gives λ_max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K.

questions.q: A star has λ_max = 290 nm. Its surface temperature is about:
The Stefan–Boltzmann constant σ is:
questions.why: σ = 2π⁵k_B⁴/(15h³c²) = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

questions.q: A body at 600 K radiates P. At 300 K the same body radiates:
questions.why: Halving T reduces σT⁴ by 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: Planck's law at high frequency approaches:
questions.why: For hν ≫ k_BT the −1 is negligible, leaving u ∝ ν³e^(−hν/k_BT).

questions.q: The entropy of blackbody radiation in volume V is proportional to:
questions.why: S = (4/3)aT³V follows from U = aT⁴V and dS = dU/T at constant V.

questions.q: The ideal-gas T_c for BEC depends on density as:
questions.why: T_c ∝ (n/2.612)^(2/3) from the condition nλ³ = 2.612 with λ ∝ T^(−1/2).

questions.q: Below T_c, the fraction of atoms in excited states at T = T_c/4 is:
Doubling the density of an ideal Bose gas changes T_c by a factor of:
questions.why: T_c ∝ n^(2/3), so doubling n multiplies T_c by 2^(2/3).

courses.title: Unit 5 · Fermi–Dirac statistics: electrons and stars
courses.summary: The Fermi–Dirac distribution and its behaviour at zero and finite temperature, the free-electron gas with Fermi energy, mean energy and degeneracy pressure, the small electronic heat capacity of metals, and degeneracy pressure in white dwarfs and neutron stars including Chandrasekhar's limit.
outcomes: Derive and evaluate the Fermi–Dirac occupancy at any temperature
Compute Fermi energy, Fermi temperature and mean energy of an electron gas
Calculate degeneracy pressure and explain why it does not vanish at T = 0
Explain why electronic heat capacity is small and linear in T
Explain how electron degeneracy supports white dwarfs and state the Chandrasekhar limit

scenes.text: At a cricket match in Kolkata, fans fill the stadium from the lowest rows up, one person per seat.
At 'zero temperature' every seat below a certain row is taken and every seat above is empty. That row is the Fermi level.

steps.title: The distribution
steps.body:
Maximising W_FD = Π g_i!/[n_i!(g_i − n_i)!] at fixed N and E gives:

**f(E) = 1/[exp((E − μ)/k_BT) + 1]**

f lies between 0 and 1, as the Pauli principle requires. For metals μ ≈ E_F at ordinary temperatures.

steps.title: Shape
steps.body:
- T = 0: f = 1 for E < E_F, 0 for E > E_F (a step).
- T > 0: the step smooths over a width of a few k_BT.
- f(E_F) = ½ at any T.
- Symmetry: the probability that a state at E_F + δ is filled equals the probability that a state at E_F − δ is empty.

steps.title: Classical tail
steps.body: For E − μ ≫ k_BT, f ≈ e^(−(E−μ)/k_BT), the Boltzmann form. This is why electrons in a lightly doped semiconductor conduction band can be treated classically.

activity.prompt: Find the Fermi–Dirac occupancy of a state 0.050 eV above E_F at 300 K (k_BT = 0.02585 eV), to three decimals.

quiz.q: At any temperature, f(E_F) equals:
quiz.why: At E = E_F the exponential is 1, so f = 1/(1 + 1) = ½.

quiz.q: At T = 0 the FD distribution is:
quiz.why: All states below E_F are filled and all above are empty, giving a sharp step.

quiz.q: For E − μ ≫ k_BT, the FD function approaches:
options: the BE function with large n
quiz.why: The +1 becomes negligible next to the large exponential, leaving e^(−(E−μ)/k_BT).

scenes.text: Cool a block of copper towards absolute zero. A classical gas inside would lose all its pressure.
The electrons instead push outward with a pressure of about 400,000 atmospheres, purely from the Pauli principle.

steps.title: Fermi energy
steps.body:
Density of states with spin factor 2: g(E) = (V/2π²)(2m/ħ²)^(3/2) √E.

Filling up to E_F with N electrons:

**E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3)**

T_F = E_F/k_B, v_F = √(2E_F/m).

steps.title: Energy and pressure at T = 0
steps.body:
- Mean energy per electron: **⟨E⟩ = (3/5)E_F**
- Total energy: U₀ = (3/5)NE_F
- Degeneracy pressure: **P = (2/3)U₀/V = (2/5)nE_F**
- Bulk modulus B = (5/3)P

steps.title: Solved: copper
steps.body:
n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, E_F = 7.0 eV.

- ⟨E⟩ = 0.6 × 7.0 = **4.2 eV** (compare (3/2)k_BT = 0.039 eV at 300 K)
- P = 0.4 × 8.5 × 10²⁸ × 7.0 × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = **3.8 × 10¹⁰ Pa**, about 3.8 × 10⁵ atm

It is balanced by the attraction of the positive ions.

steps.title: Common slip
steps.body: Remember the spin factor 2 in g(E). Without it, k_F would be (6π²n)^(1/3) and E_F would be too large by 2^(2/3).

activity.prompt: Silver has E_F = 5.5 eV. Find the mean energy per conduction electron at T = 0, in eV.

quiz.q: The mean energy of a free-electron gas at T = 0 is:
quiz.why: Averaging E over g(E) ∝ √E from 0 to E_F gives ∫E^(3/2)/∫E^(1/2) = (3/5)E_F.

quiz.q: Degeneracy pressure exists at T = 0 because:
options: the Pauli principle forces electrons into high-momentum states
quiz.why: Electrons cannot all occupy the lowest state, so they fill momentum states up to p_F and exert pressure.

quiz.q: Degeneracy pressure is:
quiz.why: P = (2/3)(U/V) = (2/3)(3/5)nE_F = (2/5)nE_F for a non-relativistic gas.

lessons.title: Electron gas at T > 0: heat capacity

scenes.text: Classical theory says metal electrons should add (3/2)R to the molar heat capacity. Measurements show only about 1% of that.
Sommerfeld's 1928 answer: only electrons within about k_BT of the Fermi level can absorb heat.

steps.title: Sommerfeld estimate
steps.body:
Only a fraction ≈ T/T_F of electrons near E_F can be thermally excited, each gaining ≈ k_BT. So U − U₀ ∝ N k_BT²/T_F and C_el ∝ T.

Exact result (Sommerfeld expansion):

**C_el = (π²/2) Nk_B (T/T_F)**

steps.title: Separating electrons and phonons
steps.body: At low T: C = γT + βT³ (electrons + Debye phonons). Plot C/T against T²: a straight line with intercept γ and slope β. For copper γ ≈ 0.69 mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻². Below about 1 K the electronic term dominates.

steps.title: Thermionic emission
steps.body:
Electrons in the high-energy tail of f(E) with energy above E_F + φ (work function) can escape. The current density follows the Richardson–Dushman law:

J = A T² exp(−φ/k_BT), A ≈ 1.2 × 10⁶ A m⁻² K⁻²

This was the basis of vacuum tubes and electron guns.

steps.title: Chemical potential shift
steps.body: μ(T) = E_F[1 − (π²/12)(k_BT/E_F)²]. For copper at 300 K the shift is only about 10⁻⁵ E_F, so μ ≈ E_F is an excellent approximation.

activity.prompt: Silver has T_F = 6.4 × 10⁴ K. Find C_el as a percentage of the classical (3/2)Nk_B at 300 K using (π²/3)(T/T_F) (two decimals).

more electrons are in the high-energy tail of f(E)

scenes.text: In 1930, nineteen-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar sailed from India to Cambridge and worked out white-dwarf physics on the voyage.
He found that above about 1.4 solar masses, electron degeneracy cannot hold a star up. He received the Nobel Prize in 1983.

steps.title: White dwarfs
steps.body: When a Sun-like star exhausts its fuel, its core contracts to about Earth's size: densities ~10⁹ kg/m³. Electrons are fully degenerate (T ≪ T_F, even at 10⁷ K), and their **degeneracy pressure** balances gravity.

steps.title: Scaling laws
steps.body:
- Non-relativistic: P ∝ n^(5/3). Balancing gravity gives R ∝ M^(−1/3): heavier white dwarfs are **smaller**.
- Relativistic (p_F ≫ m_ec): P ∝ n^(4/3). Pressure and gravity scale the same way with R, so stability fails above a critical mass.

steps.title: Chandrasekhar limit
steps.body: **M_Ch ≈ 1.4 M_☉** (for a carbon–oxygen composition with two nucleons per electron). Above this, the core collapses further: electrons combine with protons into neutrons, forming a **neutron star** supported by neutron degeneracy and nuclear forces, or a black hole if heavier still.

steps.title: Solved: compression
steps.body:
A white dwarf in the non-relativistic regime is compressed so that n increases by a factor of 8.

- P ∝ n^(5/3) → 8^(5/3) = 2⁵ = **32 times** larger pressure
- E_F ∝ n^(2/3) → 8^(2/3) = **4 times** larger

| | MB | BE | FD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Particles | distinguishable | bosons | fermions |
| Occupancy | e^(−(E−μ)/kT) | 1/(e^x − 1) | 1/(e^x + 1) |
| Low-T behaviour | classical | condensation | Fermi sea |
| Examples | dilute gases | photons, ⁴He | electrons, neutrons |
