uni-bsc-phy-thermal-physics.title: B.Sc Physics · Thermal Physics (full paper)
uni-bsc-phy-thermal-physics.description: Unit-by-unit Thermal Physics: laws of thermodynamics, entropy and engines, thermodynamic potentials and Maxwell relations, kinetic theory of gases, and blackbody radiation, with solved numericals and a revision/lab unit. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Physics (Hons) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Zeroth and first law of thermodynamics
courses.summary: Thermodynamic systems, equilibrium and temperature (zeroth law), quasi-static work, internal energy and the first law, heat capacities and adiabatic processes of an ideal gas.
outcomes: Define system, surroundings, state variables and thermodynamic equilibrium
State the zeroth law and explain why it makes temperature measurable
Compute work in isothermal, isobaric, isochoric and adiabatic processes
Apply the first law dU = δQ − δW to ideal-gas processes
Derive Cp − Cv = R and PV^γ = constant

lessons.title: Systems, equilibrium and the zeroth law

scenes.text: Meera's mother waits a full minute before reading the thermometer under Meera's tongue. Why not read it at once?
The thermometer must reach thermal equilibrium with the body. Only then do they share one property: temperature.

steps.title: System, surroundings, boundary
steps.body:
- **Open system**: exchanges matter and energy (a boiling open pot).
- **Closed system**: exchanges energy, not matter (gas in a piston).
- **Isolated system**: exchanges neither (ideal thermos flask).

A system is described by **state variables** (P, V, T, U, S). **Intensive** variables (P, T, density) do not depend on size; **extensive** ones (V, U, S, mass) scale with size.

steps.title: Thermodynamic equilibrium and the zeroth law
steps.body:
Thermodynamic equilibrium = mechanical (no unbalanced force), thermal (uniform T) and chemical (no net reaction/diffusion) equilibrium together.

**Zeroth law**: if A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. It lets us define a state function called temperature and use a thermometer (C) to compare A and B without touching them together.

steps.title: Equation of state and exact differentials
steps.body:
An **equation of state** links state variables, e.g. ideal gas PV = nRT, or van der Waals (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT.

State functions have **exact differentials**: dU integrates to U₂ − U₁ independent of path, and ∮dU = 0. Heat and work are **path functions**, written δQ and δW (inexact). Test: for dF = M dx + N dy, F is exact if ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x.

steps.title: Solved: is the differential exact?
steps.body:
Check dF = (2xy) dx + (x²) dy.
- M = 2xy → ∂M/∂y = 2x
- N = x² → ∂N/∂x = 2x
- Equal, so dF is exact; F = x²y + const.

Now δW = P dV for an ideal gas written in (T, V): δW = (RT/V) dV + 0·dT (1 mol). ∂(RT/V)/∂T = R/V ≠ ∂(0)/∂V = 0 → inexact, so work depends on path.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a body 'contains heat'. It contains internal energy; heat is energy in transit.
- Treating temperature as extensive: joining two cups at 40 °C gives 40 °C, not 80 °C.
- Forgetting that equilibrium needs mechanical and chemical balance too, not only equal T.

statements.s: Pressure is an intensive variable.
statements.why: Splitting a gas sample in half leaves its pressure unchanged.

statements.s: Work done by a gas is a state function.
statements.why: Work depends on the path on the P–V diagram, so δW is inexact.

statements.s: The zeroth law is what makes a thermometer meaningful.
statements.why: It guarantees that two bodies each in equilibrium with the thermometer are in equilibrium with each other.

statements.s: An isolated system can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings.
statements.why: That describes a closed system; an isolated system exchanges neither.

quiz.q: Which quantity is extensive?
quiz.why: Internal energy doubles when the amount of substance doubles, so it is extensive, while T, P and density do not.

quiz.q: For dF = M dx + N dy to be exact we need:
quiz.why: Equality of the mixed partial derivatives ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x is the condition that M dx + N dy is the differential of some function F.

quiz.q: Gas in a sealed steel cylinder heated on a stove is a:
quiz.why: Heat crosses the wall but no matter does, which is the definition of a closed system.

scenes.text: Steam lifts the cooker's weight and escapes with a whistle. Heat from the flame became partly internal energy of steam and partly work lifting the weight.
The first law is the bookkeeping rule for exactly this split.

steps.title: Quasi-static work
steps.body:
For a gas pushing a piston slowly (quasi-statically), work done BY the gas is

W = ∫ P dV (area under the curve on a P–V diagram).

- Isochoric (V const): W = 0
- Isobaric: W = P(V₂ − V₁)
- Isothermal ideal gas: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
- Adiabatic: W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1)

In a cycle, net work = area enclosed (clockwise → positive work by gas).

steps.title: The first law
steps.body:
dU = δQ − δW (sign convention: Q into system positive, W by system positive).

Internal energy U is a state function. For an ideal gas U depends on T only (Joule's free-expansion result), so ΔU = n Cv ΔT for ANY process. Free expansion into vacuum: W = 0, Q = 0 → ΔU = 0 → T unchanged (ideal gas).

steps.title: Solved: isothermal expansion
steps.body:
1 mol of ideal gas expands isothermally at 300 K from 10 L to 20 L.
- W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 1 × 8.314 × 300 × ln 2
- = 2494.2 × 0.6931 = **1729 J**
- ΔU = 0 (T constant) → Q = W = 1729 J absorbed.

steps.title: Solved: isobaric heating
steps.body:
2 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is heated at constant pressure by 100 K. Cv = 3R/2, Cp = 5R/2.
- Q = nCpΔT = 2 × 20.785 × 100 = **4157 J**
- ΔU = nCvΔT = 2 × 12.471 × 100 = **2494 J**
- W = Q − ΔU = **1663 J** (= nRΔT = 2 × 8.314 × 100 ✓)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing sign conventions: chemistry texts often write ΔU = Q + W (W on system). Pick one and state it.
- Using ln with litres vs m³ — the ratio V₂/V₁ is dimensionless, so units cancel, but P must be in Pa when you use W = PΔV.
- Assuming Q = 0 in an isothermal process; actually ΔU = 0 and Q = W.

activity.prompt: 3 mol of ideal gas expand isothermally at 400 K until the volume triples. Find the work done by the gas in J (R = 8.314 J/mol·K, ln 3 = 1.0986).

quiz.q: In free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum:
quiz.why: No piston is pushed and the walls are insulated, so Q = W = 0 and the first law gives ΔU = 0, hence T is unchanged for an ideal gas.

quiz.q: Net work in a cyclic process equals:
options: area enclosed on the P–V diagram
quiz.why: Over a cycle ΔU = 0 and the net work equals the area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, ΔU = nCvΔT holds for:
quiz.why: Ideal-gas internal energy depends on temperature only, so ΔU = nCvΔT applies to every process between the same temperatures.

scenes.text: Rahul pumps his tyre fast and the pump barrel warms up. No flame touched it.
Rapid compression is nearly adiabatic: work done on the air raises its temperature.

steps.title: Cp − Cv = R (Mayer's relation)
steps.body:
At constant volume: δQ = dU = n Cv dT.
At constant pressure: δQ = dU + P dV = n Cv dT + nR dT (since PV = nRT gives P dV = nR dT).
So n Cp dT = n(Cv + R) dT → **Cp − Cv = R** (per mole).

γ = Cp/Cv: monatomic 5/3 ≈ 1.67, diatomic (room T) 7/5 = 1.40.

steps.title: Deriving PV^γ = constant
steps.body:
Adiabatic: δQ = 0 → n Cv dT = −P dV.
Differentiate PV = nRT: P dV + V dP = nR dT.
Eliminate dT: P dV + V dP = −(R/Cv) P dV → V dP = −γ P dV (because 1 + R/Cv = γ).
Integrate: ln P + γ ln V = const → **PV^γ = const**, equivalently TV^(γ−1) = const and T^γ P^(1−γ) = const.

The adiabatic curve is γ times steeper than the isotherm through the same point: (dP/dV)_ad = −γP/V.

steps.title: Solved: adiabatic compression of air
steps.body:
Air (γ = 1.4) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to one-tenth its volume (as in a diesel engine).
- T₂ = T₁ (V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 300 × 10^0.4
- 10^0.4 = 2.512 → T₂ = **754 K** (≈ 481 °C) — hot enough to ignite diesel fuel.

steps.title: Solved: adiabatic work
steps.body:
1 mol of monatomic gas cools adiabatically from 400 K to 300 K.
- W = n Cv (T₁ − T₂) = 1 × 1.5 × 8.314 × 100 = **1247 J** done by the gas.
- Equivalent to (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(2/3) = 1247 J ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using T in °C in TV^(γ−1) = const. Always use kelvin.
- Using γ = 1.67 for air; air is diatomic, γ ≈ 1.4.
- Thinking 'adiabatic' means 'isothermal'. Adiabatic means no heat exchange; temperature changes.

activity.prompt: A monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) at 27 °C is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Find the final temperature in kelvin.

quiz.q: For a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature γ is about:
quiz.why: A diatomic gas has 5 active degrees of freedom at room temperature, so Cv = 5R/2, Cp = 7R/2 and γ = 7/5 = 1.40.

quiz.q: Slope of an adiabat compared with an isotherm at the same point is:
quiz.why: The isotherm has dP/dV = −P/V while the adiabat has dP/dV = −γP/V, so the adiabat is steeper by a factor γ.

quiz.q: Cp − Cv = R holds exactly for:
quiz.why: Mayer's relation uses PV = nRT in the derivation, so it is exact only for an ideal gas, per mole.

lessons.title: Lab: indicator diagrams and multi-step cycles

scenes.text: Railway engineers once clipped an 'indicator' to steam cylinders to draw P–V loops while the engine ran.
The area of the loop told them the work per stroke. You will do the same on paper.

steps.title: Method for any cycle
steps.body:
1. Tabulate each corner state (P, V, T) using PV = nRT.
2. For each leg find W (area under leg), ΔU = nCvΔT and Q = ΔU + W.
3. Check: ΣΔU = 0 and ΣW = ΣQ = enclosed area.
4. Efficiency of an engine cycle = W_net / Q_in (sum only positive Q).

steps.title: Units trick
steps.body: 1 L·atm = 101.3 J. Keep P in atm and V in L during the table, then convert work at the end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting heat rejected in Q_in — efficiency uses only heat absorbed.
- Forgetting the sign of work on compression legs (negative).
- Reading T off the diagram instead of computing from PV = nRT.

activity.prompt: A gas cycle on a P–V diagram is a rectangle with pressures 2×10⁵ Pa and 5×10⁵ Pa and volumes 1×10⁻³ m³ and 4×10⁻³ m³. Net work per cycle (J)?

quiz.q: 1 L·atm is approximately:
quiz.why: 1 atm = 1.013×10⁵ Pa and 1 L = 10⁻³ m³, so their product is about 101.3 J.

quiz.q: In engine-cycle efficiency, the denominator is:
quiz.why: Efficiency is the net work out divided by the heat taken in from hot sources, so only positive heat inputs are summed.

quiz.q: For a full cycle, ΣΔU equals:
quiz.why: Internal energy is a state function, so returning to the starting state gives a total change of zero.

questions.q: The zeroth law allows us to define:
questions.why: Transitivity of thermal equilibrium means all bodies in mutual equilibrium share one property, temperature.

questions.q: Work done by 1 mol ideal gas expanding isothermally at 300 K from V to 2V is about:
For an isochoric process:
questions.why: With no volume change the gas does no P dV work, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU.

questions.q: PV^γ = const applies to a:
questions.why: The derivation assumes δQ = 0, ideal gas and quasi-static steps; free expansion is not quasi-static.

questions.q: Cv for a monatomic ideal gas (per mole) is:
questions.why: Three translational degrees of freedom each contribute R/2, giving Cv = 3R/2.

questions.q: Air at 300 K compressed adiabatically to V/10 (γ = 1.4) reaches about:
Heat is a path function because:
questions.why: The heat exchanged between two states depends on the process, which is what an inexact differential means.

questions.q: 2 mol monatomic gas heated 100 K at constant P absorbs about:
On a P–V diagram, a clockwise cycle means:
options: net work done by the gas is positive
questions.why: Going clockwise, the expansion leg lies at higher pressure than the compression leg, so the gas does net positive work.

questions.q: The ratio of adiabatic to isothermal slope at a point is:
questions.why: Adiabat slope −γP/V divided by isotherm slope −P/V gives γ.

questions.q: 1 mol monatomic gas cooling adiabatically by 100 K does work of about:
Which pair is extensive?
questions.why: Volume and internal energy both scale with the amount of matter, so both are extensive.

questions.q: Mayer's relation Cp − Cv = R uses:
questions.why: At constant pressure P dV = nR dT from the ideal gas law, which supplies the extra R.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Second law, Carnot engines and entropy
courses.summary: Reversible and irreversible processes, Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements, heat engines and refrigerators, Carnot cycle and Carnot's theorem, thermodynamic temperature, Clausius inequality and entropy changes in real processes.
outcomes: State and show the equivalence of the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements
Analyse the Carnot cycle and compute efficiency and COP
Explain Carnot's theorem and the thermodynamic temperature scale
Use the Clausius inequality and the principle of increase of entropy
Calculate entropy changes for phase change, heating, mixing and gas expansion

lessons.title: Second law: engines, refrigerators and the two statements

story.title: Why can't a ship run on sea heat?

scenes.text: The ocean holds enormous internal energy. Ananya asks why a ship can't simply draw heat from the sea and turn all of it into propeller work.
Energy conservation would allow it. The second law forbids it: you need a colder body to dump heat into.

steps.title: Heat engine and refrigerator
steps.body:
**Engine**: absorbs Q₁ from a hot reservoir at T₁, does work W, rejects Q₂ to a cold reservoir at T₂. η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.

**Refrigerator**: work W moves Q₂ from cold to hot. COP (refrigerator) = Q₂/W; COP (heat pump) = Q₁/W = 1 + COP_ref.

steps.title: The two statements
steps.body:
- **Kelvin–Planck**: no cyclic device can absorb heat from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work.
- **Clausius**: no cyclic device can transfer heat from a colder to a hotter body with no other effect.

Equivalence (proof sketch): if a 'perfect refrigerator' existed, attach it to an ordinary engine; the pair then takes heat from the hot reservoir only and converts it fully to work, violating Kelvin–Planck. Conversely a perfect engine driving an ordinary refrigerator violates Clausius.

steps.title: Reversible vs irreversible
steps.body: A reversible process can be retraced so that system AND surroundings return to their initial states. It must be quasi-static and free of dissipation (friction, viscosity, electrical resistance, heat flow across finite ΔT, free expansion, mixing). All real processes are irreversible; reversible ones are limiting ideals.

steps.title: Solved: engine and refrigerator numbers
steps.body:
(a) An engine takes 5000 J and rejects 3500 J per cycle: W = 1500 J, η = 1500/5000 = **30 %**.
(b) A fridge removes 300 J from its freezer per cycle using 100 J of work: COP = 300/100 = **3**; heat dumped into the kitchen = 400 J.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking COP must be < 1 like efficiency. COP of good refrigerators is 2–6.
- Saying the second law forbids converting work fully into heat. That is allowed (friction does it); the reverse in a cycle is forbidden.
- Calling any slow process reversible: slow heat flow across a finite temperature gap is still irreversible.

statements.s: A cyclic engine can convert all the heat from one reservoir into work if it is frictionless.
statements.why: Kelvin–Planck forbids it regardless of friction; some heat must be rejected.

statements.s: COP of a heat pump equals 1 + COP of the same device used as a refrigerator.
statements.why: Q₁/W = (Q₂ + W)/W = COP_ref + 1.

statements.s: Heat flow across a finite temperature difference is irreversible.
statements.why: It generates entropy and cannot be reversed without external work.

statements.s: Violating the Clausius statement would also violate Kelvin–Planck.
statements.why: The two statements are logically equivalent.

quiz.q: An engine absorbs 800 J and rejects 600 J. Its efficiency is:
Which process is reversible in the ideal limit?
quiz.why: A frictionless quasi-static isothermal expansion can be retraced exactly, while the others are inherently dissipative.

quiz.q: The Clausius statement concerns:
options: heat flowing from cold to hot unaided
complete conversion of work to heat
quiz.why: Clausius says heat cannot pass from a colder to a hotter body without some other effect such as work input.

lessons.title: Carnot cycle, Carnot's theorem and absolute temperature

scenes.text: In 1824 a young French engineer asked: what is the best any heat engine could possibly do?
His answer depends only on the two reservoir temperatures — not on steam, air or any working substance.

steps.title: The four strokes
steps.body:
1. Isothermal expansion at T₁: absorbs Q₁ = nRT₁ ln(V₂/V₁).
2. Adiabatic expansion: T₁ → T₂.
3. Isothermal compression at T₂: rejects Q₂ = nRT₂ ln(V₃/V₄).
4. Adiabatic compression back to the start.

The adiabats give V₂/V₁ = V₃/V₄, so Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁ and
**η_Carnot = 1 − T₂/T₁**.

steps.title: Carnot's theorem
steps.body:
(i) No engine working between two reservoirs is more efficient than a reversible engine between the same reservoirs.
(ii) All reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have equal efficiency.

Proof idea: run a supposedly better engine to drive a reversed Carnot engine; the combination would move heat from cold to hot with no work input — violating Clausius.

steps.title: Thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale
steps.body: Because Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁ for any reversible engine, Kelvin defined temperature through heat ratios, independent of any substance. Fixing the triple point of water at 273.16 K sets the scale; it coincides with the ideal-gas scale.

steps.title: Solved: Carnot engine and refrigerator
steps.body:
(a) Engine between 500 K and 300 K: η = 1 − 300/500 = **40 %**. With Q₁ = 1000 J, W = 400 J, Q₂ = 600 J.
(b) Carnot refrigerator keeping 273 K inside a 300 K room: COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂) = 273/27 = **10.1**. Real fridges reach about a third of this.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in 1 − T₂/T₁: 1 − 27/227 is wrong; use 300/500.
- Thinking a Carnot engine has 100 % efficiency; that would need T₂ = 0 K.
- Assuming real engines can match Carnot by using better fuel; the limit depends only on temperatures.

activity.prompt: A Carnot engine works between 800 K and 300 K and absorbs 2000 J per cycle from the hot reservoir. How much work (J) does it do per cycle?

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency between 400 K and 300 K is:
quiz.why: η = 1 − 300/400 = 0.25, so a Carnot engine can convert at most a quarter of the heat into work.

quiz.q: Efficiency of a reversible engine depends on:
quiz.why: Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, fixed by T₁ and T₂ alone.

quiz.q: In the Carnot cycle, the two adiabats ensure that:
quiz.why: Applying TV^(γ−1) = const on both adiabats gives equal volume ratios, which makes Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁.

scenes.text: An ice cube melts in Kiran's hand, never the other way round. Energy would be conserved either way.
Entropy is the quantity that tells which direction nature takes.

steps.title: Clausius inequality
steps.body:
For any cycle, ∮ δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality for a reversible cycle.

Because ∮ δQ_rev/T = 0, the quantity dS = δQ_rev/T is an exact differential: **entropy S is a state function** (unit J/K).

For an irreversible process between states 1 and 2: S₂ − S₁ > ∫ δQ/T.

steps.title: Principle of increase of entropy
steps.body:
For an isolated system (δQ = 0): ΔS ≥ 0. Entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) never decreases; it stays constant only for reversible processes.

T dS = dU + P dV (combined first and second law) — valid between any two equilibrium states because all terms are state functions.

Statistically S = k_B ln W (Boltzmann): entropy measures the number of microstates.

steps.title: Solved: ideal gas expansion
steps.body:
1 mol ideal gas doubles its volume isothermally: ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = 8.314 × 0.693 = **5.76 J/K**.
General ideal gas: ΔS = nCv ln(T₂/T₁) + nR ln(V₂/V₁).
In free expansion (V → 2V) the gas's ΔS is the same 5.76 J/K (state function), but the surroundings change by 0, so ΔS_universe = +5.76 J/K: irreversible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ΔS = Q/T for a process where T changes; integrate ∫ mc dT/T instead.
- Computing ΔS for an irreversible process using the actual Q; use a reversible path between the same end states.
- Claiming the entropy of a system can never decrease; only the total for an isolated system cannot (a fridge interior loses entropy).

activity.prompt: Find the entropy change (J/K) when 2 kg of water at 100 °C (373 K) is converted to steam at the same temperature. Latent heat of vaporisation = 2.26×10⁶ J/kg.

quiz.q: For a reversible cycle, ∮δQ/T is:
quiz.why: The Clausius inequality becomes an equality for reversible cycles, so ∮δQ/T = 0, which is why entropy is a state function.

quiz.q: Entropy of an isolated system undergoing an irreversible process:
quiz.why: The principle of increase of entropy says ΔS > 0 for any irreversible change in an isolated system.

quiz.q: The relation T dS = dU + P dV holds for:
quiz.why: Every term is a state function, so the identity holds between any two nearby equilibrium states regardless of the actual path.

lessons.title: Lab: entropy generated when hot and cold water mix

scenes.text: Sunil mixes a bucket of boiling-hot water with cold tap water for a comfortable bath.
Energy balances perfectly — yet entropy of the universe goes up. Let us measure how much.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Measure masses m₁, m₂ and temperatures T₁ (hot), T₂ (cold) in kelvin.
2. Mix in an insulated calorimeter and record final T_f.
3. Theory: T_f = (m₁T₁ + m₂T₂)/(m₁ + m₂) for the same liquid (neglect calorimeter).
4. ΔS = m₁c ln(T_f/T₁) + m₂c ln(T_f/T₂). The first term is negative, the second positive; the sum is always positive.

steps.title: Why always positive
steps.body: For equal masses ΔS = mc ln[T_f²/(T₁T₂)] and T_f = (T₁+T₂)/2 is the arithmetic mean, which is always ≥ the geometric mean √(T₁T₂). So ΔS ≥ 0, equal only when T₁ = T₂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C inside the logarithm.
- Rounding T_f early: small ΔS is a difference of large numbers, so keep 4 significant figures.
- Ignoring the calorimeter's water equivalent in real data.

activity.prompt: 0.5 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.5 kg at 10 °C in an insulated vessel (c = 4186 J/kg·K). Find the total entropy change in J/K (use kelvin = °C + 273.15).

quiz.q: In mixing hot and cold water, the hot water's entropy:
quiz.why: The hot water loses heat and cools, so ∫mc dT/T is negative for it, though the cold water gains more.

quiz.q: For equal masses, ΔS ≥ 0 follows from:
options: AM ≥ GM of the two temperatures
quiz.why: ΔS = mc ln[T_f²/(T₁T₂)] with T_f the arithmetic mean, and the arithmetic mean is never less than the geometric mean.

quiz.q: Entropy change in this experiment is computed using:
options: the actual irreversible heat over T_f
a reversible path between the same end states
quiz.why: Entropy is a state function, so we evaluate it along an imagined reversible heating or cooling path between the same initial and final states.

questions.q: Kelvin–Planck statement forbids:
options: complete conversion of work into heat
a cyclic engine with a single reservoir producing net work
heat flow from hot to cold
questions.why: No cyclic device can take heat from one reservoir and turn it entirely into work.

questions.q: Carnot efficiency between 500 K and 300 K is:
COP of a Carnot refrigerator between 273 K and 300 K is about:
Entropy change when 1 kg ice melts at 273 K (L = 3.34×10⁵ J/kg):
For one mole of ideal gas doubling volume isothermally, ΔS is:
Carnot's theorem implies that an irreversible engine between T₁ and T₂ has:
options: lower efficiency than a reversible one
questions.why: No engine beats a reversible engine between the same reservoirs; irreversible ones do worse.

questions.q: Boltzmann's entropy formula is:
questions.why: S = k_B ln W links entropy to the number of microstates W.

questions.q: Which is NOT a source of irreversibility?
questions.why: A quasi-static frictionless process is the reversible ideal; the others dissipate.

questions.q: Heating 1 kg water from 273 K to 373 K changes its entropy by about:
The thermodynamic temperature scale is fixed by assigning:
options: 273.16 K to the triple point of water
questions.why: The Kelvin scale (before the 2019 SI redefinition fixed k_B) was defined by setting the triple point of water at 273.16 K.

questions.q: For an irreversible process between states 1 and 2:
questions.why: The Clausius inequality gives S₂ − S₁ > ∫δQ/T along an irreversible path.

questions.q: A heat pump with refrigerator COP 4 has heating COP:
questions.why: COP_heat pump = COP_ref + 1 = 5.

questions.q: Mixing 1 kg water at 80 °C with 1 kg at 20 °C produces entropy of about:
questions.why: Summing 4186 ln(323/353) + 4186 ln(323/293) gives about +36 J/K.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Thermodynamic potentials, Maxwell relations and phase change
courses.summary: Internal energy, enthalpy, Helmholtz and Gibbs functions with their natural variables; derivation of the four Maxwell relations; TdS equations and the general Cp − Cv; Clausius–Clapeyron equation and first/second-order transitions; Joule–Thomson effect and inversion temperature.
outcomes: Write dU, dH, dF, dG in natural variables and state when each is minimised
Derive all four Maxwell relations from exact differentials
Use the TdS equations to obtain Cp − Cv = TVα²/κ_T
Apply the Clausius–Clapeyron equation to boiling and melting
Explain Joule–Thomson cooling and compute the van der Waals inversion temperature

scenes.text: A battery at room temperature and pressure can only give you part of its chemical energy as electrical work.
Gibbs free energy is the account that tells you exactly how much.

steps.title: Definitions and differentials
steps.body:
Starting from dU = T dS − P dV:
- **Enthalpy** H = U + PV → dH = T dS + V dP
- **Helmholtz** F = U − TS → dF = −S dT − P dV
- **Gibbs** G = H − TS → dG = −S dT + V dP

Natural variables: U(S,V), H(S,P), F(T,V), G(T,P). These are Legendre transforms of U.

steps.title: Physical meaning
steps.body:
- ΔH = heat absorbed at constant pressure (e.g. reaction enthalpy, latent heat).
- −ΔF = maximum total work obtainable at constant T.
- −ΔG = maximum non-PV (useful) work at constant T and P.
- Equilibrium: at fixed T, V the system minimises F; at fixed T, P it minimises G. Two phases coexist when their molar Gibbs functions are equal: g₁ = g₂.

steps.title: Solved: reading derivatives
steps.body:
From dG = −S dT + V dP:
- (∂G/∂T)_P = −S and (∂G/∂P)_T = V.

For 1 mol ideal gas at constant T: dG = V dP = RT dP/P → G(P₂) − G(P₁) = RT ln(P₂/P₁).
At 300 K, compressing from 1 bar to 10 bar: ΔG = 8.314 × 300 × ln 10 = 2494 × 2.303 = **5743 J**.

steps.title: Memory aid: thermodynamic square
steps.body: Write the square with corners V F T / U · G / S H P ("Valid Facts and Theoretical Understanding Generate Solutions to Hard Problems"). Each potential sits between its two natural variables; arrows give signs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying F is minimised at constant T and P; that is G.
- Forgetting that H, F, G are state functions — they are, because U, P, V, T, S are.
- Writing dG = −S dT − V dP (wrong sign on V dP).

activity.prompt: 1 mol of ideal gas is compressed isothermally at 400 K from 2 bar to 8 bar. Find ΔG in J (R = 8.314 J/mol·K, ln 4 = 1.3863).

quiz.q: Natural variables of the Gibbs function are:
quiz.why: dG = −S dT + V dP, so G is naturally a function of temperature and pressure.

quiz.q: At constant T and V a system in equilibrium minimises:
quiz.why: Helmholtz free energy F = U − TS decreases in spontaneous processes at fixed T and V and is minimum at equilibrium.

quiz.q: (∂H/∂S)_P equals:
quiz.why: From dH = T dS + V dP, the coefficient of dS at constant pressure is T.

scenes.text: No instrument measures entropy directly, yet engineers need (∂S/∂P)_T for steam tables.
Maxwell relations swap it for (∂V/∂T)_P — something you can read off a thermometer and a measuring cylinder.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
If dZ = M dx + N dy is exact, (∂M/∂y)_x = (∂N/∂x)_y. Apply to each potential:
1. dU = T dS − P dV → (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V
2. dH = T dS + V dP → (∂T/∂P)_S = (∂V/∂S)_P
3. dF = −S dT − P dV → (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V
4. dG = −S dT + V dP → (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P

steps.title: TdS equations
steps.body:
Writing S(T,V) and S(T,P) and using relations 3 and 4:
- T dS = Cv dT + T(∂P/∂T)_V dV (first TdS equation)
- T dS = Cp dT − T(∂V/∂T)_P dP (second TdS equation)

Equating them gives the general result
**Cp − Cv = T V α² / κ_T**, with α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)_P (expansivity) and κ_T = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)_T (isothermal compressibility). Since κ_T > 0, Cp ≥ Cv always.

steps.title: Solved: ideal-gas check
steps.body:
For PV = RT (1 mol): α = 1/T, κ_T = 1/P.
Cp − Cv = T V (1/T²)/(1/P) = PV/T = **R** ✓ — Mayer's relation is a special case.

steps.title: Solved: energy equation
steps.body:
From dU = T dS − P dV and Maxwell 3: (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P.
- Ideal gas: T(R/V) − P = 0 → U independent of V.
- van der Waals (P = RT/(V−b) − a/V²): (∂U/∂V)_T = **a/V²** > 0, so a real gas cools on free expansion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Losing the minus signs in relations 1 and 4 — derive, don't memorise blindly.
- Mixing up which variable is held constant; the held variable is the partner from the same potential.
- Using Cp − Cv = R for solids or liquids, where Cp − Cv is small and given by TVα²/κ_T.

statements.s: (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V follows from dF.
statements.why: dF = −S dT − P dV; equating mixed partials gives this relation.

statements.s: For a van der Waals gas (∂U/∂V)_T = 0.
statements.why: It equals a/V², which is positive because of molecular attraction.

statements.s: Cp can be smaller than Cv for a stable substance.
statements.why: Cp − Cv = TVα²/κ_T and κ_T > 0 for stability, so Cp ≥ Cv.

statements.s: For water at 4 °C, where α = 0, Cp = Cv.
statements.why: With zero expansivity the difference TVα²/κ_T vanishes.

quiz.q: Maxwell relation from dG is:
quiz.why: dG = −S dT + V dP, and cross-differentiating −S and V gives −(∂S/∂P)_T = (∂V/∂T)_P.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, α equals:
quiz.why: V = RT/P gives (∂V/∂T)_P = R/P = V/T, so α = (1/V)(V/T) = 1/T.

quiz.q: (∂U/∂V)_T for a van der Waals gas is:
quiz.why: Using T(∂P/∂T)_V − P with P = RT/(V−b) − a/V² leaves a/V².

scenes.text: At a Himalayan camp the water boils well below 100 °C and the dal never cooks properly.
A pressure cooker raises the pressure and the boiling point. Clausius–Clapeyron gives the slope.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
On the coexistence curve g₁(T,P) = g₂(T,P). Moving along it, dg₁ = dg₂:
−s₁ dT + v₁ dP = −s₂ dT + v₂ dP
→ dP/dT = (s₂ − s₁)/(v₂ − v₁). With s₂ − s₁ = L/T:

**dP/dT = L / [T (v₂ − v₁)]** (L, v per kg or per mole consistently).

steps.title: Solved: boiling water
steps.body:
At 373 K: L = 2.26×10⁶ J/kg, v_steam = 1.67 m³/kg, v_water = 0.001 m³/kg.
- dT/dP = T Δv / L = 373 × 1.669 / 2.26×10⁶ = **2.75×10⁻⁴ K/Pa**
- Per atmosphere (1.013×10⁵ Pa): ≈ 28 K/atm as a local slope. (The curve flattens, so a cooker at +1 atm reaches about 120 °C, not 128 °C.)

steps.title: Solved: melting ice under pressure
steps.body:
At 273 K: L = 3.34×10⁵ J/kg, v_water = 1.000×10⁻³, v_ice = 1.091×10⁻³ m³/kg.
- dT/dP = 273 × (−9.1×10⁻⁵)/3.34×10⁵ = **−7.4×10⁻⁸ K/Pa** ≈ −0.0075 K/atm.
- Ice expands on freezing, so pressure LOWERS its melting point — but only slightly.

steps.title: Order of a transition (Ehrenfest)
steps.body:
- **First order**: first derivatives of G (S, V) jump → latent heat and volume change (melting, boiling).
- **Second order**: G and its first derivatives continuous, second derivatives (Cp, α, κ_T) jump — e.g. superconducting transition at zero field, He I → He II (λ-point, strictly a continuous transition with a logarithmic Cp).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing per-mole L with per-kg volumes.
- Using the slope over large pressure ranges; integrate with v_g ≈ RT/P for vapour instead: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(L/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
- Claiming skating works only because of pressure melting; the effect is far too small (surface premelting and friction heating matter more).

activity.prompt: Using dT/dP = 2.75×10⁻⁴ K/Pa for water near 100 °C, by how many kelvin does the boiling point rise if the pressure increases by 1.0×10⁴ Pa?

quiz.q: Along a coexistence curve, the two phases have equal:
quiz.why: Phase equilibrium at given T and P requires equal molar Gibbs free energies, which is the starting point of the Clausius–Clapeyron derivation.

quiz.q: The melting point of ice decreases with pressure because:
quiz.why: Water occupies less volume than ice, so v₂ − v₁ < 0 and dT/dP is negative.

quiz.q: A second-order transition (Ehrenfest) shows a discontinuity in:
quiz.why: In a second-order transition G, S and V are continuous while second derivatives such as Cp jump.

lessons.title: Lab: Joule–Thomson expansion and inversion temperature

scenes.text: Oxygen plants liquefy air by forcing compressed gas through a valve, again and again.
Each throttling step cools the gas a little — if it starts below its inversion temperature.

steps.title: Porous-plug experiment
steps.body:
Gas at P₁ is pushed steadily through a porous plug to lower P₂ in an insulated pipe. Work done on the gas P₁V₁ − P₂V₂ plus Q = 0 gives U₁ + P₁V₁ = U₂ + P₂V₂: **enthalpy is constant** (isenthalpic, irreversible).

Joule–Thomson coefficient μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)_H = (1/Cp)[T(∂V/∂T)_P − V]. Ideal gas: μ_JT = 0.

steps.title: van der Waals result
steps.body:
At low pressure a van der Waals gas gives μ_JT ≈ (1/Cp)(2a/RT − b).
- Cooling (μ > 0) when T < T_i = **2a/(Rb)** (attraction dominates).
- Heating when T > T_i (repulsion/finite size dominates).
Hydrogen and helium have very low T_i, so they must be pre-cooled before throttling.

steps.title: Solved: nitrogen
steps.body:
N₂: a = 0.137 Pa·m⁶/mol², b = 3.87×10⁻⁵ m³/mol.
T_i = 2 × 0.137 / (8.314 × 3.87×10⁻⁵) = 0.274 / 3.218×10⁻⁴ = **≈ 850 K**.
The measured value (about 620 K) is lower — the van der Waals model is only qualitative — but either way room-temperature N₂ cools on throttling.

steps.title: Procedure (demonstration set-up)
steps.body:
1. Pass the gas through the plug at a steady flow.
2. Record P₁, P₂ with gauges and T₁, T₂ with thermocouples on both sides.
3. Repeat for several ΔP; plot ΔT against ΔP — the slope is μ_JT.
4. Repeat at a higher inlet temperature to see μ_JT shrink.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling J–T expansion adiabatic reversible; it is irreversible and isenthalpic, not isentropic.
- Expecting cooling for every gas; above T_i the gas warms.
- Confusing it with free (Joule) expansion, where U (not H) is constant.

activity.prompt: Using van der Waals constants a = 0.364 Pa·m⁶/mol² and b = 4.27×10⁻⁵ m³/mol (CO₂), estimate the inversion temperature 2a/(Rb) in kelvin (R = 8.314).

quiz.q: In the Joule–Thomson process the conserved quantity is:
quiz.why: The flow-work balance gives U₁ + P₁V₁ = U₂ + P₂V₂, so enthalpy is unchanged across the plug.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas μ_JT is:
quiz.why: For an ideal gas T(∂V/∂T)_P = V, so the bracket in μ_JT vanishes and there is no temperature change.

quiz.q: Hydrogen must be pre-cooled before J–T liquefaction because:
options: its inversion temperature is far below room temperature
quiz.why: Above its low inversion temperature (about 200 K) hydrogen warms on throttling, so it must first be cooled below T_i.

questions.q: dF equals:
questions.why: F = U − TS gives dF = dU − T dS − S dT = −S dT − P dV.

questions.q: Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)_T equals:
questions.why: It follows from the exactness of dF = −S dT − P dV.

questions.q: Cp − Cv in general equals:
questions.why: Equating the two TdS equations gives Cp − Cv = TVα²/κ_T.

questions.q: Latent heat is a signature of a transition of:
questions.why: A jump in entropy between phases means a latent heat, the hallmark of a first-order transition.

questions.q: Clausius–Clapeyron equation:
questions.why: Equating dg along the coexistence curve and using Δs = L/T gives dP/dT = L/(TΔv).

questions.q: Pressure lowers the melting point of ice by about:
Van der Waals inversion temperature is:
questions.why: Setting 2a/RT − b = 0 gives T_i = 2a/(Rb).

questions.q: −ΔG at constant T and P equals:
questions.why: The decrease of G is the maximum useful work other than P dV work available at fixed T and P.

questions.q: (∂U/∂V)_T for a van der Waals gas:
questions.why: The energy equation T(∂P/∂T)_V − P leaves a/V² for van der Waals.

questions.q: ΔG for isothermal compression of 1 mol ideal gas from 1 to 10 bar at 300 K is about:
Joule–Thomson expansion is:
questions.why: Throttling keeps H constant but generates entropy, so it is irreversible.

questions.q: The local slope dT/dP of water's boiling curve at 100 °C is about:

courses.title: Unit 4 · Kinetic theory of gases and real gases
courses.summary: Pressure from molecular collisions, Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution and characteristic speeds, law of equipartition and specific heats, mean free path, transport phenomena (viscosity, thermal conduction, diffusion), van der Waals gas and critical constants.
outcomes: Derive P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩ and relate kinetic energy to temperature
Use the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution to find v_mp, ⟨v⟩ and v_rms
Apply equipartition to predict Cv and γ, and state where it fails
Compute mean free path and explain its pressure and temperature dependence
Relate viscosity, conductivity and diffusion to λ and ⟨v⟩
Derive critical constants of a van der Waals gas

lessons.title: Pressure of an ideal gas and molecular speeds

scenes.text: A balloon left on the terrace at noon swells tight. Nothing was blown in — the molecules just hit the walls harder.
Kinetic theory turns that picture into P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body:
- Molecules are point particles in random motion; their own volume is negligible.
- No forces except during brief elastic collisions.
- Large numbers, so averages are meaningful; Newtonian mechanics holds.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
A molecule hitting a wall normal to x transfers 2mvₓ. In a cube of side L it returns every 2L/vₓ, so its average force is mvₓ²/L. Summing over N molecules: F = (Nm/L)⟨vₓ²⟩. With ⟨vₓ²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3 (isotropy):

P = (1/3)(Nm/V)⟨v²⟩ = **(1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩**.

Compare with PV = Nk_BT: (1/2)m⟨v²⟩ = **(3/2)k_BT**. Temperature measures the mean translational KE. v_rms = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M).

steps.title: Solved: rms speed of nitrogen
steps.body:
N₂ at 300 K, M = 0.028 kg/mol:
v_rms = √(3 × 8.314 × 300 / 0.028) = √(2.672×10⁵) = **517 m/s** — faster than sound in air (≈ 346 m/s), as expected since sound speed = √(γRT/M).

steps.title: Solved: KE per molecule
steps.body: Mean translational KE at 27 °C: (3/2)k_BT = 1.5 × 1.381×10⁻²³ × 300 = **6.21×10⁻²¹ J** ≈ 0.039 eV, independent of the gas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M in g/mol in √(3RT/M); it must be kg/mol.
- Thinking heavier gases have higher mean KE; at the same T all have equal mean KE, heavier ones move slower.
- Writing ⟨v⟩² for ⟨v²⟩ — the mean of the square is larger than the square of the mean.

activity.prompt: Find v_rms of hydrogen molecules (M = 0.002 kg/mol) at 300 K in m/s (R = 8.314).

quiz.q: In kinetic theory, the pressure of a gas is P =
quiz.why: Momentum transfer to the walls averaged over three equivalent directions gives P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩.

quiz.q: Mean translational KE per molecule is:
quiz.why: Equating (1/3)Nm⟨v²⟩ with Nk_BT gives (1/2)m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT.

quiz.q: If T is quadrupled, v_rms becomes:
quiz.why: v_rms is proportional to √T, so increasing T fourfold doubles the rms speed.

scenes.text: In a marathon a few runners sprint ahead and a few lag; most are near the middle.
Gas molecules spread out the same way, and Maxwell found the exact curve in 1860.

steps.title: The distribution
steps.body:
Fraction of molecules with speeds between v and v + dv:

f(v) dv = 4π (m/2πk_BT)^(3/2) v² e^(−mv²/2k_BT) dv

The v² factor (volume of a velocity shell) makes f(0) = 0; the exponential kills high speeds. ∫₀^∞ f(v) dv = 1. Raising T flattens the curve and shifts the peak right, keeping the area 1.

steps.title: Three characteristic speeds
steps.body:
- Most probable (df/dv = 0): v_mp = √(2k_BT/m)
- Mean: ⟨v⟩ = √(8k_BT/πm)
- rms: v_rms = √(3k_BT/m)

Ratio v_mp : ⟨v⟩ : v_rms = 1 : 1.128 : 1.225.

steps.title: Why the Moon has no atmosphere
steps.body: Escape speed from the Moon is 2.4 km/s. Even if typical speeds are lower, the high-speed tail of the Maxwell distribution keeps leaking molecules away over geological time. Earth (11.2 km/s) retains N₂ and O₂ but has lost most of its primordial hydrogen and helium.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ordering the speeds wrongly: v_mp < ⟨v⟩ < v_rms always.
- Forgetting the v² factor and treating f(v) as a plain Gaussian centred at zero (that is the distribution of one velocity component vₓ).
- Assuming all molecules have speed v_rms.

activity.prompt: For a gas whose most probable speed is 400 m/s, what is the rms speed in m/s? (v_rms/v_mp = √(3/2))

quiz.q: The correct order of speeds is:
quiz.why: The ratio 1 : 1.128 : 1.225 shows the most probable speed is smallest and rms largest.

quiz.q: As temperature increases, the Maxwell speed peak:
options: shifts to higher v and lowers
quiz.why: v_mp ∝ √T moves right, and since the area stays 1 the broader curve has a lower peak.

quiz.q: The v² factor in f(v) arises from:
options: the volume of a spherical shell in velocity space
quiz.why: All velocity vectors of magnitude v lie on a shell of area 4πv², which multiplies the Gaussian factor.

lessons.title: Equipartition, specific heats and mean free path

scenes.text: Equipartition predicted Cv = 7R/2 for hydrogen, but experiments at room temperature gave 5R/2.
The missing piece was quantum mechanics: vibrations are 'frozen out' at low temperature.

steps.title: Law of equipartition
steps.body:
In classical thermal equilibrium every quadratic term in the energy has mean value (1/2)k_BT.
- Monatomic: 3 translational → U = (3/2)RT per mole, Cv = 3R/2, γ = 5/3.
- Rigid diatomic: 3 trans + 2 rot → Cv = 5R/2, γ = 7/5.
- With vibration (kinetic + potential): +2 terms → Cv = 7R/2, γ = 9/7.
In general γ = 1 + 2/f. Dulong–Petit for solids: 6 terms per atom → Cv = 3R.

steps.title: Where it fails
steps.body: Equipartition works only when k_BT is much larger than the energy-level spacing. Vibrational levels of H₂ are spaced ~0.5 eV ≫ k_BT (0.026 eV at 300 K), so vibration does not contribute at room temperature; solids' Cv falls below 3R at low T (Einstein/Debye models).

steps.title: Mean free path
steps.body:
A molecule of diameter d sweeps a collision cylinder of cross-section σ = πd². Allowing for motion of all molecules (relative speed √2⟨v⟩):

**λ = 1/(√2 π d² n) = k_BT/(√2 π d² P)**

λ ∝ T/P. Collision frequency = ⟨v⟩/λ.

steps.title: Solved: air at STP-like conditions
steps.body:
d = 3.7×10⁻¹⁰ m, T = 300 K, P = 1.013×10⁵ Pa.
- πd² = 4.30×10⁻¹⁹ m²; √2πd²P = 6.16×10⁻¹⁴ N/m
- k_BT = 4.14×10⁻²¹ J
- λ = 4.14×10⁻²¹/6.16×10⁻¹⁴ = **6.7×10⁻⁸ m ≈ 67 nm** — about 200 molecular diameters.
- With ⟨v⟩ ≈ 475 m/s, collision rate ≈ 7×10⁹ per second.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using radius instead of diameter in σ = πd².
- Forgetting the √2 factor from relative motion.
- Thinking λ depends on molecular mass at fixed n; it depends on n and d only.

activity.prompt: Under the conditions of the solved example λ = 6.7×10⁻⁸ m at 1.013×10⁵ Pa. Find λ at the same temperature but a vacuum of 1 Pa, in millimetres.

quiz.q: γ for a gas with 6 active quadratic degrees of freedom is:

lessons.title: Transport phenomena and the van der Waals gas

scenes.text: Thomas Andrews (1869) squeezed CO₂ at 35 °C and it refused to turn liquid at any pressure.
Below 31 °C it liquefied easily. He had discovered the critical temperature.

steps.title: Transport coefficients
steps.body:
Molecules carry momentum, energy and mass over a distance ≈ λ before colliding. Elementary kinetic theory gives:
- Viscosity η = (1/3) ρ ⟨v⟩ λ
- Thermal conductivity K = (1/3) ρ ⟨v⟩ λ c_v (c_v per kg) → K = η c_v
- Diffusion D = (1/3) ⟨v⟩ λ → D = η/ρ

Since ρλ is independent of pressure, **η and K of a gas do not depend on pressure** (Maxwell's surprising prediction, confirmed experimentally) and grow as √T.

steps.title: van der Waals equation
steps.body:
(P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT per mole.
- a/V² corrects for intermolecular attraction (reduces wall pressure).
- b ≈ 4 × (volume of molecules per mole) corrects for finite size.

Critical point: inflection with dP/dV = d²P/dV² = 0 gives
V_c = 3b, T_c = 8a/(27Rb), P_c = a/(27b²), and P_cV_c/RT_c = 3/8 = 0.375 (real gases ≈ 0.27–0.30).

steps.title: Andrews' isotherms
steps.body: Below T_c an isotherm has a flat liquid–vapour coexistence section; the van der Waals curve instead wiggles, and Maxwell's equal-area construction replaces the wiggle with the flat line. Above T_c no liquefaction occurs at any pressure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a gas's viscosity rises with pressure like a liquid's; for a dilute gas it is pressure-independent.
- Swapping the factors in T_c = 8a/(27Rb).
- Using litres and atm values of a, b with R = 8.314 J/mol·K — keep SI units throughout.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Thermal radiation, revision, practicals & exam
courses.summary: Blackbody radiation, Kirchhoff's law, Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien laws, Rayleigh–Jeans and Planck's law; standard practicals (Lee's disc conductivity, Stefan's law check) and a formula sheet with previous-year-style problems and a full-paper exam.
outcomes: State Kirchhoff's law and the properties of a perfect blackbody
Use Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien displacement laws in numericals
Obtain the Rayleigh–Jeans and Wien limits from Planck's law

Revise the whole Thermal Physics paper with a formula sheet and mixed problems

lessons.title: Blackbody radiation: Kirchhoff, Stefan and Wien

scenes.text: A village blacksmith judges iron by colour: dull red, then orange, then yellow-white as it heats.
He is reading Wien's displacement law with his eyes.

steps.title: Blackbody and Kirchhoff's law
steps.body:
A **blackbody** absorbs all radiation falling on it (absorptivity a = 1). A small hole in a cavity with blackened walls is a practical blackbody (Ferry's or Wien's cavity).

**Kirchhoff's law**: at a given temperature and wavelength, emissive power / absorptivity is the same for all bodies and equals the blackbody emissive power: e_λ/a_λ = E_λ(black). Good absorbers are good emitters.

steps.title: Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien laws
steps.body:
- Total power radiated per unit area: **E = σT⁴**, σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. A grey body: E = εσT⁴.
- Net loss to surroundings at T₀: P = εσA(T⁴ − T₀⁴).
- **Wien displacement**: λ_max T = b = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K.
- Energy density u = (4σ/c)T⁴; radiation pressure = u/3.

steps.title: Solved: temperature of the Sun
steps.body:
Sunlight peaks near λ_max = 500 nm.
T = b/λ_max = 2.898×10⁻³/5.0×10⁻⁷ = **5800 K** (surface temperature ≈ 5770 K).

steps.title: Solved: heat loss from a person
steps.body:
Skin at 310 K, ε = 0.97, area 1.8 m², room walls at 298 K.
- T⁴ − T₀⁴ = 9.235×10⁹ − 7.886×10⁹ = 1.349×10⁹ K⁴
- P = 0.97 × 5.67×10⁻⁸ × 1.8 × 1.349×10⁹ = **≈ 134 W** — comparable to the body's resting metabolic rate, which is why clothing matters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in T⁴ (catastrophic: 37⁴ vs 310⁴).
- Forgetting that the body also absorbs from the surroundings; use T⁴ − T₀⁴.
- Confusing Wien's displacement law with Wien's radiation formula.

activity.prompt: The Earth's thermal emission peaks near λ_max = 10 µm. Using b = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K, find the corresponding temperature in kelvin.

quiz.q: If the absolute temperature of a blackbody doubles, its radiated power becomes:
quiz.why: Power is proportional to T⁴ and 2⁴ = 16.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's law implies that:
quiz.why: The ratio e/a is universal, so a body with high absorptivity at a wavelength also has high emissivity there.

quiz.q: As temperature rises, λ_max:
quiz.why: λ_max = b/T, so hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths, shifting from red towards blue.

scenes.text: Classical physics predicted that a warm oven should emit infinite energy at short wavelengths.
In 1900 Planck rescued physics by assuming energy comes in quanta hν — the birth of quantum theory.

steps.title: Planck's radiation law
steps.body:
Energy density per unit wavelength:

u(λ,T) dλ = (8πhc/λ⁵) · 1/(e^(hc/λk_BT) − 1) dλ

In frequency: u(ν,T) dν = (8πhν³/c³) · 1/(e^(hν/k_BT) − 1) dν.

Idea: number of cavity modes per unit volume = 8πν²dν/c³; average energy per mode = hν/(e^(hν/kT) − 1) instead of the classical k_BT.

steps.title: The two limits
steps.body:
- Long λ (hc/λkT ≪ 1): e^x − 1 ≈ x → u = 8πk_BT/λ⁴ — **Rayleigh–Jeans law**, which diverges as λ → 0 (ultraviolet catastrophe).
- Short λ (x ≫ 1): u ≈ (8πhc/λ⁵) e^(−hc/λkT) — **Wien's law**.

Integrating Planck's law over all λ gives the T⁴ law with σ = 2π⁵k⁴/(15c²h³); setting du/dλ = 0 gives λ_maxT = hc/(4.965k) = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K.

steps.title: Solved: which regime?
steps.body:
For λ = 1 mm at T = 300 K: x = hc/λkT = (6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸)/(10⁻³ × 1.381×10⁻²³ × 300) = 1.988×10⁻²⁵/4.143×10⁻²⁴ = **0.048** ≪ 1 → Rayleigh–Jeans works well (microwave/radio astronomy uses it).
For λ = 500 nm at 300 K: x ≈ 96 → deep Wien regime, emission negligible.

steps.title: Cosmic microwave background
steps.body: The CMB is the most perfect blackbody spectrum ever measured, with T = 2.725 K; by Wien's law its peak lies near 1.06 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing λ⁴ in the Planck wavelength form; it is λ⁵ (λ⁴ appears in Rayleigh–Jeans).
- Assuming the peak in ν-form occurs at c/λ_max; the frequency and wavelength peaks are not related by ν = c/λ.

statements.s: Rayleigh–Jeans law agrees with experiment at long wavelengths.
statements.why: In the limit hc/λkT ≪ 1 Planck's law reduces to it.

statements.s: Planck assumed oscillator energies are multiples of hν.
statements.why: Quantising energy gives mean energy hν/(e^(hν/kT) − 1).

statements.s: Wien's formula fails at short wavelengths.
statements.why: Wien's formula is the short-wavelength limit; it fails at long wavelengths.

statements.s: Integrating Planck's law over all wavelengths gives a T⁴ dependence.
statements.why: The integral yields the Stefan–Boltzmann law.

quiz.q: The ultraviolet catastrophe refers to the failure of:
quiz.why: Rayleigh–Jeans predicts energy density growing as 1/λ⁴, which diverges at short wavelengths.

quiz.q: Mean energy per mode in Planck's theory is:
quiz.why: Averaging quantised energies nhν with Boltzmann weights gives hν/(e^(hν/kT) − 1).

quiz.q: Peak of the 2.725 K CMB spectrum (in wavelength) lies near:

lessons.title: Lab: thermal conductivity of a bad conductor by Lee's disc

scenes.text: Your lab partner wants to know whether cardboard or ebonite is the better insulator for a hot-box project.
Lee's disc gives a number in W/m·K for each.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Measure the specimen thickness d (screw gauge, several places) and disc radius r (vernier).
2. Place the specimen between the steam chamber and the brass disc; pass steam.
3. Wait for steady state: thermometers T₁ (steam side) and T₂ (disc) constant for 10 min.
4. Remove the specimen; heat the disc directly about 10 °C above T₂.
5. Let it cool in air; record temperature every 30 s through T₂.
6. Plot the cooling curve; find slope dT/dt at T₂.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
At steady state heat conducted through the specimen = heat lost by the disc at T₂:

K π r² (T₁ − T₂)/d = m s (dT/dt)|_T₂

→ **K = m s (dT/dt) d / [π r² (T₁ − T₂)]** (simplified form, ignoring the small correction for the disc's curved surface).

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why must the specimen be thin and wide? So that heat flow is one-dimensional and edge losses are small.
- Why find dT/dt exactly at T₂? The steady-state loss rate depends on the disc temperature.
- Why is the method unsuitable for metals? With large K, T₁ − T₂ would be too small to measure accurately (use Searle's method instead).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking readings before steady state is reached.
- Using the slope at room temperature instead of at T₂.
- Forgetting to convert d from mm to m.

activity.prompt: In a Lee's disc run: m = 0.90 kg, s = 380 J/kg·K, dT/dt at T₂ = 0.012 K/s, d = 2.5 mm, r = 0.06 m, T₁ − T₂ = 15 K. Find K in W/m·K.

quiz.q: In Lee's method the disc's rate of heat loss is found from:
quiz.why: The slope of the cooling curve at the steady temperature T₂ times m s gives the rate at which the disc loses heat.

quiz.q: Lee's disc is suitable for:
options: poor conductors like ebonite or cardboard
quiz.why: Poor conductors give a measurable temperature drop across a thin specimen, which the method needs.

quiz.q: Steady state means:
options: the disc is at room temperature
quiz.why: At steady state the heat flowing in equals the heat lost, so the thermometer readings remain constant.

lessons.title: Revision: formula sheet and previous-year-style problems

scenes.text: Priya has one evening left before her Thermal Physics exam and a pile of notes.
One sheet of formulas, a few classic problems, and she is ready.

steps.title: Formula sheet I — laws and processes
steps.body:
- dU = δQ − δW; W_iso = nRT ln(V₂/V₁); PV^γ = const; W_ad = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ−1)
- Cp − Cv = R (ideal); = TVα²/κ_T (general)
- η_Carnot = 1 − T₂/T₁; COP_ref = T₂/(T₁ − T₂)
- dS = δQ_rev/T; ΔS_ideal = nCv ln(T₂/T₁) + nR ln(V₂/V₁)

steps.title: Formula sheet II — potentials, kinetic theory, radiation
steps.body:
- dH = TdS + VdP; dF = −SdT − PdV; dG = −SdT + VdP; four Maxwell relations
- dP/dT = L/(TΔv); μ_JT = (1/Cp)[T(∂V/∂T)_P − V]; T_i = 2a/Rb
- v_mp : ⟨v⟩ : v_rms = √2 : √(8/π) : √3 (× √(kT/m)); λ = 1/(√2πd²n)
- T_c = 8a/27Rb, P_c = a/27b², V_c = 3b
- E = σT⁴; λ_maxT = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K

steps.title: Problem 1 (5 marks)
steps.body:
A reversible engine works between 227 °C and 27 °C and rejects 1200 J per cycle. Find the work per cycle.
- T₁ = 500 K, T₂ = 300 K; Q₁ = Q₂T₁/T₂ = 1200 × 5/3 = 2000 J
- W = Q₁ − Q₂ = **800 J**

steps.title: Problem 2 (5 marks)
steps.body:
At what temperature is v_rms of O₂ equal to v_rms of H₂ at 27 °C?
- v_rms ∝ √(T/M) → T_O₂/32 = 300/2 → T = **4800 K**

steps.title: Problem 3 (long answer outline)
steps.body: 'Derive the Clausius–Clapeyron equation and use it to explain the working of a pressure cooker.' Outline: (i) equal g on coexistence curve; (ii) dg = −s dT + v dP for each phase; (iii) Δs = L/T; (iv) dP/dT = L/TΔv > 0 for boiling, so higher P → higher boiling point → faster cooking.

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body: Long questions usually ask for one derivation (Carnot efficiency, Maxwell relations, Clausius–Clapeyron, P = ρ⟨v²⟩/3, Planck limits) plus one numerical. Write assumptions, draw the P–V or T–S diagram, and box final answers with units.

uni-bsc-phy-waves-oscillations.title: B.Sc. Physics · Waves & Oscillations
uni-bsc-phy-waves-oscillations.description: Simple harmonic motion, damped and forced oscillations, superposition and coupled oscillators, wave motion, standing waves, acoustics and Fourier analysis, with the standard practicals and exam practice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. Physics (Hons./Programme) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Simple Harmonic Motion
courses.summary: The differential equation of SHM and its solution, phase, energy, spring–mass and pendulum systems, combinations of springs, and the LC circuit as an electrical oscillator.
outcomes: Write and solve the SHM differential equation with initial conditions
Compute displacement, velocity, acceleration and energy at any instant
Find periods of spring, pendulum and LC systems
Map mechanical oscillators onto electrical analogues

scenes.text: Struck lightly, a tuning fork hums at exactly 256 Hz whether you hit it softly or hard.
That amplitude-independent frequency is the signature of simple harmonic motion.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A system executes SHM when its restoring force is proportional to displacement: F = −kx. Newton's law gives ẍ + ω²x = 0 with ω = √(k/m). General solution x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), where A (amplitude) and φ (initial phase) come from initial conditions. Period T = 2π/ω, independent of A.

steps.title: Velocity and acceleration
steps.body: v = −Aω sin(ωt + φ) = ±ω√(A² − x²); a = −ω²x. Velocity leads displacement by π/2; acceleration is π out of phase with displacement. v_max = Aω at x = 0; a_max = Aω² at x = ±A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing f and ω (ω = 2πf); assuming every periodic motion is SHM (a bouncing ball is periodic but not SHM); forgetting that a = −ω²x needs x in metres for a in m/s².

activity.prompt: A particle in SHM has amplitude 0.1 m and period 0.5 s. Its maximum speed (m/s)?

quiz.q: In SHM the acceleration is:
options: Proportional to x and opposite to it
quiz.why: From ẍ = −ω²x, the acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium.

quiz.q: Velocity in SHM leads displacement by:
quiz.why: Differentiating cos gives −sin = cos(θ + π/2), a quarter-cycle lead.

quiz.q: The period of SHM depends on:
quiz.why: T = 2π/ω is fixed by the system (k and m), not by how it is started.

scenes.text: A child on a swing is momentarily still at the top and fastest at the bottom.
Energy sloshes between potential and kinetic, twice every cycle, while the total stays fixed.

steps.title: Energy expressions
steps.body: U = ½kx² = ½kA² cos²(ωt + φ); K = ½mv² = ½kA² sin²(ωt + φ) = ½k(A² − x²). Total E = ½kA² = ½mω²A², constant. Energy ∝ A² and ∝ ω².

steps.title: Time averages
steps.body: Over a cycle ⟨cos²⟩ = ⟨sin²⟩ = ½, so ⟨K⟩ = ⟨U⟩ = E/2. Both K and U oscillate at 2ω — twice the oscillator's frequency.

steps.title: Worked example: from energy to speed
steps.body: A 0.5 kg mass on the same spring: v_max = √(2E/m) = √4 = 2 m/s. Check: ω = √(200/0.5) = 20 rad/s, Aω = 2 m/s. ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying K = U at x = A/2 (at A/2, U is only a quarter of E); forgetting that doubling amplitude quadruples energy.

activity.prompt: For SHM of amplitude 0.2 m, at what displacement (m) are kinetic and potential energies equal?

quiz.q: Total energy of SHM is proportional to:
quiz.why: E = ½kA², so energy scales with the square of amplitude.

quiz.q: Kinetic energy in SHM oscillates at frequency:
quiz.why: sin² has half the period of sin, so K repeats twice per cycle.

quiz.q: At x = A/2, the fraction of energy that is kinetic is:
quiz.why: U = ½k(A/2)² = E/4, so K = 3E/4.

scenes.text: A motorcycle's front forks hold two springs side by side; a train buffer stacks springs end to end.
How springs are combined changes the stiffness — and the bounce frequency.

steps.title: Spring–mass systems
steps.body: T = 2π√(m/k). Parallel springs: k = k₁ + k₂. Series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. A vertical spring has the same T as a horizontal one: gravity only shifts the equilibrium by mg/k. Cutting a spring in half doubles k.

steps.title: Pendulums
steps.body: Simple pendulum: torque −mgl sinθ ≈ −mglθ for small θ, giving T = 2π√(l/g). Compound pendulum: T = 2π√(I/(mgh)) = 2π√((k² + h²)/(gh)). Torsion pendulum: T = 2π√(I/C).

steps.title: Worked example: springs
steps.body: m = 0.5 kg, k = 50 N/m: T = 2π√0.01 = 0.628 s. Two such springs in parallel: k = 100, T = 0.444 s. In series: k = 25, T = 0.889 s.

steps.title: Worked example: seconds pendulum
steps.body: A seconds pendulum has T = 2 s: l = gT²/4π² = 9.8 × 4/39.48 ≈ 0.993 m. On the Moon (g ≈ 1.62 m/s²) the same pendulum would have T = 2π√(0.993/1.62) ≈ 4.92 s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Swapping series and parallel formulas (springs are opposite to resistors); applying T = 2π√(l/g) to large amplitudes, where T increases (about 0.4% longer at 15°).

activity.prompt: Springs of 100 N/m and 300 N/m are joined in series and carry 0.75 kg. Period of oscillation (s)?

quiz.q: Two identical springs k in parallel have effective constant:
quiz.why: Parallel springs share the load at equal extension, so their stiffnesses add.

quiz.q: A spring cut into two equal halves; each half has constant:
quiz.why: Each half stretches half as much under the same force, so its stiffness doubles.

quiz.q: A vertical spring–mass oscillator has period:
quiz.why: Gravity only moves the equilibrium position; the restoring force about it is still −kx.

scenes.text: Turning an old radio's dial changes a variable capacitor in an LC circuit.
Charge oscillates between capacitor and inductor exactly like a mass on a spring.

steps.title: LC oscillations
steps.body: Kirchhoff's loop: L dI/dt + q/C = 0 with I = dq/dt → q̈ + q/(LC) = 0. So q = Q₀ cos(ω₀t + φ) with ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Energy oscillates between the capacitor (q²/2C) and inductor (½LI²); total Q₀²/2C is constant (no resistance).

steps.title: Analogy table
steps.body: x ↔ q, v ↔ I, m ↔ L, k ↔ 1/C, damping b ↔ R, force F ↔ emf. Kinetic energy ½mv² ↔ magnetic energy ½LI²; potential ½kx² ↔ electric q²/2C.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: L = 10 mH, C = 1 μF: LC = 10⁻⁸ s², ω₀ = 10⁴ rad/s, f = 10⁴/2π ≈ 1592 Hz. If Q₀ = 5 μC: I_max = ω₀Q₀ = 0.05 A, energy = Q₀²/2C = 25 × 10⁻¹²/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = 12.5 μJ.

steps.title: Where LC circuits live
steps.body: Radio tuning circuits, oscillators in transmitters, metal detectors, and wireless charging coils all rely on LC resonance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using ω = √(LC) instead of 1/√(LC); forgetting unit prefixes (mH = 10⁻³ H, μF = 10⁻⁶ F).

activity.prompt: An LC circuit has L = 25 mH and C = 0.1 μF. Natural frequency f in Hz?

quiz.q: In the analogy, the inductance L corresponds to:
quiz.why: L dI/dt plays the role of m dv/dt, so L is the electrical inertia.

quiz.q: Natural angular frequency of an LC circuit:
quiz.why: The equation q̈ + q/(LC) = 0 gives ω₀² = 1/(LC).

quiz.q: Capacitance corresponds to:
quiz.why: The capacitor term q/C matches kx, so 1/C ↔ k.

questions.why: A linear restoring force −kx gives ẍ + (k/m)x = 0.

questions.why: v_max = Aω = 4 × 5 = 20 cm/s.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Damped & Forced Oscillations
courses.summary: Damped oscillator in its three regimes, logarithmic decrement, relaxation time and quality factor, forced oscillations, amplitude and velocity resonance, power absorption, bandwidth and the series LCR circuit.
outcomes: Solve the damped oscillator and classify under-, critical and over-damping
Compute logarithmic decrement, relaxation time and Q
Derive steady-state amplitude and phase of a driven oscillator
Relate sharpness of resonance to Q in mechanical and LCR systems

scenes.text: A car without shock absorbers bounces for many cycles after a speed-breaker; one with worn shocks bounces twice.
Good shocks bring it back smoothly with no overshoot — close to critical damping.

steps.title: Equation
steps.body: With a viscous force −bv: mẍ + bẋ + kx = 0, or ẍ + 2γẋ + ω₀²x = 0 with γ = b/2m and ω₀ = √(k/m). Trying x = e^{αt}: α = −γ ± √(γ² − ω₀²).

steps.title: Three regimes
steps.body: Underdamped (γ < ω₀): x = A₀e^{−γt} cos(ω′t + φ), ω′ = √(ω₀² − γ²) — oscillation with decaying amplitude. Critically damped (γ = ω₀): x = (A + Bt)e^{−γt}, fastest return without oscillation. Overdamped (γ > ω₀): sum of two decaying exponentials, slow non-oscillatory return.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: m = 0.5 kg, k = 50 N/m, b = 2 kg/s. ω₀ = 10 rad/s, γ = 2/(2 × 0.5) = 2 s⁻¹ < ω₀ → underdamped. ω′ = √(100 − 4) = √96 ≈ 9.80 rad/s. Amplitude falls by e in 1/γ = 0.5 s. Critical damping would need b = 2√(mk) = 2 × 5 = 10 kg/s.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Galvanometers and analogue meters are designed near critical damping so the needle settles quickly; door closers are slightly overdamped to avoid slamming.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Defining γ as b/m in some books and b/2m in others — check which convention a formula uses. The damped frequency ω′ is LOWER than ω₀, not higher.

activity.prompt: With ω₀ = 10 rad/s, classify each damping constant γ.

quiz.q: A damped oscillator returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating when:
quiz.why: Critical damping γ = ω₀ gives the quickest non-oscillatory approach.

quiz.why: The characteristic roots give an oscillatory part with ω′ = √(ω₀² − γ²).

lessons.title: Log decrement, relaxation time & Q factor

scenes.text: A temple bell rings for many seconds; a cardboard box thuds and stops at once.
The quality factor Q measures how many oscillations the energy survives.

steps.title: Measures of damping
steps.body: Amplitude A(t) = A₀e^{−γt}; energy E(t) = E₀e^{−2γt}. Relaxation time τ = 1/(2γ): energy falls to 1/e. Logarithmic decrement λ = ln(Aₙ/Aₙ₊₁) = γT′. Quality factor Q = ω₀τ = ω₀/(2γ) = 2π × (energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle), for light damping.

steps.title: Worked example: from the earlier oscillator
steps.body: ω₀ = 10 rad/s, γ = 2 s⁻¹: τ = 0.25 s, Q = 10/4 = 2.5 — heavily damped. T′ = 2π/9.80 ≈ 0.641 s, λ = 2 × 0.641 ≈ 1.28: each swing is e^{−1.28} ≈ 0.28 of the previous one.

steps.title: Worked example: half amplitude in 10 cycles
steps.body: A pendulum (T ≈ 1 s, ω₀ ≈ 2π) halves its amplitude in 10 oscillations: γ × 10 s = ln2 → γ ≈ 0.0693 s⁻¹. Q = 2π/(2 × 0.0693) ≈ 45. λ = ln2/10 ≈ 0.069.

steps.title: Typical Q values
steps.body: Car suspension ≈ 1; guitar string ≈ 10³; quartz watch crystal ≈ 10⁴–10⁵; superconducting microwave cavities exceed 10¹⁰.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Energy decays at 2γ, amplitude at γ — don't mix them. Q = ω₀/2γ assumes light damping.

activity.prompt: An oscillator with ω₀ = 400 rad/s has its amplitude decay as e^{−4t} (t in s). What is its Q?

quiz.why: ln(Aₙ/Aₙ₊₁) = ln(e^{γT′}) = γT′.

quiz.q: Relaxation time τ is the time for energy to fall to:
quiz.why: E = E₀e^{−2γt} reaches E₀/e when t = 1/(2γ) = τ.

quiz.q: A higher Q means:
quiz.why: Q = ω₀/2γ grows as γ falls, so high-Q systems ring for many cycles.

scenes.text: Marching troops are ordered to break step when crossing suspension bridges.

steps.title: Equation and steady state
steps.body: ẍ + 2γẋ + ω₀²x = (F₀/m) cos ωt. After transients die out, x = A cos(ωt − δ) with A = (F₀/m)/√((ω₀² − ω²)² + 4γ²ω²) and tanδ = 2γω/(ω₀² − ω²). The system oscillates at the DRIVER's frequency.

steps.title: Resonance
steps.body: Amplitude resonance at ω_r = √(ω₀² − 2γ²), slightly below ω₀, with A_max = F₀/(2mγ√(ω₀² − γ²)). Velocity (and power) resonance occurs exactly at ω = ω₀. Phase: δ → 0 well below resonance, π/2 at ω₀, → π well above.

steps.title: Engineering
steps.body: Machinery mounts, tall buildings (tuned mass dampers) and aircraft wings are designed to keep natural frequencies away from driving frequencies; MRI and radio receivers exploit resonance deliberately.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a driven system oscillates at ω₀ in steady state; forgetting the transient; assuming amplitude resonance is exactly at ω₀ for heavy damping.

quiz.q: Amplitude resonance frequency is:
quiz.why: Maximising A(ω) gives ω_r = √(ω₀² − 2γ²), just below ω₀.

lessons.title: Power, bandwidth & the series LCR circuit

scenes.text: Dozens of FM stations fill the air, yet the radio plays one cleanly.
A high-Q tuned circuit responds strongly only in a narrow band around its resonance.

steps.title: Average power and bandwidth
steps.body: Mean power absorbed P(ω) = (F₀²γω²/m)/((ω₀² − ω²)² + 4γ²ω²), maximum at ω₀. It falls to half at ω ≈ ω₀ ± γ (light damping), so the full width at half power Δω = 2γ and Q = ω₀/Δω.

steps.title: Series LCR
steps.body: L q̈ + R q̇ + q/C = E₀ cos ωt. Impedance Z = √(R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²). At resonance ω₀ = 1/√(LC): Z = R (minimum), current is maximum and in phase with emf. Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C). Voltage across L or C at resonance = Q × source voltage.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: L = 0.1 H, C = 10 μF, R = 10 Ω, E_rms = 5 V. ω₀ = 1/√(10⁻⁶) = 1000 rad/s, f₀ ≈ 159 Hz. Q = 1000 × 0.1/10 = 10, bandwidth Δω = 100 rad/s (≈ 15.9 Hz). I_rms = 5/10 = 0.5 A; V_L = V_C = 50 V rms — ten times the supply.

steps.title: Lab tip
steps.body: In the LCR resonance practical, plot current vs frequency, mark I_max/√2, read f₁ and f₂, and compute Q = f₀/(f₂ − f₁).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Half-POWER points correspond to I_max/√2, not I_max/2. Voltage magnification means capacitor ratings must exceed Q × supply voltage.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Superposition & Coupled Oscillators
courses.summary: Superposition of collinear harmonic oscillations of equal and unequal frequency (beats), perpendicular oscillations and Lissajous figures, and coupled pendulums with normal modes and energy exchange.
outcomes: Add collinear SHMs analytically and with phasors
Explain and calculate beat frequency
Predict Lissajous figures and read frequency ratios from them
Find normal-mode frequencies of two coupled oscillators

scenes.text: Two loudspeakers play the same tone; walking between them, the sound swells and fades.
At each point the two vibrations add with a different phase — rotating arrows (phasors) make the sum easy.

steps.title: Same frequency
steps.body: x₁ = a₁ cos ωt, x₂ = a₂ cos(ωt + δ). The sum is another SHM of the same ω: x = R cos(ωt + θ), with R² = a₁² + a₂² + 2a₁a₂ cosδ and tanθ = a₂ sinδ/(a₁ + a₂ cosδ).

steps.title: Phasor picture
steps.body: Represent each SHM by a vector of length a rotating at ω; the projection on the x-axis is the displacement. Adding SHMs = adding vectors tip-to-tail. δ = 0 gives R = a₁ + a₂ (constructive); δ = π gives |a₁ − a₂| (destructive).

steps.title: Worked example: N equal phasors
steps.body: N oscillations of amplitude a with successive phase difference δ: R = a sin(Nδ/2)/sin(δ/2). For N = 3, δ = 2π/3 the phasors form a closed triangle and R = 0 — the basis of diffraction-grating minima (optics).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding amplitudes directly when δ ≠ 0; using degrees in one place and radians in another; forgetting that superposition requires a linear system.

activity.prompt: Two SHMs of equal amplitude 5 cm and the same frequency differ in phase by 120°. Resultant amplitude (cm)?

quiz.why: With δ = π, R = |a₁ − a₂| = 0: complete cancellation.

Superposition of two same-frequency collinear SHMs is:
quiz.why: A sum of cosines of the same ω is a single cosine of that ω with new amplitude and phase.

scenes.text: A musician plucks two strings meant to be in unison and hears a slow wah-wah-wah.
She tightens one until the throbbing slows and vanishes — the beat frequency has gone to zero.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: x = a cos ω₁t + a cos ω₂t = 2a cos((ω₁ − ω₂)t/2) cos((ω₁ + ω₂)t/2). A fast oscillation at the average frequency is modulated by a slow envelope. Loudness peaks whenever the envelope's magnitude peaks, i.e. |f₁ − f₂| times per second: beat frequency f_b = |f₁ − f₂|.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz: f_b = 4 Hz, heard tone ≈ 258 Hz, loudness maxima every 0.25 s.

steps.title: Worked example: unknown fork
steps.body: An unknown fork gives 5 beats/s with a 512 Hz fork, so it is 507 or 517 Hz. Loading the unknown with wax LOWERS its frequency. If beats increase to 7/s, it moved away from 512, so it was already below: 507 Hz. If beats decreased, it was 517 Hz.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Tuning instruments, measuring small frequency differences, and the 'wow' sound of twin-engine propeller aircraft when engines run at slightly different speeds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the beat frequency is (f₁ − f₂)/2 — that is the envelope's mathematical frequency, but loudness peaks twice per envelope cycle. Beats are audible clearly only when f_b is below about 10–15 Hz.

activity.prompt: An unknown fork gives 5 beats/s with a 512 Hz fork. After loading the unknown with a little wax, beats rise to 8/s. Unknown fork's original frequency (Hz)?

quiz.q: Beat frequency of 440 Hz and 444 Hz:
quiz.why: f_b = |f₁ − f₂| = 4 Hz.

quiz.q: Filing the prongs of a tuning fork:
quiz.why: Removing mass from the prongs reduces inertia, raising the frequency, whereas loading lowers it.

quiz.q: The pitch heard during beats corresponds to:
quiz.why: The carrier oscillation is at the average frequency (f₁ + f₂)/2.

scenes.text: In the lab, one signal drives the CRO's horizontal plates and another the vertical plates.
A circle, a figure of eight, a slanted line — each pattern encodes a frequency ratio and a phase.

steps.title: Same frequency
steps.body: x = a cos ωt, y = b cos(ωt + δ). Eliminating t: x²/a² + y²/b² − (2xy/ab) cosδ = sin²δ. δ = 0: straight line y = (b/a)x. δ = π: y = −(b/a)x. δ = π/2: ellipse with axes along x and y (a circle if a = b). Other δ: tilted ellipse.

steps.title: Different frequencies
steps.body: For a rational ratio the figure closes. Reading the ratio: f_y/f_x = (number of tangent points on a horizontal edge of the bounding box)/(number on a vertical edge). Example: x = sin ωt, y = sin 2ωt gives a figure-of-eight touching the top twice and each side once → f_y : f_x = 2 : 1.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: On a CRO, an unknown signal on Y and 50 Hz on X produce a pattern touching the top edge 3 times and the side edge 1 time. f_y = 3 × 50 = 150 Hz. If the figure slowly rotates, the ratio is slightly off and the rate of rotation measures the mismatch.

steps.title: Phase measurement
steps.body: For a same-frequency ellipse, sinδ = (y-intercept)/(maximum y) = y₀/b. This is a standard way to measure phase shifts in RC circuits on a CRO.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Inverting the tangency ratio; counting a corner point as two tangencies; ignoring that an irrational ratio never closes.

scenes.text: Two pendulums are joined by a weak spring. Start one swinging and leave the other still.
Slowly the first stops and the second swings fully, then they swap back — energy flows to and fro.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body: Two identical pendulums (mass m, length l) coupled by a spring k: mẍ₁ = −(mg/l)x₁ − k(x₁ − x₂), mẍ₂ = −(mg/l)x₂ + k(x₁ − x₂). Normal coordinates q₁ = x₁ + x₂ and q₂ = x₁ − x₂ decouple them.

steps.title: Normal modes
steps.body: In-phase mode (q₁): spring never stretched, ω₁ = √(g/l). Out-of-phase mode (q₂): ω₂ = √(g/l + 2k/m), higher. Any motion is a superposition of the two modes. Starting with one bob displaced excites both equally; they beat, so energy moves completely between pendulums with exchange period T_ex = 2π/(ω₂ − ω₁).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: g/l = 9 s⁻² → ω₁ = 3.00 rad/s. If 2k/m = 0.61 s⁻², ω₂ = √9.61 = 3.10 rad/s. T_ex = 2π/0.10 ≈ 62.8 s: one pendulum goes from full swing to rest in half of that, ≈ 31 s.

steps.title: Beyond two masses
steps.body: N coupled masses have N normal modes; in the continuum limit these become the standing waves of a string, and in crystals the quantised modes are phonons.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking the coupled system has a single frequency; putting the factor 2 in the wrong mode (only the out-of-phase mode stretches the spring, by 2x).
