courses.title: Unit 4 · Wave Motion
courses.summary: The one-dimensional wave equation, travelling harmonic waves, wave speed on strings and in fluids (Newton–Laplace), energy, intensity, impedance and reflection, decibels and the Doppler effect.
outcomes: Read amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed from a wave function
Derive v = √(T/μ) and the speed of sound in gases
Compute intensity, sound level and reflection coefficients
Apply the Doppler formula for moving sources and observers

scenes.text: At a cricket match a 'Mexican wave' races around the stands at tens of metres per second.
Yet no spectator leaves their seat — the pattern travels, the medium only oscillates locally.

steps.title: The wave equation
steps.body: Any shape moving without change at speed v is y = f(x − vt) (to +x) or g(x + vt) (to −x). Both satisfy ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²y/∂t², the 1-D wave equation. Because it is linear, superposition holds.

steps.title: Harmonic waves
steps.body: y = A sin(kx − ωt + φ), wave number k = 2π/λ, angular frequency ω = 2πf, phase speed v = ω/k = fλ. Particle velocity ∂y/∂t = −Aω cos(kx − ωt) is different from wave speed. Transverse waves: particle motion ⊥ propagation (string, light); longitudinal: parallel (sound).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: y = 0.02 sin(4πx − 400πt) (SI). A = 0.02 m, k = 4π → λ = 0.5 m, ω = 400π → f = 200 Hz, v = ω/k = 100 m/s in +x. Maximum particle speed Aω = 0.02 × 400π ≈ 25.1 m/s.

steps.title: Worked example: phase difference
steps.body: For λ = 0.5 m, two points 0.125 m apart differ in phase by kΔx = 4π × 0.125 = π/2. Points one full λ apart oscillate in phase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing particle velocity with wave velocity; reading the sign wrongly — (kx − ωt) moves toward +x, (kx + ωt) toward −x.

activity.prompt: A wave is y = 0.05 sin(2πx − 680πt) in SI units. Its speed in m/s?

quiz.q: y = A sin(kx + ωt) travels:
quiz.why: Keeping kx + ωt constant as t increases requires x to decrease.

quiz.q: Wave speed equals:
quiz.why: A point of constant phase moves at dx/dt = ω/k.

quiz.q: Sound in air is a:
quiz.why: Air molecules oscillate along the direction of propagation in compressions and rarefactions.

scenes.text: Newton calculated sound's speed in air assuming constant temperature and got about 280 m/s — measured values were near 330 m/s.
Laplace realised compressions are too fast for heat to flow: the process is adiabatic.

steps.title: Transverse wave on a string
steps.body: Take a small element dx of a string with tension T and mass per length μ. The net vertical force is T(∂y/∂x)|ₓ₊dₓ − T(∂y/∂x)|ₓ = T(∂²y/∂x²)dx. Newton: μ dx ∂²y/∂t² = T ∂²y/∂x² dx → wave equation with v = √(T/μ).

steps.title: Longitudinal waves in fluids
steps.body: v = √(B/ρ), where B is the bulk modulus. Newton used isothermal B = P: v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m/s for air. Laplace's correction uses adiabatic B = γP: v = √(γP/ρ). In solids (thin rod) v = √(Y/ρ).

steps.title: Worked example: string
steps.body: Steel wire, T = 100 N, μ = 0.01 kg/m: v = √10⁴ = 100 m/s. Quadrupling tension doubles v.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking sound speed in air depends on pressure at fixed temperature (it doesn't — P/ρ stays constant); using μ in g/m without converting to kg/m.

activity.prompt: A sonometer wire has linear density 4 g/m and tension 64 N. Transverse wave speed (m/s)?

quiz.q: Laplace's correction replaces isothermal with:
quiz.why: Compressions in a sound wave happen too quickly for heat exchange, so B = γP.

quiz.q: Speed of sound in an ideal gas is proportional to:
quiz.why: v = √(γRT/M) scales as the square root of absolute temperature.

quiz.q: Doubling string tension multiplies wave speed by:
quiz.why: v = √(T/μ), so doubling T increases v by √2.

scenes.text: Before an ultrasound scan, the technician spreads gel on the skin.
Without it, an air gap would reflect almost all the sound — an impedance mismatch.

steps.title: Energy and intensity
steps.body: For a harmonic wave in a medium of density ρ, energy density averaged over time is ½ρω²A², and intensity (power per area) I = ½ρvω²A². For a string, power P = ½μvω²A². Intensity ∝ A²ω². From a point source I ∝ 1/r².

steps.title: Impedance and reflection
steps.body: Characteristic impedance: string Z = √(Tμ) = μv; fluid Z = ρv. At a boundary, amplitude reflection r = (Z₁ − Z₂)/(Z₁ + Z₂), transmission t = 2Z₁/(Z₁ + Z₂). Energy reflected fraction R = r². Matched impedances give no reflection; a fixed end (Z₂ → ∞) reflects with phase inversion.

steps.title: Worked example: reflection
steps.body: Air Z ≈ 415 kg m⁻² s⁻¹, water ≈ 1.48 × 10⁶. r ≈ (1.48 × 10⁶ − 415)/(1.48 × 10⁶ + 415) ≈ 0.9994; R ≈ 0.9989 — over 99.8% of sound energy is reflected at an air–water surface.

steps.title: Decibels
steps.body: Sound level β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀), I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². 60 dB (conversation) → I = 10⁻⁶ W/m². Doubling intensity adds ≈ 3 dB; ten times adds 10 dB. Doubling distance from a point source subtracts ≈ 6 dB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding decibel values arithmetically (two 60 dB sources make ≈ 63 dB, not 120 dB); forgetting that intensity scales with ω² as well as A².

activity.prompt: A machine produces 70 dB at a point. Ten identical machines running together produce what sound level (dB)?

quiz.q: Intensity of a wave is proportional to:
quiz.why: I = ½ρvω²A², quadratic in amplitude.

quiz.q: Reflection at a perfectly matched boundary is:
quiz.why: With Z₁ = Z₂, r = 0 and all energy is transmitted.

quiz.q: Intensity of an 80 dB sound:

scenes.text: An ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and drops in pitch the instant it passes.
The same physics lets traffic radar measure car speeds and astronomers measure stellar motion.

steps.title: General formula (sound)
steps.body: f′ = f (v + v_o)/(v − v_s), where v is sound speed in the medium, v_o the observer's speed TOWARD the source and v_s the source's speed TOWARD the observer (use negative values for motion away). A moving source changes the wavelength; a moving observer changes the rate of meeting crests.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Siren 500 Hz, ambulance at 30 m/s, v = 340 m/s, observer at rest. Approaching: 500 × 340/310 ≈ 548 Hz. Receding: 500 × 340/370 ≈ 459 Hz. The drop heard as it passes is about 89 Hz.

steps.title: Worked example: reflection from a moving car
steps.body: A stationary radar-like sound source at f hits a car approaching at u. The car receives f₁ = f(v + u)/v and re-emits as a moving source: f₂ = f₁ v/(v − u) = f(v + u)/(v − u). For u ≪ v, Δf ≈ 2fu/v.

steps.title: Light
steps.body: For light, only relative velocity matters: f′ = f√((1 + β)/(1 − β)) for approach, β = v/c. Receding galaxies show a redshift, the observational basis of Hubble's law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sign errors — decide 'toward' or 'away' for each, then check that approaching gives a HIGHER frequency. Wind changes v relative to the ground and must be included.

activity.prompt: A 600 Hz source moves toward a stationary observer at 40 m/s; sound speed 340 m/s. Frequency heard (Hz)?

quiz.why: Crests bunch up ahead of a moving source, shortening the wavelength there.

quiz.why: Motion away from us lowers the observed frequency, shifting spectral lines toward red.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Standing Waves, Acoustics & Fourier Analysis
courses.summary: Stationary waves on strings and in air columns, normal modes and harmonics, end correction and the resonance tube, phase and group velocity with dispersion, and Fourier series of periodic waveforms.
outcomes: Derive node/antinode positions and normal-mode frequencies
Analyse open and closed pipes including end correction
Distinguish phase velocity from group velocity
Expand simple periodic signals in Fourier series

scenes.text: Pluck a sitar string and lightly touch its midpoint: the low note vanishes and an octave rings out.
Touching forces a node there, killing all modes except those with a node at the middle.

steps.title: Formation
steps.body: Superpose y₁ = A sin(kx − ωt) and y₂ = A sin(kx + ωt): y = 2A sin kx cos ωt. Every point oscillates in phase (or antiphase) with amplitude 2A|sin kx|. Nodes at kx = nπ (x = nλ/2); antinodes midway. Energy does not travel along a standing wave.

steps.title: Normal modes of a string
steps.body: Fixed at x = 0 and x = L requires sin kL = 0 → L = nλ/2. Frequencies fₙ = n v/(2L) = (n/2L)√(T/μ), n = 1, 2, 3… All harmonics are present. Laws of strings: f ∝ 1/L, ∝ √T, ∝ 1/√μ.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: L = 0.6 m, v = 240 m/s: f₁ = 240/1.2 = 200 Hz; f₂ = 400 Hz; f₃ = 600 Hz. Touching at L/3 leaves modes with a node there: n = 3, 6, 9… → lowest 600 Hz.

steps.title: Melde's experiment
steps.body: A string attached to an electrically driven tuning-fork prong forms p loops over length l. Transverse arrangement (prong vibrates ⊥ string): f = (p/2l)√(T/μ). Longitudinal arrangement (prong vibrates along the string): the string vibrates at f/2, so f = (p/l)√(T/μ). Example: l = 1 m, T = 0.5 N, μ = 5 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m, p = 4 loops (transverse): f = 2 × √1000 ≈ 63.2 Hz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying nodes are λ apart (they are λ/2 apart); forgetting the factor of 2 between Melde's transverse and longitudinal arrangements.

activity.prompt: A 0.8 m string fixed at both ends has wave speed 320 m/s. Frequency of its third harmonic (Hz)?

quiz.q: Distance between adjacent nodes is:
quiz.why: Nodes occur where sin kx = 0, at x = nλ/2.

quiz.q: In a standing wave, energy:
quiz.why: Equal waves travelling in opposite directions carry equal and opposite energy flux.

quiz.q: Quadrupling string tension changes the fundamental frequency by:
quiz.why: f ∝ √T, so 4× tension gives 2× frequency.

lessons.title: Air columns, end correction & the resonance tube

scenes.text: A bamboo flute is open at both ends; covering holes changes its effective length.
A test tube (closed at one end) sounds an octave lower than an open tube of the same length — and only odd harmonics.

steps.title: Boundary conditions
steps.body: Displacement node at a closed end, antinode at an open end (pressure node). Closed pipe: L = (2n − 1)λ/4 → f = (2n − 1)v/4L — odd harmonics only. Open pipe: L = nλ/2 → f = nv/2L — all harmonics.

steps.title: End correction
steps.body: The antinode forms slightly beyond the open end, at e ≈ 0.6r (r = tube radius). Closed pipe: f = v/4(L + 0.6r). Open pipe: f = v/2(L + 1.2r).

steps.title: Resonance tube method
steps.body: A 512 Hz fork over a water-filled tube: first resonance at L₁ = 16.0 cm, second at L₂ = 49.5 cm. L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 (end correction cancels) → λ = 0.67 m, v = 512 × 0.67 ≈ 343 m/s. End correction e = (L₂ − 3L₁)/2 = (49.5 − 48)/2 = 0.75 cm.

steps.title: Worked example: pipes
steps.body: v = 340 m/s, L = 0.5 m (ignore end correction). Closed: f₁ = 340/2 = 170 Hz, next 510 Hz. Open: f₁ = 340 Hz, next 680 Hz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using L₁ = λ/4 directly (it ignores the end correction); expecting even harmonics in a closed pipe.

activity.prompt: Resonance tube with a 480 Hz fork: first resonance at 17.0 cm, second at 53.0 cm. Speed of sound (m/s)?

quiz.q: A closed pipe produces:
quiz.why: A node at one end and antinode at the other allow only L = (2n − 1)λ/4.

quiz.q: In the resonance tube, L₂ − L₁ equals:
quiz.why: Successive resonances add half a wavelength, and the end correction cancels in the difference.

quiz.q: End correction for a pipe of radius r at one open end is about:
quiz.why: Experiment and theory give the antinode about 0.6r beyond an open end.

scenes.text: Watch a wave group behind a boat on deep water: individual crests appear at the back of the group, race forward and vanish at the front.
The crests move at the phase velocity; the group — and the energy — moves at half that speed.

steps.title: Wave groups
steps.body: Add two waves of nearby ω, k: y = 2A cos(Δk x/2 − Δω t/2) sin(k̄x − ω̄t). The carrier moves at v_p = ω/k; the envelope at v_g = Δω/Δk → dω/dk. Energy and information travel at v_g (in normal media).

steps.title: Relations
steps.body: v_g = v_p + k dv_p/dk = v_p − λ dv_p/dλ. Non-dispersive medium (v_p independent of λ, e.g. sound in air, light in vacuum): v_g = v_p. Normal dispersion (dv_p/dλ > 0): v_g < v_p.

steps.title: Worked example: deep water
steps.body: Deep-water waves: ω = √(gk), so v_p = √(g/k) and v_g = dω/dk = ½√(g/k) = v_p/2. For λ = 10 m: v_p = √(9.8 × 10/2π) ≈ 3.95 m/s, v_g ≈ 1.98 m/s.

steps.title: Worked example: matter waves
steps.body: For a free particle, ω = ħk²/2m: v_p = ħk/2m but v_g = ħk/m = p/m — the group velocity is the particle's classical velocity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Concluding relativity is violated when v_p > c (e.g. in waveguides or plasma) — signals travel at v_g < c. Using Δω/Δk for widely different components.

activity.prompt: Match each wave to its v_g/v_p ratio.

quiz.q: Group velocity is defined as:
quiz.why: The envelope's speed is Δω/Δk, which becomes dω/dk in the limit.

quiz.q: In a non-dispersive medium:
quiz.why: If v_p is independent of k then ω = v_p k and dω/dk = v_p.

quiz.q: Energy in a wave packet travels at:
quiz.why: Energy is concentrated in the envelope, which moves at the group velocity.

scenes.text: A harmonium and a flute both play 'Sa' at 261.6 Hz, yet you can tell them apart instantly.
Their waveforms contain the same fundamental but different mixtures of harmonics.

steps.title: Fourier's theorem
steps.body: Any reasonable periodic function of period T = 2π/ω can be written f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ[aₙ cos nωt + bₙ sin nωt], with aₙ = (2/T)∫ f(t) cos nωt dt and bₙ = (2/T)∫ f(t) sin nωt dt over one period. Even functions have only cosines; odd functions only sines.

steps.title: Worked example: square wave
steps.body: f = +1 for 0 < ωt < π, −1 for π < ωt < 2π (odd). bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nθ dθ (doubling for symmetry) = (2/nπ)(1 − cos nπ) → 4/(nπ) for odd n, 0 for even. f = (4/π)[sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + …]; b₁ ≈ 1.273, b₃ ≈ 0.424.

steps.title: Worked example: sawtooth
steps.body: f(θ) = θ for −π < θ < π (odd): bₙ = 2(−1)^(n+1)/n. f = 2[sin θ − ½ sin 2θ + ⅓ sin 3θ − …]. Both odd and even harmonics appear, falling as 1/n.

steps.title: Gibbs phenomenon
steps.body: Near a jump, partial Fourier sums overshoot by about 9% of the jump, however many terms are taken; the overshoot narrows but does not shrink.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting a₀/2 for signals with a DC offset; integrating over the wrong interval; assuming a square wave contains even harmonics.

activity.prompt: For a square wave of amplitude 1 (as above), what is the Fourier coefficient b₅? Give 4 decimal places.

quiz.why: bₙ = (2/nπ)(1 − cos nπ) vanishes for even n, leaving odd sine terms.

quiz.q: The timbre of an instrument is determined by:
quiz.why: Different harmonic mixtures give different waveform shapes for the same pitch.

quiz.q: An even function's Fourier series contains:
quiz.why: For f(−t) = f(t) all bₙ integrals vanish by symmetry.

questions.why: Space and time parts are separated, so the pattern does not move.

questions.why: Allowed harmonics are 1, 3, 5…, so the second overtone is the 5th harmonic.

An open pipe and a closed pipe have the same fundamental. Ratio L_open/L_closed:
questions.why: v/2L_o = v/4L_c gives L_o = 2L_c.

questions.why: ω = √(gk) gives dω/dk = ω/2k.

questions.why: v_g = v_p − λ dv_p/dλ = aλ − aλ = 0.

questions.why: bₙ ∝ 1/n for odd n, so b₃/b₁ = 1/3.

questions.why: bₙ = 2(−1)^(n+1)/n gives b₂ = −1.

questions.why: Partial sums overshoot by roughly 9% regardless of the number of terms.

questions.why: Perceived pitch corresponds to the fundamental (repetition) frequency.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, Practicals & Exam
courses.summary: A formula sheet for Waves & Oscillations and the standard practicals — Melde's experiment, the sonometer (laws of strings and AC frequency) and series LCR resonance — with procedures, observation calculations, viva points and a mixed exam.
outcomes: Recall key results across all units
Determine fork frequency by Melde's method
Verify the laws of strings and find AC mains frequency with a sonometer
Find resonant frequency, bandwidth and Q of an LCR circuit

scenes.text: Kabir pins one sheet above his desk the week before exams.
Each line is a result plus the condition it needs — the most-tested combination.

steps.title: SHM
steps.body: ẍ + ω²x = 0, x = A cos(ωt + φ), v = ω√(A² − x²), E = ½kA². T: spring 2π√(m/k); pendulum 2π√(l/g); LC 2π√(LC). Springs: parallel k₁ + k₂; series k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).

steps.title: Damped & forced
steps.body: γ = b/2m; ω′ = √(ω₀² − γ²); λ = γT′; τ = 1/2γ; Q = ω₀/2γ = ω₀/Δω. Forced: A = (F₀/m)/√((ω₀² − ω²)² + 4γ²ω²), tanδ = 2γω/(ω₀² − ω²). LCR: ω₀ = 1/√(LC), Q = ω₀L/R.

steps.title: Superposition
steps.body: R² = a₁² + a₂² + 2a₁a₂ cosδ; beats f₁ − f₂; Lissajous f_y/f_x = horizontal/vertical tangencies; coupled modes √(g/l), √(g/l + 2k/m).

steps.title: Waves
steps.body: v = fλ = ω/k; string √(T/μ); gas √(γP/ρ) ∝ √T; rod √(Y/ρ). I = ½ρvω²A²; β = 10 log(I/10⁻¹²); r = (Z₁ − Z₂)/(Z₁ + Z₂). Doppler f′ = f(v + v_o)/(v − v_s).

steps.title: Standing waves & Fourier
steps.body: String fₙ = nv/2L; closed pipe (2n − 1)v/4L; open nv/2L; e = 0.6r; L₂ − L₁ = λ/2. v_g = dω/dk = v_p − λ dv_p/dλ. Square wave (4/π)Σ sin nωt/n (odd n).

quiz.q: Which oscillator has period independent of g?
quiz.why: T = 2π√(m/k) contains no g; gravity only shifts equilibrium.

quiz.q: Resonance in a series LCR circuit gives:
quiz.why: Reactances cancel, leaving pure resistance, so current and emf are in phase.

quiz.q: Sound speed in air does not change with:
quiz.why: At fixed T, P/ρ is constant, so √(γP/ρ) is unchanged.

lessons.title: Lab: Melde's experiment — frequency of a fork

scenes.text: A thread tied to an electrically maintained fork passes over a pulley to a small pan of weights.
Adjust the load until the thread breaks into clear, steady loops; count them.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Find μ by weighing a known length of the thread. 2) Transverse arrangement: set the fork so its prong vibrates perpendicular to the thread. 3) Adjust pan weight (T = (m_pan + m)g) and length l until p well-defined loops appear. 4) Record p, l, T. 5) Repeat with different loads. 6) Turn the fork for the longitudinal arrangement and repeat.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body: Transverse: f = (p/2l)√(T/μ). Longitudinal: f = (p/l)√(T/μ). A useful check: p²T should be constant for fixed l and f.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Loops not sharply defined (nodes blurred); forgetting the pan's mass in T; friction at the pulley; thread μ not uniform.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why does the string vibrate at f/2 in the longitudinal mode? (It is pulled once per prong cycle but completes only half its own oscillation each pull.) Why is p²T constant? (f, l, μ fixed ⇒ p√T is fixed.)

activity.prompt: Transverse Melde setup: l = 1.2 m, p = 6 loops, T = 0.6 N, μ = 6 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m. Fork frequency (Hz)?

quiz.q: Changing from transverse to longitudinal arrangement with the same T and l, the number of loops:
quiz.why: The string vibrates at f/2 in the longitudinal mode, so it forms half as many loops.

quiz.q: In Melde's experiment, p²T is constant because:
options: f, l and μ are fixed
quiz.why: From f = (p/2l)√(T/μ), with f, l, μ fixed, p√T and hence p²T are constant.

quiz.q: Tension in the thread is:
quiz.why: The entire hanging mass, including the pan, provides the tension.

lessons.title: Lab: Sonometer — laws of strings & AC frequency

scenes.text: A steel wire stretches over two movable bridges on a hollow wooden box; a tiny paper rider sits mid-wire.
When the vibrating length matches resonance, the rider leaps off.

steps.title: Laws of strings
steps.body: f = (1/2l)√(T/μ). Law of length: f ∝ 1/l at fixed T (fl constant, using forks of different f). Law of tension: l ∝ √T at fixed f (l²/T constant). Law of mass: f ∝ 1/√μ.

steps.title: AC frequency method
steps.body: Pass mains AC (through a step-down transformer) through a non-magnetic wire placed between the poles of a horseshoe magnet. The force on the wire reverses each half cycle, so it vibrates at the mains frequency f. Adjust the bridges for maximum vibration: f = (1/2l)√(T/μ). (With an electromagnet driving a steel wire instead, the wire is attracted twice per cycle and vibrates at 2f.)

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: T = 0.5 kg × 9.8 = 4.9 N, μ = 4.9 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m → v = √10⁴ = 100 m/s. Resonant length l = 1.0 m → f = 100/2 = 50 Hz, matching Indian mains.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Wire not uniform; bridges not sharp; reading the resonance by ear alone; magnet not centred between bridges; forgetting the hanger mass.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why the hollow box? (Forced vibration of the box and air increases loudness.) Why use a non-magnetic wire with a permanent magnet? (So the force comes only from the current, giving frequency f.)

activity.prompt: AC sonometer: load 0.4 kg (g = 9.8), μ = 4.9 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m, resonant length 0.90 m with a permanent magnet. Mains frequency (Hz)?

quiz.q: In the AC sonometer with a permanent magnet, the wire vibrates at:
quiz.why: The force IL × B reverses once per half cycle, completing one oscillation per AC cycle.

quiz.q: Law of tension states that at constant f:
quiz.why: f = (1/2l)√(T/μ) fixed requires l ∝ √T.

quiz.q: Why is a paper rider used?
quiz.why: At resonance the wire's amplitude becomes large enough to throw the rider off.

scenes.text: A signal generator feeds a series LCR circuit; a student sweeps frequency and reads current.
The readings rise to a sharp peak and fall — a resonance curve.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Connect L, C, R in series with an AC milliammeter and signal generator (constant output voltage). 2) Vary f in steps, finer near the peak; record I. 3) Plot I vs f. 4) Read f₀ at I_max. 5) Draw a line at I_max/√2; read f₁ and f₂. 6) Q = f₀/(f₂ − f₁). 7) Compare with 1/(2π√(LC)) and (1/R)√(L/C).

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: L = 10 mH, C = 1 μF → theoretical f₀ = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1592 Hz. With total R = 10 Ω (including coil): Q = (1/10)√(10⁻²/10⁻⁶) = 10, so bandwidth ≈ 159 Hz.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Generator voltage drooping near resonance (check it at each step); the coil's own resistance makes measured Q smaller than (1/R)√(L/C) with R = resistor alone; meter loading.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why is it called an acceptor circuit? (It accepts maximum current at f₀.) What changes with larger R? (Lower, broader peak; same f₀.) What is a parallel LCR called? (Rejector circuit — minimum current at resonance.)

quiz.why: Q = ω₀L/R falls, so the curve becomes lower and wider while f₀ = 1/2π√(LC) is unchanged.

quiz.why: It passes maximum current at f₀.

quiz.why: Power ∝ I², so half power corresponds to I_max/√2.

Learners can apply conservation of energy and momentum to collisions
