Learners can derive escape and orbital speeds and use Kepler's laws

lessons.title: Newton's laws and frames of reference

story.title: The bathroom scale in the lift

scenes.text: Arjun carries a bathroom scale into his hostel lift for fun. As the lift starts upward the reading jumps from 60 kg to 72 kg.
His weight did not change, so what did the scale really measure? The answer is the normal force — and the lift is a non-inertial frame.

steps.title: The three laws, stated carefully
steps.body:
- **First law** defines an *inertial frame*: a frame in which a body with zero net force keeps constant velocity.
- **Second law**: F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass, F_net = ma.
- **Third law**: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on *different* bodies.

In a frame accelerating with acceleration a₀, Newton's second law works only if you add a **pseudo force** −m a₀ on every body. Rotating frames add centrifugal (mω²r outward) and Coriolis (−2m ω × v) terms.

steps.title: Solved: block sliding down a rough incline
steps.body:
A 5 kg block slides down a 30° incline with μk = 0.2. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8 m/s²).

- Along the incline: mg sinθ − f = ma
- Normal: N = mg cosθ, so f = μk mg cosθ
- a = g(sinθ − μk cosθ) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.2 × 0.866)
- a = 9.8 × 0.3268 = **3.20 m/s²** (mass cancels)

steps.title: Solved: apparent weight in a lift
steps.body:
A 60 kg student stands on a scale in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s².

- In the lift frame add pseudo force ma downward: N − mg − ma = 0
- N = m(g + a) = 60 × 11.8 = **708 N**
- The scale (calibrated in kg-wt) reads 708/9.8 ≈ 72.2 kg

If the lift falls freely (a = g downward), N = 0: weightlessness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting an action–reaction pair on the same free-body diagram (they act on different bodies, so they never cancel).
- Adding pseudo forces while working in the ground (inertial) frame — use one frame only.
- Writing f = μN for static friction always; μs N is only the *maximum* static friction.
- Forgetting that mass cancels in incline problems, then plugging in a wrong mass.

steps.title: Exam habit
steps.body: Always draw a free-body diagram, choose axes along and perpendicular to the motion, and state which frame you are in before writing equations.

activity.prompt: A 50 kg person stands on a scale in a lift that accelerates DOWNWARD at 1.8 m/s². Take g = 9.8 m/s². What normal force (in N) does the scale exert?

quiz.q: A frame in which a free particle moves with constant velocity is called:
quiz.why: An inertial frame is one where a free particle (no force) moves at constant velocity, which is what Newton's first law defines.

quiz.q: In a lift accelerating upward at a, the apparent weight of mass m is:
quiz.why: In a lift accelerating upward, N − mg = ma, so the normal force (apparent weight) is m(g + a).

quiz.q: The pseudo force in a frame with acceleration a₀ is:
quiz.why: In a frame with acceleration a₀, an observer sees a pseudo force −m a₀, opposite to the frame's acceleration.

quiz.q: For a block sliding down a rough incline, acceleration depends on:
quiz.why: For sliding down a rough incline, ma = mg sin θ − μk mg cos θ, so a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ). The mass cancels.

quiz.q: The Coriolis force on a body moving with velocity v in a frame rotating with ω is:
quiz.why: In a frame rotating with angular velocity ω, the Coriolis force on a particle of velocity v is −2m ω × v. It vanishes if v = 0 or v is parallel to ω.

scenes.text: Priya flicks the striker at a coin of equal mass. The striker stops dead and the coin shoots off with the striker's speed.
That is a head-on elastic collision of equal masses — velocities are exchanged. Let us see why.

steps.title: Work–energy and conservative forces
steps.body:
- Work W = ∫ F · dr; the **work–energy theorem**: W_net = ΔK.
- A force is **conservative** if its work is path-independent ⇔ ∮F·dr = 0 ⇔ ∇ × F = 0. Then F = −∇U.
- Gravity and spring forces are conservative; friction is not.
- With only conservative forces, K + U = constant.

Momentum p = mv is conserved whenever the net external force is zero, regardless of whether energy is conserved.

steps.title: Solved: 1-D elastic collision
steps.body:
A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg ball at rest, head-on and elastically.

- v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂) = (1/3)(3) = **1 m/s**
- v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂) = (4/3)(3) = **4 m/s**
- Check momentum: 2×3 = 2×1 + 1×4 = 6 ✓
- Check KE: ½·2·9 = 9 J = ½·2·1 + ½·1·16 = 1 + 8 ✓

steps.title: Solved: spring compression
steps.body:
A 0.5 kg block at 2 m/s on a smooth floor hits a spring (k = 200 N/m). Maximum compression?

- ½mv² = ½kx²
- x = v√(m/k) = 2 × √(0.5/200) = 2 × 0.05 = **0.10 m**

steps.title: Coefficient of restitution
steps.body: e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach). e = 1 elastic, 0 < e < 1 inelastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic (bodies stick). In a perfectly inelastic collision of m₁ (speed u) with m₂ at rest, the KE lost is fraction m₂/(m₁ + m₂) of the initial KE.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming KE is conserved in every collision — only momentum is guaranteed (if no external impulse).
- Using speeds instead of velocities with signs in 1-D formulas.
- Calling friction conservative because it is 'constant'.
- Forgetting that F = −dU/dx has a minus sign: force points downhill on the potential curve.

statements.s: Momentum is conserved in an inelastic collision if no external force acts.
statements.why: Momentum conservation needs only zero external impulse.

statements.s: If ∇ × F = 0 everywhere in a simply connected region, F can be written as −∇U.
statements.why: That is the test for a conservative force.

statements.s: In a perfectly inelastic collision kinetic energy is conserved.
statements.why: Maximum KE is lost when bodies stick together.

statements.s: In a head-on elastic collision of equal masses with one at rest, the moving body stops.
statements.why: Velocities are exchanged.

quiz.q: The work–energy theorem states that net work equals:
quiz.why: The work–energy theorem says that the net work on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, W_net = ΔK.

quiz.q: A force field is conservative if:
quiz.why: A force is conservative when its curl is zero, ∇ × F = 0, so that work is path independent (in a simply connected region).

quiz.q: For e = 0 the collision is:
quiz.why: Coefficient of restitution e = 0 means the bodies do not separate after collision; they stick together, which is perfectly inelastic.

quiz.q: A 1 kg mass at 4 m/s sticks to an identical mass at rest. Final speed:
quiz.why: Momentum conservation: 1 × 4 = (1 + 1)v, so v = 2 m/s.

quiz.q: In the case above, the fraction of KE lost is:
quiz.why: Initial KE = ½ × 1 × 16 = 8 J. Final KE = ½ × 2 × 2² = 4 J, so half is lost, i.e. a fraction of 1/2.

lessons.title: Rigid bodies: moment of inertia, torque, rolling

scenes.text: In the lab, Kabir releases a ring and a solid disc of the same mass and radius from the top of a ramp.
The disc wins every time. Mass and radius are equal — so the difference must lie in how mass is distributed: the moment of inertia.

steps.title: Rotational quantities
steps.body:
- Moment of inertia I = Σ mᵢrᵢ² = ∫ r² dm (about a stated axis)
- Torque τ = r × F; τ = Iα for a fixed axis
- Angular momentum L = Iω; dL/dt = τ_ext, so L is conserved when τ_ext = 0
- Rotational KE = ½Iω²

**Parallel axis theorem**: I = I_cm + Md². **Perpendicular axis theorem** (plane laminae only): I_z = I_x + I_y.

steps.title: Solved: rod about one end
steps.body:
A uniform rod (mass M, length L) has I_cm = ML²/12.

- Distance from centre to end d = L/2
- I_end = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + 3ML²/12 = **ML²/3**

Similarly a ring about a diameter: I_z = MR² = I_x + I_y with I_x = I_y ⇒ I_diameter = MR²/2.

steps.title: Solved: rolling without slipping
steps.body:
For a body rolling down an incline of angle θ: a = g sinθ /(1 + I/MR²).

- Ring: I/MR² = 1 ⇒ a = g sinθ/2
- Disc: I/MR² = 1/2 ⇒ a = (2/3) g sinθ
- Solid sphere: 2/5 ⇒ a = (5/7) g sinθ

Disc on 30°: a = (2/3)(9.8)(0.5) = **3.27 m/s²**. Solid sphere beats disc beats ring.

steps.title: Conservation of angular momentum
steps.body: A skater pulling her arms in reduces I, so ω rises (Iω constant). Rotational KE ½Iω² = L²/2I actually *increases* — the extra energy comes from the work her muscles do pulling the arms in.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to 3-D bodies like a sphere — it is valid only for flat laminae.
- Using parallel-axis shift from a non-centre-of-mass axis (d must be measured from the CM axis).
- Forgetting rotational KE when using energy conservation for rolling bodies.
- Assuming static friction does work in pure rolling (it does none: contact point is momentarily at rest).

activity.prompt: Match each body to its moment of inertia about the stated axis.

quiz.q: The parallel axis theorem is I = I_cm + Md², where d is measured from:
quiz.why: In I = I_cm + Md², d is the distance between the new axis and the parallel axis through the centre of mass. The shift must start from the CM axis.

quiz.q: The perpendicular axis theorem applies to:
quiz.why: The perpendicular axis theorem (I_z = I_x + I_y) holds only for planar bodies (laminae), where all mass lies in one plane.

quiz.q: Which reaches the bottom of an incline first (rolling, same M and R)?
quiz.why: For rolling, a = g sin θ/(1 + I/MR²). The solid sphere has the smallest I/MR² (2/5), so the largest acceleration and it arrives first; the ring (1) is last.

quiz.q: For pure rolling, the velocity of the contact point is:
quiz.why: In pure rolling the translation speed v at the contact point is cancelled by the rotational speed ωR = v in the opposite direction, so the contact point is momentarily at rest.

quiz.q: If a skater halves her moment of inertia, her angular speed:
quiz.why: With no external torque, angular momentum Iω is conserved, so halving I doubles ω.

quiz.q: Fraction of total KE that is rotational for a rolling disc:
quiz.why: For a disc, K_rot = ½(½MR²)(v/R)² = ¼Mv² and K_trans = ½Mv², so the fraction rotational is (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3.

scenes.text: Meera watches a launch broadcast and hears the commentator say a probe needs about 11.2 km/s to leave Earth for good.
She sets kinetic energy equal to the gravitational binding energy and gets the same number on a napkin.

steps.title: Central forces and Kepler
steps.body:
- Newton's law: F = GMm/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; potential energy U = −GMm/r
- A **central force** has zero torque about the centre ⇒ angular momentum conserved ⇒ motion in a plane and equal areas in equal times (**Kepler II**)
- **Kepler I**: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus
- **Kepler III**: T² ∝ a³; for circular orbits T² = 4π²r³/GM
- g at height h: g' = g R²/(R + h)²; for h ≪ R, g' ≈ g(1 − 2h/R)

steps.title: Solved: escape and orbital speed
steps.body:
Take g = 9.8 m/s², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.

- Escape: ½mv² = GMm/R ⇒ vₑ = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) = √(1.254 × 10⁸) ≈ **11.2 km/s**
- Orbit just above surface: mv²/R = mg ⇒ v₀ = √(gR) ≈ **7.9 km/s**
- So vₑ = √2 v₀

steps.title: Solved: g at the height of a satellite
steps.body:
Find g at h = 320 km.

- R + h = 6720 km; R/(R + h) = 6400/6720 = 0.9524
- g' = 9.8 × (0.9524)² = 9.8 × 0.907 = **8.89 m/s²**
- Astronauts float not because g is zero but because they are in free fall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating gravitational PE as mgh far from the surface — use −GMm/r.
- Thinking escape speed depends on the launch direction or the mass of the projectile (it does not, ignoring air).
- Using the diameter instead of the radius, or km instead of m.
- Writing total energy of a circular orbit as positive; it is E = −GMm/2r (bound).

activity.prompt: Complete the orbital relations.
activity.text: For a circular orbit, kinetic energy is GMm/(2r), potential energy is −GMm/r, so total energy is ___ times the potential energy, and escape speed is √___ times orbital speed near the surface.

quiz.q: Kepler's second law is a consequence of conservation of:
quiz.why: Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) follows from conservation of angular momentum, since a central force exerts no torque.

quiz.q: For a circular orbit, T² is proportional to:
quiz.why: Setting gravity equal to centripetal force gives T² = 4π²r³/(GM), so T² ∝ r³ (Kepler's third law).

quiz.q: Escape speed from Earth's surface is about:
quiz.why: Escape speed v = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s. 7.9 km/s is the orbital speed near the surface.

quiz.q: Total energy of a satellite in circular orbit of radius r is:
quiz.why: In a circular orbit K = GMm/2r and U = −GMm/r, so E = K + U = −GMm/2r (negative, so it is bound).

quiz.q: For h ≪ R, g at height h is approximately:
quiz.why: g(h) = g R²/(R + h)² = g(1 + h/R)⁻² ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for h ≪ R.

questions.q: Newton's first law is used to define:
questions.why: Newton's first law tells us that a body with no net force moves with constant velocity, and this identifies the inertial frames.

questions.q: Unit of moment of inertia:
questions.why: Moment of inertia I = Σmr² has the unit kg m².

questions.q: Which force is non-conservative?
questions.why: Kinetic friction does work that depends on the path taken and dissipates energy as heat, so it is non-conservative. Gravity, spring and electrostatic forces are conservative.

questions.q: A 70 kg man in a freely falling lift reads on the scale:
questions.why: In free fall, the lift and the man accelerate at g, so N = m(g − g) = 0 and the scale reads zero (apparent weightlessness).

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through one end perpendicular to it is:
questions.why: By the parallel axis theorem, I = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + ML²/4 = ML²/3.

questions.q: Equal areas in equal times holds for any:
questions.why: Equal areas in equal times follows from conservation of angular momentum, which holds for any central force, not only inverse-square forces.

questions.q: A 4 kg block on a 37° smooth incline (sin37° = 0.6) has acceleration (g = 10 m/s²):
questions.why: On a smooth incline a = g sin θ = 10 × 0.6 = 6 m/s². The mass does not matter.

questions.q: Assertion: In pure rolling, static friction does no work. Reason: The contact point has zero instantaneous velocity.
options: Both true, reason does not explain
questions.why: Both true: at the contact point of pure rolling the velocity is zero, so the power of static friction f·v is zero and it does no work. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A 3 kg ball at 4 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. Velocity of the 3 kg ball after collision:
questions.why: For an elastic head-on collision, v₁ = ((m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂))u₁ = (2/4) × 4 = 2 m/s.

questions.q: A solid sphere rolls down a 30° incline. Its acceleration (g = 9.8 m/s²) is about:
questions.why: For a solid sphere, a = g sin θ/(1 + 2/5) = (5/7)g sin θ = (5/7)(9.8)(0.5) = 3.5 m/s².

questions.q: Case: A satellite orbits at r = 2R (R = Earth radius). Its orbital speed compared to a surface-skimming orbit v₀ is:
questions.why: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) ∝ 1/√r. At r = 2R the speed is v₀/√2.

questions.q: A spring (k = 800 N/m) is compressed 5 cm and launches a 0.125 kg ball on a smooth floor. Launch speed:
questions.why: Spring energy ½kx² becomes kinetic ½mv², so v = x√(k/m) = 0.05 × √(800/0.125) = 0.05 × 80 = 4 m/s.

questions.q: A disc of mass 2 kg, radius 0.1 m spins at 10 rad/s. A 0.5 kg lump of putty sticks to its rim. New angular speed:
Energy needed to move a 1000 kg satellite from a circular orbit of radius 2R to one of radius 4R (GMm/R = 6.27 × 10¹⁰ J):
questions.why: Orbital energy is −GMm/2r. ΔE = GMm/2 × (1/2R − 1/4R) = GMm/(8R) = 6.27 × 10¹⁰/8 ≈ 7.8 × 10⁹ J.

questions.q: In a frame rotating with angular velocity ω, a particle at rest at distance r experiences:
questions.why: A particle at rest in the rotating frame has zero velocity there, so the Coriolis force (∝ v) is zero. Only the centrifugal force mω²r acts.

courses.title: Electricity & Magnetism · fields to Maxwell
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: The Electricity & Magnetism core paper: Gauss's law, potential and capacitors with dielectrics, magnetostatics, electromagnetic induction and Maxwell's equations.
outcomes: Learners can use Gauss's law for symmetric charge distributions
Learners can compute capacitance, stored energy and dielectric effects
Learners can apply Biot–Savart and Ampère's laws
Learners can state Maxwell's equations and use Faraday's law

scenes.text: A long charged plastic pipe sits in a dusty workshop. Sana wonders how strong its field is at her hand, 10 cm away.
Instead of summing infinite little charges, she imagines a coaxial cylinder around it — Gauss's law does the rest.

steps.title: Flux and Gauss's law
steps.body:
- Electric flux Φ = ∮ E · dA
- **Gauss's law (integral)**: ∮ E · dA = q_enc/ε₀, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²
- **Differential form**: ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀ (via the divergence theorem)
- Electrostatic field is conservative: ∇ × E = 0

Gauss's law is always true, but is *useful* for computing E only when symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar) makes |E| constant over the Gaussian surface.

steps.title: Solved: infinite line charge
steps.body:
Line charge density λ. Choose a coaxial cylinder of radius r, length l.

- Flux only through curved surface: E(2πrl) = λl/ε₀
- E = λ/(2πε₀r) = 2kλ/r
- For λ = 2 μC/m, r = 0.1 m: E = 2 × 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶/0.1 = **3.6 × 10⁵ N/C**

steps.title: Solved: uniformly charged sphere
steps.body:
Total charge Q, radius R.

- Outside (r ≥ R): E = kQ/r²
- Inside (r < R): q_enc = Q r³/R³ ⇒ E(4πr²) = Qr³/(ε₀R³) ⇒ **E = kQr/R³**
- E grows linearly inside, peaks at the surface, falls as 1/r² outside.

Infinite sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking flux depends on the Gaussian surface's size — it depends only on enclosed charge.
- Using Gauss's law to 'find' E for an asymmetric distribution (the law holds, but E is not constant on the surface).
- Mixing σ/(2ε₀) (isolated sheet) with σ/ε₀ (just outside a conductor).
- Forgetting E inside a conductor in electrostatics is zero.

activity.prompt: How does E vary with distance r from each charge distribution?

items.text: Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere

quiz.q: Gauss's law in differential form is:
quiz.why: Gauss's law in differential form is ∇·E = ρ/ε₀. ∇ × E = 0 is the electrostatic curl condition and ∇·B = 0 is for magnetism.

quiz.q: Field of an infinite line charge varies as:
quiz.why: For an infinite line charge, Gauss's law over a cylinder gives E = λ/(2πε₀r), so E ∝ 1/r.

quiz.q: Flux through a closed surface with no enclosed charge is:
quiz.why: By Gauss's law, flux = q_enclosed/ε₀. With no enclosed charge, the net flux is zero.

quiz.q: Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, E at r = R/2 equals (E_s at surface):
quiz.why: Inside a uniformly charged sphere, E = ρr/(3ε₀) ∝ r. At r = R/2 it is half the value at the surface.

quiz.q: Field near an infinite plane sheet of charge density σ:
quiz.why: For an infinite sheet, flux leaves both faces: 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/2ε₀.

scenes.text: Rohit opens an old camera flash (safely discharged by his teacher) and finds a fat capacitor inside.
It slowly stores energy from a small battery and dumps it in a millisecond. Capacitance, voltage and ½CV² explain the flash.

steps.title: Potential and capacitance
steps.body:
- E = −∇V; V(r) = kq/r for a point charge; Poisson's equation ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀ (Laplace's where ρ = 0)
- Capacitance C = Q/V; parallel plates C = ε₀A/d
- Energy U = ½CV² = Q²/2C; energy density u = ½ε₀E²
- Series: 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ; parallel: C = ΣCᵢ

A dielectric of constant κ multiplies C by κ. Polarisation P creates bound charges; **D = ε₀E + P = ε₀κE** and ∇ · D = ρ_free.

steps.title: Solved: battery connected vs disconnected
steps.body:
Insert a slab (κ) fully:

- **Battery connected** (V fixed): C → κC, Q → κQ, U = ½CV² → κU.
- **Battery disconnected** (Q fixed): C → κC, V → V/κ, U = Q²/2C → U/κ. The field pulls the slab in, doing work.

Two 6 μF capacitors in series give 3 μF; in parallel 12 μF.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the series formula for parallel capacitors (opposite of resistors!).
- Forgetting whether the battery stays connected when a dielectric is inserted.
- Writing E = +∇V (sign error): field points toward decreasing potential.
- Using mm or cm² without converting to SI.

activity.prompt: Two capacitors, 4 μF and 12 μF, are in series across 16 V. What is the charge on each (in μC)?

quiz.q: Relation between field and potential:
quiz.why: The electric field is the negative gradient of the potential, E = −∇V, so it points toward decreasing potential.

quiz.q: Capacitors 2 μF and 3 μF in parallel give:
quiz.why: Capacitances in parallel add: 2 + 3 = 5 μF.

quiz.q: With the battery disconnected, inserting a dielectric makes the stored energy:
quiz.why: With the battery disconnected, charge Q stays fixed. U = Q²/2C, and C → κC, so U decreases by a factor κ.

quiz.q: Energy density of an electric field in vacuum:
quiz.why: The energy density of an electric field in vacuum is u = ½ε₀E².

quiz.q: ∇ · D equals:
quiz.why: Gauss's law for D states ∇·D = ρ_free. D is sourced by free charge only, while bound charge is accounted for by polarisation.

scenes.text: On a field trip, Nikhil's compass needle swings when he walks under a DC power cable.
Current makes magnetic fields. Biot–Savart gives the field of any wire; Ampère's law gives it fast when there is symmetry.

steps.title: Laws of magnetostatics
steps.body:
- Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B); on a wire F = I L × B
- **Biot–Savart**: dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂ / r², μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A
- **Ampère's law**: ∮ B · dl = μ₀ I_enc; differential: ∇ × B = μ₀J
- No magnetic monopoles: ∇ · B = 0

Results: long wire B = μ₀I/(2πr); centre of a circular loop B = μ₀I/(2R); long solenoid B = μ₀nI inside, ≈ 0 outside.

steps.title: Solved: field of a wire and a solenoid
steps.body:
- Wire, I = 10 A, r = 5 cm: B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10/0.05 = **4 × 10⁻⁵ T** (comparable to Earth's field)
- Solenoid, n = 1000 turns/m, I = 2 A: B = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 2 ≈ **2.51 × 10⁻³ T**

steps.title: Solved: force between parallel wires
steps.body:
Two long wires 0.1 m apart carry 5 A each in the same direction.

- Force per length F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 25/0.1 = **5 × 10⁻⁵ N/m**, attractive
- Opposite currents repel. (This force once defined the ampere.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Ampère's law where B is not constant along the loop (e.g. a short finite wire).
- Forgetting the cross product direction — use the right-hand rule.
- Thinking magnetic force does work on a charge (v × B is ⊥ v, so it never changes speed).
- Confusing n (turns per metre) with N (total turns).

activity.prompt: Match the current configuration to its magnetic field.
pairs: Long straight wire at distance r
Centre of circular loop radius R
Inside toroid radius r, N turns

quiz.q: ∇ · B = 0 means:
quiz.why: ∇·B = 0 means that magnetic field lines have no beginning or end, i.e. there are no isolated magnetic monopoles.

quiz.q: Magnetic force on a moving charge does:
quiz.why: The magnetic force F = qv × B is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and cannot change the particle's speed.

quiz.q: Two parallel wires with currents in the same direction:
quiz.why: Parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, while opposite currents repel.

quiz.q: Field at the centre of a loop of radius 0.1 m with 1 A:
quiz.why: At the centre of a circular loop B = μ₀I/2R = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1/(2 × 0.1) = 2π × 10⁻⁶ T.

quiz.q: Ampère's law in differential form (static):
quiz.why: For steady currents Ampère's law in differential form is ∇ × B = μ₀J. (∇ × E = −∂B/∂t is Faraday's law.)

scenes.text: Ishita's cycle lamp glows brighter the faster she pedals. A magnet spins inside a coil in the dynamo.
Changing flux makes an emf — Faraday's law. Maxwell later added one term that predicted light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

steps.title: Faraday, Lenz and inductance
steps.body:
- **Faraday**: ε = −dΦ_B/dt (N turns: −N dΦ/dt); differential: ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t
- **Lenz**: the induced current opposes the change that produced it (the minus sign; energy conservation)
- Motional emf ε = Blv
- Self-inductance L = NΦ/I; long solenoid L = μ₀n²Al; energy ½LI²

steps.title: Maxwell's equations
steps.body:
- ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀
- ∇ · B = 0
- ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t
- ∇ × B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t

The last term is Maxwell's **displacement current** (ε₀ ∂E/∂t), needed so that charge conservation holds (e.g. between capacitor plates). In free space they give waves with speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

steps.title: Solved: motional and coil emf
steps.body:
- A 0.2 m rod moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T: ε = Blv = 0.5 × 0.2 × 4 = **0.4 V**
- A 100-turn coil of area 0.02 m² in B = 0.5 T is pulled out in 0.1 s: ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.02 × 0.5/0.1 = **10 V**

steps.title: Solved: check c from constants
steps.body: μ₀ε₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² = 1.112 × 10⁻¹⁷ s²/m². c = 1/√(1.112 × 10⁻¹⁷) ≈ **3.0 × 10⁸ m/s** — Maxwell's great unification of light with electromagnetism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a large flux gives emf — only a *changing* flux does.
- Dropping N for multi-turn coils.
- Calling displacement current a flow of charge; it is a changing electric field.
- Getting Lenz direction wrong: oppose the *change*, not the field itself.

activity.prompt: Order the reasoning that leads Maxwell to the displacement current.
items: Take the divergence of ∇ × B = μ₀J
Divergence of a curl is zero, so ∇ · J = 0
But continuity requires ∇ · J = −∂ρ/∂t, not zero, when charge builds up
Use ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀ to write ∂ρ/∂t = ε₀ ∇ · ∂E/∂t
Add μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t to the right side of Ampère's law

quiz.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of:
quiz.why: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change causing it. If it aided the change, current and flux would grow without any work done, breaking conservation of energy.

quiz.q: Displacement current density is:
quiz.why: Maxwell added the displacement current density J_d = ε₀ ∂E/∂t to Ampère's law, so a changing electric field also produces a magnetic field.

quiz.q: Speed of EM waves in vacuum equals:
quiz.why: Maxwell's equations give a wave equation with speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The other expressions do not have units of speed.

quiz.q: Energy stored in an inductor:
quiz.why: The energy stored in an inductor carrying current I is U = ½LI², from integrating L I dI.

quiz.q: A rod 0.5 m moves at 2 m/s across B = 0.2 T. EMF:
quiz.why: Motional emf = Blv = 0.2 × 0.5 × 2 = 0.2 V.

questions.q: SI unit of electric flux:
questions.why: Electric flux Φ = E·A, so its unit is (N/C) × m² = N m²/C. V/m and N/C are units of field.

questions.q: Which Maxwell equation expresses the absence of magnetic monopoles?
questions.why: ∇·B = 0 says that B has no sources or sinks, which expresses the absence of magnetic monopoles.

questions.q: The field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is:
questions.why: In equilibrium, free charges inside a conductor rearrange until the net field inside is zero, since any field would keep them moving.

questions.q: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is proportional to:
questions.why: For a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d, so it is proportional to plate area A and inversely proportional to separation d.

questions.q: A charge moving parallel to B experiences:
questions.why: The magnetic force is F = qv × B. When v is parallel to B, the cross product is zero, so no force acts.

questions.q: The minus sign in Faraday's law represents:
questions.why: The minus sign in Faraday's law ε = −dΦ/dt says that the induced emf opposes the change in flux, which is Lenz's law.

questions.q: Three 3 μF capacitors in series have equivalent capacitance:
questions.why: In series, 1/C = 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1, so C = 1 μF.

questions.q: Assertion: Gauss's law can find E of a finite charged rod easily. Reason: Gauss's law is valid for any closed surface.
questions.why: The reason is true because Gauss's law holds for any closed surface. But a finite rod lacks the symmetry needed to pull E out of the integral, so the assertion is false.

questions.q: A solenoid of 500 turns over 0.25 m carries 1 A. B inside:
A 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores:
Case: A sphere of radius 0.1 m holds 1 nC uniformly through its volume. E at r = 0.05 m (k = 9 × 10⁹):
questions.why: Inside a uniformly charged sphere E = kQr/R³ = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹ × 0.05/(0.1)³ = 0.45/10⁻³ = 450 N/C.

questions.q: A flat coil of 50 turns, area 0.01 m², rotates at ω = 100 rad/s in B = 0.4 T. Peak emf:
A capacitor charged and disconnected from the battery has a slab κ = 4 inserted. Initial energy 8 mJ. Final energy:
questions.why: With the battery disconnected, charge is fixed. Capacitance rises by κ = 4, so U = Q²/2C falls to 8 mJ/4 = 2 mJ.

questions.q: Between the plates of a charging capacitor (circular plates radius R, displacement current I_d), B at radius r < R is:
questions.why: Ampère–Maxwell law over a loop of radius r < R encloses displacement current I_d r²/R². So B × 2πr = μ₀I_d r²/R², giving B = μ₀I_d r/(2πR²).

questions.q: Energy stored in a 0.5 m long air solenoid, n = 1000/m, A = 10 cm², I = 2 A:

courses.title: Waves & Optics · oscillations, interference, diffraction
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Simple harmonic, damped and forced oscillations, the wave equation and superposition, interference (Young, thin films, Newton's rings), diffraction gratings and polarisation.
outcomes: Learners can solve SHM, damping and resonance problems
Learners can use the wave equation and standing-wave conditions
Learners can compute fringe widths, ring diameters and grating angles
Learners can apply Malus's and Brewster's laws

scenes.text: Tara reads about footbridges that swayed when crowds walked in step with the bridge's natural frequency.
Natural frequency, damping and resonance — the same maths as a mass on a spring.

steps.title: The equations
steps.body:
- SHM: m ẍ + kx = 0 ⇒ x = A sin(ωt + φ), ω = √(k/m), T = 2π/ω
- Energy E = ½kA², shared between K and U
- **Damped**: m ẍ + bẋ + kx = 0. Light damping: x = A e^(−bt/2m) cos(ω′t + φ), ω′ = √(ω² − b²/4m²). Critical damping when b² = 4mk; overdamped beyond.
- **Forced**: driving F₀ cos ωt gives steady amplitude A = (F₀/m)/√((ω₀² − ω²)² + (bω/m)²). Resonance near ω = ω₀; sharpness measured by quality factor Q = ω₀m/b.

steps.title: Solved: damped decay
steps.body:
Amplitude falls from 10 cm to 5 cm in 20 s. Find time to fall to 1.25 cm.

- Each 20 s halves the amplitude (exponential decay)
- 10 → 5 → 2.5 → 1.25: three half-lives = **60 s**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using frequency f where angular frequency ω is needed (ω = 2πf).
- Thinking the period of SHM depends on amplitude (not for ideal SHM).
- Assuming resonance amplitude is infinite in real systems — damping limits it.
- Confusing energy decay time with amplitude decay time (energy ∝ A², decays twice as fast).

bands.text: Underdamped: oscillates with exponentially shrinking amplitude.
Critically damped: returns to rest fastest without oscillating (car shock absorbers aim near here).
Overdamped: creeps back slowly without oscillating.

quiz.q: Angular frequency of a spring-mass system:
quiz.why: For a mass on a spring the restoring force is −kx, so ω² = k/m and ω = √(k/m). The period T = 2π/ω.

quiz.q: Critical damping occurs when:
quiz.why: For a damped oscillator, critical damping occurs when the discriminant of the auxiliary equation vanishes: b² = 4mk. Below this it is underdamped.

quiz.q: Total energy of SHM is proportional to:
quiz.why: The total energy of SHM is E = ½kA², so it is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

quiz.q: Higher Q factor means:
quiz.why: Q = ω₀m/b, so a higher Q means less damping and a sharper, taller resonance peak.

quiz.q: m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m. Period:

lessons.title: Wave equation, standing waves and beats

scenes.text: Dev tightens a sitar string and the note rises. He plays it with a tuning fork and hears a slow wah-wah.
Tension sets wave speed; standing waves set pitch; the wah-wah is beats.

steps.title: Waves in one dimension
steps.body:
- Wave equation: ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²y/∂t²; any f(x − vt) solves it
- Harmonic wave y = A sin(kx − ωt), k = 2π/λ, v = ω/k = fλ
- String: v = √(T/μ), μ = mass per length
- Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends: λₙ = 2L/n, fₙ = nv/2L
- Beats: two close frequencies f₁, f₂ give beat frequency |f₁ − f₂|

steps.title: Solved: fundamental of a string
steps.body:
T = 100 N, μ = 0.01 kg/m, L = 0.5 m.

- v = √(100/0.01) = **100 m/s**
- f₁ = v/2L = 100/1 = **100 Hz**; second harmonic 200 Hz
- To double f₁ you need 4× tension.

steps.title: Solved: beats to tune
steps.body:
A fork of 256 Hz with a string gives 4 beats/s. Tightening the string slightly makes beats *decrease*.

- String is 252 or 260 Hz
- Tightening raises its frequency; beats fall only if it was below 256
- So the string was **252 Hz**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing particle velocity (∂y/∂t) with wave velocity v.
- Using L = λ for the fundamental of a string (it is L = λ/2).
- Closed pipe allows only odd harmonics — don't use 2L.
- Forgetting μ must be in kg/m, not g/m.

activity.prompt: A 1 m string fixed at both ends carries waves at 300 m/s. What is the frequency of its THIRD harmonic (Hz)?

quiz.q: Wave speed on a string is:
quiz.why: Wave speed on a stretched string is v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length.

quiz.q: Fundamental wavelength for a string fixed at both ends:
quiz.why: A string fixed at both ends has a node at each end. The fundamental has one loop, which is half a wavelength, so λ = 2L.

quiz.q: 512 Hz and 508 Hz sound together. Beat frequency:
quiz.why: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies: 512 − 508 = 4 Hz.

quiz.q: If tension is quadrupled, fundamental frequency:
quiz.why: Fundamental frequency f = (1/2L)√(T/μ) ∝ √T. If T is 4 times larger, f becomes 2 times larger.

quiz.q: y = 0.02 sin(4x − 200t) (SI). Wave speed:
quiz.why: For y = A sin(kx − ωt), v = ω/k = 200/4 = 50 m/s.

lessons.title: Interference: Young, thin films, Newton's rings

scenes.text: Little Anu blows soap bubbles; her elder brother, a B.Sc student, sees swirling colours where the film is thinnest.
Light reflected from the two surfaces of the film interferes. Thickness decides which colour adds up.

steps.title: Conditions for interference
steps.body:
Sustained interference needs **coherent** sources (constant phase difference), similar amplitudes and small path differences.

- **YDSE**: path difference d sinθ ≈ yd/D; bright at yd/D = nλ; fringe width **β = λD/d**
- **Thin film (reflected)**: 2μt cos r = (n + ½)λ for bright, 2μt cos r = nλ for dark — an extra λ/2 arises from reflection at the denser medium
- **Newton's rings (reflected, air film)**: dark ring diameters Dₙ² = 4nλR; so λ = (D²ₙ₊ₚ − D²ₙ)/(4pR). Central spot is dark in reflection.

steps.title: Solved: Young's experiment
steps.body:
λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m, d = 0.5 mm.

- β = λD/d = 600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1/(0.5 × 10⁻³) = **1.2 mm**
- Immersing the apparatus in water (μ = 1.33) gives β/μ ≈ 0.9 mm.

steps.title: Solved: Newton's rings
steps.body:
R = 1 m, λ = 589 nm. Diameter of the 10th dark ring?

- D² = 4nλR = 4 × 10 × 589 × 10⁻⁹ × 1 = 2.356 × 10⁻⁵ m²
- D = **4.85 mm**
- Filling the gap with a liquid of μ makes D² = 4nλR/μ, so rings shrink.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the λ/2 phase change on reflection from a denser medium.
- Using radius formulas with diameters (rₙ² = nλR vs Dₙ² = 4nλR).
- Thinking two separate bulbs can give a stable pattern (not coherent).
- Mixing mm and nm — convert everything to metres.

activity.prompt: In YDSE, λ = 500 nm, slit separation 0.25 mm, screen at 1.5 m. Fringe width in mm?

quiz.q: Fringe width in YDSE:
quiz.why: The fringe width in Young's double slit experiment is β = λD/d, where D is slit-to-screen distance and d is slit separation.

quiz.q: Central spot of Newton's rings in reflected light is:
quiz.why: At the centre the air film has zero thickness, but the ray reflected at the glass plate gets a λ/2 phase shift while the other does not. They destructively interfere, so the centre is dark.

quiz.q: Coherent sources must have:
quiz.why: Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, which gives stable interference fringes.

quiz.q: Newton's ring diameters (dark) are proportional to:
quiz.why: For dark Newton's rings D² = 4nλR, so the diameter D is proportional to √n.

quiz.q: If D is doubled and d halved in YDSE, β becomes:
quiz.why: Since β = λD/d, doubling D and halving d multiplies β by 2 × 2 = 4.

scenes.text: Kiran tilts an old CD under a tube light and sees ordered rainbow bands.
The tracks act as a diffraction grating. Later her polarising sunglasses kill road glare — polarisation by reflection.

steps.title: Diffraction
steps.body:
- **Single slit** (width a): minima at a sinθ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2…); central maximum is twice as wide as the others
- **Grating** (spacing d): principal maxima at d sinθ = nλ; maximum order n < d/λ
- Resolving power of a grating: λ/Δλ = nN (N = lines illuminated)
- Fresnel (near-field) vs Fraunhofer (far-field, plane wavefronts) diffraction

steps.title: Polarisation
steps.body:
- Light is a transverse wave, so it can be polarised
- **Malus's law**: I = I₀ cos²θ for polarised light through an analyser; unpolarised light → I₀/2 through one polariser
- **Brewster's law**: tan θ_B = μ; at θ_B the reflected light is fully polarised and reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular
- Other methods: double refraction (calcite), scattering, quarter/half-wave plates

steps.title: Solved: grating orders
steps.body:
5000 lines/cm ⇒ d = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m; λ = 500 nm.

- First order: sinθ = λ/d = 0.25 ⇒ θ ≈ **14.5°**
- d/λ = 4, but n = 4 would need θ = 90° (not observable), so the highest visible order is **3**.

steps.title: Solved: polarisers and Brewster
steps.body:
- Unpolarised I₀ through two polarisers at 60°: I = (I₀/2) cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = **I₀/8**
- Glass μ = 1.5: θ_B = tan⁻¹ 1.5 ≈ **56.3°**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the grating formula for single-slit *minima* or vice versa.
- Forgetting the factor ½ for the first polariser with unpolarised light.
- Counting n = d/λ exactly as a visible order.
- Thinking sound can be polarised (it is longitudinal in air).

statements.s: The central maximum of a single slit is twice as wide as secondary maxima.
statements.why: It spans between the n = −1 and n = +1 minima.

statements.s: At Brewster's angle, the refracted light is fully polarised.
statements.why: It is the REFLECTED light that is fully polarised; the refracted beam is partially polarised.

statements.s: Polarisation proves light is transverse.
statements.why: Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised.

statements.s: A grating with more lines illuminated has higher resolving power.
statements.why: R = nN.

quiz.q: Grating equation:
quiz.why: The grating equation is d sin θ = nλ, where d is the grating spacing and n the order of the principal maximum.

quiz.q: Brewster angle satisfies:
quiz.why: At the Brewster angle reflected light is fully polarised, and tan θ_B = μ.

quiz.q: Polarised light of intensity I₀ through an analyser at 90°:
quiz.why: Malus's law gives I = I₀cos²θ. At 90°, cos 90° = 0 so no light passes.

quiz.q: Fraunhofer diffraction uses:
quiz.why: Fraunhofer diffraction assumes the source and screen are effectively at infinite distance, so the incident and diffracted wavefronts are plane.

quiz.q: Single slit width 0.1 mm, λ = 500 nm. First minimum angle (radians):
quiz.why: The first minimum is at a sin θ = λ, so sin θ = 500 × 10⁻⁹/10⁻⁴ = 5 × 10⁻³, which in radians is about 0.005.

questions.q: The period of ideal SHM depends on amplitude:
questions.why: The period of ideal SHM, T = 2π√(m/k), does not depend on amplitude. This property is called isochronism.

questions.q: Unpolarised light through one ideal polariser keeps:
questions.why: An ideal polariser passes only the component along its axis; averaged over random polarisation directions cos²θ gives ½, so half the intensity passes.

questions.q: Interference requires sources that are:
questions.why: Sustained interference needs coherent sources, with a fixed phase relationship between the waves.

questions.q: Wave y = A sin(kx − ωt) travels:
questions.why: In y = A sin(kx − ωt), constant phase means x = (ω/k)t + constant, so the wave travels in the +x direction.

questions.q: Overdamped systems:
questions.why: An overdamped system (b² > 4mk) returns slowly to equilibrium without oscillating.

questions.q: Grating spacing 1.67 μm, λ = 600 nm. Highest observable order:
questions.why: The maximum order needs sin θ ≤ 1, so n ≤ d/λ = 1670/600 ≈ 2.78. The highest observable order is therefore 2.

questions.q: Assertion: Newton's rings are circular. Reason: The air film thickness is constant along circles centred on the contact point.
options: Both true, reason does not explain
questions.why: Both true: the air film thickness is the same along any circle centred on the contact point, so equal-thickness loci are circles and the fringes are circular. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A string's fundamental is 200 Hz. Halving its length and keeping tension gives:
questions.why: For a string f ∝ 1/L at fixed tension and mass density. Halving L doubles the frequency to 400 Hz.

questions.q: Two polarisers crossed at 90° with a third at 45° between them. Output for unpolarised I₀:
questions.why: The first polariser passes I₀/2. The 45° one passes (I₀/2)cos²45° = I₀/4, and the last, at 45° to it, passes I₀/4 × ½ = I₀/8.

questions.q: In Newton's rings, D₅ = 3 mm and D₁₅ = 5 mm with R = 1 m. λ is:
A 0.5 kg mass on a spring k = 50 N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Speed at x = 0.06 m:
Case: Oil film (μ = 1.25) on water (μ = 1.33), white light at normal incidence. Minimum thickness strongly reflecting 500 nm:
questions.why: Air (1) to oil (1.25) and oil to water (1.33) both reflect from a denser medium, so both get λ/2 shifts and these cancel. A bright reflection then needs 2μt = λ, so t = 500/(2 × 1.25) = 200 nm.

questions.q: Resolving the sodium doublet (589.0, 589.6 nm) in first order needs at least:
questions.why: Resolving power λ/Δλ = nN. For n = 1: N = 589.3/0.6 ≈ 982 lines.

questions.q: A damped oscillator loses 1% of energy per cycle. Its Q factor is about:
questions.why: Q ≈ 2π × (energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle) = 2π × (1/0.01) = 2π × 100 ≈ 628.

questions.q: YDSE with λ = 600 nm: a thin glass sheet (μ = 1.5) over one slit shifts the pattern by 5 fringes. Thickness:
questions.why: The glass sheet adds an extra optical path (μ − 1)t. Shifting 5 fringes means (μ − 1)t = 5λ, so t = 5 × 600 nm/0.5 = 6000 nm = 6 μm.

courses.title: Thermal Physics · kinetic theory to Maxwell relations
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Kinetic theory of gases, the first and second laws of thermodynamics, Carnot engines and entropy, and thermodynamic potentials with Maxwell relations.
outcomes: Learners can derive pressure and rms speed from kinetic theory
Learners can compute work and heat in isothermal and adiabatic processes
Learners can apply Carnot efficiency and entropy changes
Learners can use Maxwell relations and the Clausius–Clapeyron equation

scenes.text: After a long highway drive, Faiz's tyre pressure reads higher than in the morning.
Hotter molecules hit the walls faster and harder. Kinetic theory turns that picture into P = ⅓ρv²_rms.

steps.title: Assumptions and results
steps.body:
Assumptions: many point molecules, random motion, elastic collisions, negligible forces except during collisions.

- Pressure P = ⅓ ρ v²_rms = ⅓ (N/V) m v²_rms
- Mean KE per molecule = (3/2)kT, k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K
- v_rms = √(3RT/M), v_avg = √(8RT/πM), v_mp = √(2RT/M); ratio v_mp : v_avg : v_rms = √2 : √(8/π) : √3
- **Equipartition**: ½kT per quadratic degree of freedom; monatomic Cv = (3/2)R, diatomic (rigid) Cv = (5/2)R, γ = 7/5

steps.title: Solved: rms speed of nitrogen
steps.body:
N₂ at 300 K, M = 0.028 kg/mol.

- v_rms = √(3 × 8.314 × 300/0.028) = √(2.67 × 10⁵) ≈ **517 m/s**
- To double v_rms you need 4× the absolute temperature (1200 K).

steps.title: Solved: comparing gases
steps.body:
At the same temperature, ratio of v_rms of H₂ to O₂:

- v ∝ 1/√M ⇒ √(32/2) = **4**
- This is why light gases like H₂ escape planetary atmospheres more easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M in g/mol in √(3RT/M) — must be kg/mol.
- Using °C instead of kelvin.
- Thinking all molecules move at v_rms (Maxwell distribution spreads speeds).
- Applying γ = 5/3 to diatomic gases.

quiz.q: Mean KE per molecule depends only on:
quiz.why: The mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kT, which depends only on absolute temperature, not on pressure or the gas's mass.

quiz.q: v_rms is proportional to:
quiz.why: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so it is proportional to √T.

quiz.q: γ for monatomic ideal gas:
quiz.why: For a monatomic gas Cv = 3R/2 and Cp = 5R/2, so γ = Cp/Cv = 5/3 ≈ 1.67.

quiz.q: Largest of the three speeds:
quiz.why: The three speeds are in the ratio v_mp : v_avg : v_rms = √2 : √(8/π) : √3, so v_rms is the largest.

quiz.q: At what temperature is v_rms of a gas twice its value at 27 °C?
quiz.why: v_rms ∝ √T. To double it, T must be 4 times: 4 × 300 K = 1200 K = 927 °C.

scenes.text: Pumping fast, Zoya notices the pump barrel warming up.
Rapid compression is nearly adiabatic: work done on the gas raises its internal energy and temperature.

steps.title: First law
steps.body:
dQ = dU + dW (heat added = rise in internal energy + work done BY the gas), dW = P dV. U of an ideal gas depends only on T: dU = nCv dT. Mayer's relation **Cp − Cv = R**.

- Isothermal: ΔU = 0, W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
- Adiabatic: Q = 0, PV^γ = constant, TV^(γ−1) = constant, W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1)
- Isobaric: W = PΔV; isochoric: W = 0

steps.title: Solved: isothermal expansion
steps.body:
1 mol ideal gas at 300 K doubles its volume isothermally.

- W = RT ln 2 = 8.314 × 300 × 0.693 ≈ **1729 J**
- ΔU = 0 so Q = 1729 J absorbed

steps.title: Solved: adiabatic compression
steps.body:
Air (γ = 1.4) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to half its volume.

- T₂ = T₁ (V₁/V₂)^(γ−1) = 300 × 2^0.4 = 300 × 1.32 ≈ **396 K**
- Diesel engines use much higher compression ratios to ignite fuel without a spark.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign convention mix-ups: decide whether W is by or on the gas and stick to it.
- Using PV^γ = constant for slow (quasi-static) isothermal processes.
- Writing ΔU = nCp ΔT (it is always nCv ΔT for an ideal gas).
- Forgetting that ln needs a ratio, not a difference.

activity.prompt: Sort each statement into the process it describes.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on:
quiz.why: For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so the internal energy depends only on temperature (Joule's law).

quiz.q: Cp − Cv equals:
quiz.why: Mayer's relation gives Cp − Cv = R per mole for an ideal gas.

quiz.q: Adiabatic curve on a PV diagram is ___ than an isothermal through the same point:
quiz.why: On a PV diagram the adiabatic slope is −γP/V, while the isotherm slope is −P/V. Since γ > 1 the adiabat is steeper.

quiz.q: Work in an isochoric process:
quiz.why: In an isochoric (constant volume) process dV = 0, so work done P dV is zero.

quiz.q: 2 mol of gas at 400 K expands isothermally from 10 L to 20 L. Work (approx):

lessons.title: Second law, Carnot cycle and entropy

story.title: The perfect engine that cannot exist

scenes.text: A start-up pitch claims an engine that turns ALL the heat from burning fuel into work.
Kelvin–Planck says no. Carnot tells us the best possible efficiency between two temperatures.

steps.title: Statements and Carnot
steps.body:
- **Kelvin–Planck**: no cyclic engine can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work
- **Clausius**: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot
- The two are equivalent. A **Carnot engine** (two isotherms + two adiabats) is the most efficient between T₁ (hot) and T₂ (cold): η = 1 − T₂/T₁
- Refrigerator COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂)
- **Entropy**: dS = dQ_rev/T; for an isolated system ΔS ≥ 0 (equality for reversible)

steps.title: Solved: Carnot numbers
steps.body:
Between 500 K and 300 K:

- η = 1 − 300/500 = **40%**
- For 1000 J taken in, W = 400 J and 600 J is rejected
- A refrigerator between 300 K and 270 K: COP = 270/30 = **9**

steps.title: Solved: entropy changes
steps.body:
- 1 kg of ice melting at 273 K (L = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg): ΔS = 3.34 × 10⁵/273 ≈ **1223 J/K**
- 1 mol ideal gas doubling volume isothermally: ΔS = R ln 2 ≈ **5.76 J/K**
- Free expansion into vacuum: same ΔS of the gas (state function), though Q = 0 — the process is irreversible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in Carnot efficiency.
- Thinking ΔS = Q/T for irreversible processes — compute along a reversible path between the same states.
- Believing entropy can never decrease anywhere (it can locally, if the surroundings gain more).
- Confusing COP of a refrigerator with that of a heat pump (T₁/(T₁ − T₂)).

activity.prompt: A Carnot engine works between 627 °C and 27 °C. What is its efficiency in percent?

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency depends on:
quiz.why: Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ depends only on the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, not on the working substance.

quiz.q: For an isolated system undergoing an irreversible process, ΔS is:
quiz.why: For an isolated system the entropy never decreases, and in an irreversible process ΔS > 0.

quiz.q: Entropy is a:
quiz.why: Entropy depends only on the state of the system, not on the path, so it is a state function.

quiz.q: Statement 'heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot' is due to:
quiz.why: The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body without work. The Kelvin–Planck statement is about converting heat fully to work.

quiz.q: Entropy change when 2 mol ideal gas expands isothermally to 4× volume:
quiz.why: For an isothermal ideal-gas expansion ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = 2R ln 4.

scenes.text: Grandmother's pressure cooker cooks dal faster in the hills. Why does higher pressure raise the boiling point?
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation — one of the most useful results from Maxwell relations — gives the slope of the boiling curve.

steps.title: Four potentials
steps.body:
- Internal energy: dU = T dS − P dV
- Enthalpy H = U + PV: dH = T dS + V dP
- Helmholtz F = U − TS: dF = −S dT − P dV
- Gibbs G = H − TS: dG = −S dT + V dP

Equality of mixed second derivatives gives **Maxwell relations**:
- (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V
- (∂T/∂P)_S = (∂V/∂S)_P
- (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V
- (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P

steps.title: Solved: Clausius–Clapeyron for water
steps.body:
dP/dT = L/(T(v₂ − v₁)). For water at 373 K: L = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg, v_vapour − v_liquid ≈ 1.67 m³/kg.

- dP/dT = 2.26 × 10⁶/(373 × 1.67) ≈ **3.6 kPa/K**
- So raising pressure by ~36 kPa raises the boiling point by about 10 K (roughly, since the slope changes).

steps.title: Solved: ice and pressure
steps.body: Ice melting: v_water < v_ice, so v₂ − v₁ < 0 and dP/dT < 0. Increasing pressure *lowers* the melting point of ice (slightly) — the explanation for regelation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up which variables are held constant in a Maxwell relation — derive from the potential's natural variables.
- Using molar L with specific volumes (keep units consistent).
- Forgetting that G is minimised at equilibrium at fixed T and P (F at fixed T and V).

activity.prompt: Match each potential with its natural variables.

quiz.q: Gibbs free energy is:
quiz.why: Gibbs free energy is defined as G = H − TS = U + PV − TS.

quiz.q: (∂S/∂V)_T equals:
quiz.why: From dF = −S dT − P dV, the cross-derivative equality gives (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V.

quiz.q: For ice melting, dP/dT is:
quiz.why: For ice melting the Clausius–Clapeyron equation gives dP/dT = L/(TΔV). Water is denser than ice, so ΔV < 0 and dP/dT is negative: more pressure lowers the melting point.

quiz.q: At constant T and P, equilibrium minimises:
quiz.why: At constant temperature and pressure, a system's equilibrium is where the Gibbs free energy G is a minimum.

quiz.q: Natural variables of enthalpy:
quiz.why: From dH = T dS + V dP, the natural variables of enthalpy are entropy S and pressure P.

questions.q: Absolute zero on the Celsius scale is about:
questions.why: Absolute zero, 0 K, corresponds to −273.15 °C.

questions.q: Heat engine efficiency is defined as:
questions.why: Efficiency is the useful work output divided by the heat taken in, η = W/Q₁.

questions.q: In an adiabatic process:
questions.why: An adiabatic process is one with no heat exchange with the surroundings, Q = 0.

questions.q: Degrees of freedom of a rigid diatomic molecule at room temperature:
questions.why: A rigid diatomic molecule has 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom at room temperature, so 5. Vibration is not excited yet.

questions.q: Entropy of the universe in any real process:
questions.why: Real processes are irreversible, so the total entropy of the universe always increases (second law).

questions.q: Helmholtz free energy is:
questions.why: Helmholtz free energy is F = U − TS. G = H − TS is the Gibbs free energy.

questions.q: Ratio v_rms(He)/v_rms(O₂) at the same T:
questions.why: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. For He (M = 4) and O₂ (M = 32), v_He/v_O₂ = √(32/4) = √8.

questions.q: Assertion: The adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal. Reason: γ > 1.
questions.why: Both true: the adiabat has slope −γP/V against −P/V for the isotherm, and since γ > 1 it is steeper. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A refrigerator between 27 °C and −3 °C has ideal COP:
questions.why: Ideal COP = T_cold/(T_hot − T_cold). T_cold = 270 K, T_hot = 300 K, so COP = 270/30 = 9.

questions.q: Monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 volume from 300 K. Final T:
questions.why: For an adiabatic process TV^(γ−1) is constant. T₂ = 300 × 8^(2/3) = 300 × 4 = 1200 K.

questions.q: Case: 0.5 kg of water at 100 °C boils to steam (L = 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg). Entropy change:
questions.why: Heat absorbed = mL = 0.5 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 1.13 × 10⁶ J at constant 373 K. ΔS = Q/T = 1.13 × 10⁶/373 ≈ 3030 J/K = 3.03 kJ/K.

questions.q: An engine takes 2000 J at 600 K and rejects 1200 J at 300 K. It is:
questions.why: Efficiency = (2000 − 1200)/2000 = 40%. The Carnot limit is 1 − 300/600 = 50%. Being below that, it is allowed but irreversible.

questions.q: 1 kg water at 0 °C is mixed with 1 kg at 100 °C (c = 4186 J/kg K). Total entropy change (approx):
Using a Maxwell relation, (∂S/∂P)_T for an ideal gas equals:
questions.why: From dG = −S dT + V dP, the Maxwell relation is (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P. For an ideal gas V = nRT/P, so (∂V/∂T)_P = nR/P and the result is −nR/P.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P equals:
questions.why: For an ideal gas P = nRT/V, so T(∂P/∂T)_V = nRT/V = P. Then (∂U/∂V)_T = P − P = 0.

courses.title: Elements of Modern Physics · quanta to Schrödinger
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Photoelectric and Compton effects, de Broglie waves and the uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation with its interpretation, and particle-in-a-box, tunnelling and the harmonic oscillator.
outcomes: Learners can use Einstein's photoelectric equation and the Compton shift
Learners can compute de Broglie wavelengths and uncertainty estimates
Learners can normalise wavefunctions and compute expectation values
Learners can derive particle-in-a-box energies

scenes.text: Raghav's solar calculator works under a white LED but barely under a dim red bulb, however close he holds it.
Light comes in photons; each photon's energy hν matters, not just brightness — Einstein's 1905 insight.

steps.title: Photons
steps.body:
- Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ; handy: E(eV) = 1240/λ(nm); momentum p = h/λ
- **Einstein's equation**: K_max = hν − φ = eV₀ (V₀ = stopping potential)
- Threshold frequency ν₀ = φ/h; no emission below it, whatever the intensity
- Intensity changes the *number* of photoelectrons, not their maximum energy
- **Compton shift**: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ); Compton wavelength h/m₀c = 2.43 pm

steps.title: Solved: stopping potential
steps.body:
λ = 400 nm on a metal with φ = 2.0 eV.

- E = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV
- K_max = 3.1 − 2.0 = **1.1 eV**, so V₀ = 1.1 V
- Threshold wavelength λ₀ = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm

steps.title: Solved: Compton at 90° and 180°
steps.body:
- θ = 90°: Δλ = 2.43 pm × (1 − 0) = **2.43 pm**
- θ = 180°: Δλ = 2 × 2.43 = **4.86 pm** (maximum)
- For visible light (λ ~ 500 nm) this shift is negligible, which is why Compton used X-rays.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking brighter light gives faster electrons.
- Forgetting that φ is in eV and E must be too (or both in joules).
- Expecting a visible Compton shift with visible light.
- Using the electron's rest mass for photons.

items.back: More electrons per second; same K_max
No emission at all, even at high intensity

items.front: Slope of V₀ vs ν graph
items.back: h/e — a way to measure Planck's constant

quiz.q: Stopping potential depends on:
quiz.why: By Einstein's equation eV₀ = hν − φ, so the stopping potential depends on frequency (and the metal) but not on intensity or exposure time.

quiz.q: Energy of a 620 nm photon:
Compton shift is maximum at:
quiz.why: The Compton shift is Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ), which is maximum when 1 − cos θ = 2, i.e. at 180°.

quiz.q: Slope of V₀ versus ν is:
quiz.why: From V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ/e, a graph of stopping potential against frequency has slope h/e.

quiz.q: A metal has threshold 500 nm. Light of 600 nm gives:
quiz.why: Light of 600 nm has a longer wavelength, hence lower photon energy, than the 500 nm threshold, so no photoelectrons are emitted.

lessons.title: Matter waves and the uncertainty principle

scenes.text: A biology lab shows images of a virus far smaller than any light microscope can resolve.
Electrons accelerated through high voltage have wavelengths much shorter than light — de Broglie's matter waves at work.

steps.title: de Broglie and Heisenberg
steps.body:
- de Broglie: **λ = h/p**; for an electron through V volts, λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ **1.227/√V nm**
- Confirmed by Davisson–Germer electron diffraction from nickel (1927)
- **Uncertainty**: Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2; ΔE Δt ≳ ħ/2 (ħ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
- It is a property of waves, not a fault of instruments.

steps.title: Solved: electron wavelength
steps.body:
- 100 V: λ = 1.227/10 = **0.1227 nm** (X-ray-like; diffracts from crystals)
- A 0.1 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s: λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/3 ≈ **2.2 × 10⁻³⁴ m** — far too small to notice.

steps.title: Solved: electron in an atom-sized region
steps.body:
Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m.

- Δp ≥ ħ/(2Δx) = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴/(2 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻²⁵ kg m/s
- Δv = Δp/m = 5.3 × 10⁻²⁵/9.11 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ **5.8 × 10⁵ m/s**
- Huge speed spread: electrons in atoms cannot have classical orbits.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 1.227/√V for particles other than electrons.
- Using relativistic speeds non-relativistically (above ~50 kV corrections matter).
- Thinking the uncertainty principle is about clumsy measurement only.
- Mixing h and ħ in the inequality.

activity.prompt: An electron is accelerated through 400 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength in nm? (Use λ = 1.227/√V nm.)

quiz.q: de Broglie wavelength:
quiz.why: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle is λ = h/p, where p is its momentum.

quiz.q: The Davisson–Germer experiment showed:
quiz.why: The Davisson–Germer experiment observed diffraction of electrons from a nickel crystal, confirming the wave nature of matter.

quiz.q: If an electron's kinetic energy is quadrupled, λ becomes:
quiz.why: λ = h/√(2mK), so λ ∝ 1/√K. Quadrupling K halves λ.

quiz.q: Uncertainty relation:
quiz.why: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2. The product has a lower bound, not an upper one.

quiz.q: Electron through 10 kV has λ about:

scenes.text: In a tutorial, Lata asks: if an electron is a wave, where exactly is it?
Born's answer: |ψ|² gives the probability density of finding it — quantum mechanics predicts probabilities.

steps.title: The equation and its meaning
steps.body:
- Time-dependent: iħ ∂ψ/∂t = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²ψ/∂x² + Vψ
- For stationary states ψ(x,t) = φ(x) e^(−iEt/ħ), giving the time-independent equation −(ħ²/2m) φ'' + Vφ = Eφ
- **Born rule**: |ψ|² dx = probability in dx; normalisation ∫|ψ|² dx = 1
- Acceptable ψ: single-valued, finite, continuous (and ψ' continuous where V is finite)
- Operators: p̂ = −iħ d/dx, Ĥ = p̂²/2m + V; expectation ⟨A⟩ = ∫ψ* Â ψ dx

steps.title: Solved: normalising a sine
steps.body:
ψ = A sin(πx/L) for 0 ≤ x ≤ L.

- ∫₀ᴸ A² sin²(πx/L) dx = A² L/2 = 1
- **A = √(2/L)**
- ⟨x⟩ = L/2 by symmetry

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating ψ itself as the probability (it is |ψ|², and ψ may be complex).
- Forgetting complex conjugates in expectation values.
- Dropping the factor 2 when integrating an even function over the full line.
- Believing stationary states are motionless — |ψ|² is time-independent, but the phase rotates.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to normalise a wavefunction.
items: Solve for the constant A (choose it real and positive)
Check boundary conditions are still satisfied

quiz.q: |ψ|² represents:
quiz.why: By the Born interpretation, |ψ|² is the probability density of finding the particle at a point.

quiz.q: Momentum operator in 1-D:
quiz.why: In position representation the momentum operator is p̂ = −iħ ∂/∂x. The kinetic energy operator is −ħ²/2m d²/dx².

quiz.q: Normalisation constant of ψ = A sin(πx/L) in [0, L]:
quiz.why: Normalisation requires ∫|ψ|²dx = A² ∫₀^L sin²(πx/L)dx = A²L/2 = 1, so A = √(2/L).

quiz.q: For stationary states, |ψ(x,t)|²:
quiz.why: For a stationary state ψ(x, t) = ψ(x)e^(−iEt/ħ). The phase factor has modulus 1, so |ψ|² does not change with time.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a requirement for an acceptable wavefunction?
quiz.why: A wavefunction must be single-valued, finite and continuous, but it may be complex. Only |ψ|² must be real.

lessons.title: Particle in a box, tunnelling and the oscillator

scenes.text: A QLED TV advert boasts quantum dots. Nisha learns that smaller dots glow bluer.
Confine an electron in a smaller box and its energy levels spread apart: E ∝ 1/L².

steps.title: Infinite square well
steps.body:
V = 0 inside 0 < x < L, infinite outside. ψ must vanish at the walls.

- ψₙ = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), n = 1, 2, 3…
- **Eₙ = n²h²/(8mL²)** = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²)
- Lowest energy is NOT zero (zero-point energy), consistent with uncertainty
- Levels spacing grows with n

steps.title: Solved: electron in a 1 nm box
Tunnelling and the harmonic oscillator
steps.body:
- A particle meeting a barrier V₀ > E has a decaying wave inside, ψ ∝ e^(−κx), κ = √(2m(V₀ − E))/ħ; transmission T ≈ e^(−2κa) for a thick barrier of width a. Examples: alpha decay, tunnel diodes, scanning tunnelling microscope.
- **Quantum harmonic oscillator**: Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω, evenly spaced, zero-point energy ½ħω.

steps.title: Solved: ratio questions
steps.body:
- Box width doubled ⇒ all energies become 1/4.
- Mass of particle doubled ⇒ energies halve.
- Oscillator: gap between any adjacent levels is ħω; ratio E₁/E₀ = (3/2)/(1/2) = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting the box at n = 0 (that gives ψ = 0 everywhere — not allowed).
- Thinking tunnelling violates energy conservation (E is unchanged).
- Using evenly spaced levels for the box (they go as n²) or n² for the oscillator (evenly spaced).

activity.prompt: Match the system to its energy formula or feature.

quiz.q: Ground-state energy of a particle in an infinite well is:
quiz.why: For an infinite well Eₙ = n²h²/8mL². The ground state n = 1 gives h²/8mL², which is non-zero (zero-point energy).

quiz.q: E₃/E₁ for an infinite well:
quiz.why: Eₙ ∝ n², so E₃/E₁ = 9/1 = 9.

quiz.q: Zero-point energy of a harmonic oscillator:
quiz.why: The levels of a quantum harmonic oscillator are (n + ½)ħω. For n = 0 the zero-point energy is ½ħω.

quiz.q: Tunnelling probability decreases when the barrier is:
quiz.why: The tunnelling probability goes like e^(−2κa), so it decreases rapidly as the barrier width a increases.

quiz.q: Halving the box width multiplies energies by:
quiz.why: E ∝ 1/L². Halving L multiplies E by 4.

questions.q: Photon energy formula:
questions.why: Planck–Einstein relation: the energy of a photon is E = hν, with h Planck's constant and ν the frequency.

questions.q: Wave nature of electrons was confirmed by:
questions.why: Davisson and Germer's electron diffraction from a nickel crystal confirmed de Broglie's wave nature of electrons.

questions.q: |ψ|² is:
questions.why: |ψ|² is the probability density of finding the particle (Born rule).

questions.q: Work function 4.2 eV. Threshold wavelength:
questions.why: λ_threshold = 1240 eV·nm/φ = 1240/4.2 ≈ 295 nm.

questions.q: Compton wavelength of the electron:
questions.why: The Compton wavelength of an electron is h/m₀c = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m = 2.43 pm.

questions.q: Particle-in-a-box levels scale as:
questions.why: For a particle in a box Eₙ = n²h²/8mL², so the levels scale as n².

questions.q: Assertion: Photoelectric emission is instantaneous even in dim light. Reason: Energy is delivered in photons, not spread continuously.
questions.why: Both true: each photon gives all its energy to one electron, so emission is immediate even when intensity is low, if the frequency is high enough. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A proton and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. They have the same:
questions.why: λ = h/p, so equal wavelength means equal momentum. Their speeds and energies differ because the masses differ.

questions.q: Light of 250 nm on a metal of φ = 2.96 eV. K_max:
Case: An electron in a box of 0.5 nm. E₁ ≈ (use E₁ = 0.376 eV for 1 nm):
questions.why: E ∝ 1/L². Halving L from 1 nm to 0.5 nm multiplies E by 4: 0.376 × 4 = 1.50 eV.

questions.q: Probability of finding a particle in the ground state of a box between 0 and L/2:
questions.why: The ground-state |ψ₁|² = (2/L)sin²(πx/L) is symmetric about L/2, so the probability in 0 to L/2 is half the total, 1/2.

questions.q: X-rays of 0.100 nm Compton-scatter at 90°. Scattered λ:
For ψ₁ in an infinite well, ⟨p⟩ equals:
questions.why: ψ₁ is a real standing wave, an equal superposition of +p and −p, so the average momentum ⟨p⟩ = 0 even though its kinetic energy is not zero.

questions.q: For ψ = √a e^(−a|x|), probability of |x| < 1/a:
Minimum KE of an electron confined to 10⁻¹⁴ m (nuclear size), estimated from p ≈ ħ/Δx, is of order:
questions.why: p ≈ 10⁻²⁰ kg m/s ⇒ pc ≈ 20 MeV — far above the electron's rest energy, one reason electrons are not nuclear constituents.

courses.title: B.Sc Physics · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Formula sheets for every core paper, a solved mixed practice paper and a 20-question mock exam spanning all units.
outcomes: Learners can recall all core formulas with units
Learners can choose the right method for mixed problems
Learners can manage time in a university theory paper

scenes.text: Two days before the semester exam, Aditya has one page left in his notebook.
He writes every formula with its condition of validity — the condition is what examiners test.

steps.title: Mechanics
steps.body:
- a(incline, rough) = g(sinθ − μcosθ); pseudo force −ma₀
- Elastic 1-D: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂)
- I = I_cm + Md² (any body); I_z = I_x + I_y (laminae)
- Rolling: a = g sinθ/(1 + I/MR²)
- vₑ = √(2gR), v₀ = √(gR), E_orbit = −GMm/2r, T² = 4π²r³/GM

steps.title: Electricity & Magnetism
steps.body:
- ∮E·dA = q/ε₀; line λ/2πε₀r; sheet σ/2ε₀; inside sphere kQr/R³
- C = κε₀A/d; U = ½CV²; u = ½ε₀E²
- Wire μ₀I/2πr; loop centre μ₀I/2R; solenoid μ₀nI; F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd
- ε = −N dΦ/dt; ε = Blv; ε_peak = NBAω; L = μ₀n²Al; U = ½LI²
- Maxwell: ∇·E = ρ/ε₀, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t

steps.title: How to use a formula sheet
steps.body: Next to each formula write: when it applies, when it fails, and one number you can sanity-check against (e.g. Earth's field ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁵ T, vₑ = 11.2 km/s).

steps.title: Top 5 exam slips
steps.body:
- Units (mm, cm², g/mol)
- Sign conventions (work by vs on, E = −∇V)
- Series vs parallel capacitors
- Applying symmetry laws without symmetry
- Forgetting rotational KE in rolling

quiz.q: Escape speed is √2 times:
quiz.why: Escape speed vₑ = √(2GM/R) and the near-surface orbital speed v₀ = √(GM/R). So vₑ = √2 v₀.

quiz.q: Capacitors in parallel:
quiz.why: Capacitors in parallel have the same voltage, and the charges add, so the capacitances add directly: C = ΣCᵢ.

quiz.q: The perpendicular axis theorem fails for:
quiz.why: The perpendicular axis theorem holds only for planar laminae. A solid sphere is a three-dimensional body, so it fails there.

quiz.q: Magnetic field outside an ideal long solenoid:
quiz.why: For an ideal long solenoid, B is uniform inside (μ₀nI) and essentially zero outside.

quiz.q: Lenz's law reflects conservation of:
quiz.why: Lenz's law reflects conservation of energy: if the induced current aided the change, energy would be created from nothing.

scenes.text: Four friends split the syllabus, each writing one sheet for the others.
They quiz each other: say the formula, its condition and a quick example.

steps.title: Waves & Optics
steps.body:
- ω = √(k/m); E = ½kA²; critical damping b² = 4mk; Q = ω₀m/b
- v = √(T/μ); fₙ = nv/2L; beats |f₁ − f₂|
- β = λD/d; thin film (reflected, one phase flip) dark: 2μt cos r = nλ; Newton's rings Dₙ² = 4nλR/μ
- Single slit minima a sinθ = nλ; grating d sinθ = nλ; R = nN
- Malus I = I₀cos²θ; Brewster tanθ_B = μ

steps.title: Thermal
steps.body:
- P = ⅓ρv²_rms; v_rms = √(3RT/M); KE = (3/2)kT
- Cp − Cv = R; W_iso = nRT ln(V₂/V₁); PV^γ = const; W_ad = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1)
- η_Carnot = 1 − T₂/T₁; COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂); dS = dQ_rev/T
- dU = TdS − PdV; F = U − TS; G = H − TS; dP/dT = L/(TΔv)

steps.title: Modern
steps.body:
- K_max = hν − φ; E(eV) = 1240/λ(nm); Δλ = 2.43 pm (1 − cosθ)
- λ = h/p; λₑ = 1.227/√V nm; ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2
- Eₙ(box) = n²h²/8mL²; Eₙ(oscillator) = (n + ½)ħω; T ≈ e^(−2κa)

steps.title: Top 5 slips
steps.body:
- °C in thermodynamic formulas
- Missing the λ/2 reflection phase
- Counting the n = d/λ grating order
- Using 1.227/√V for protons
- Starting a box at n = 0

activity.prompt: Match formula to topic.

quiz.q: Beats between 440 Hz and 437 Hz:
quiz.why: The beat frequency is the difference of the frequencies: 440 − 437 = 3 Hz.

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency between 400 K and 300 K:
Electron through 25 V, λ ≈:
Quantum oscillator level spacing:
quiz.why: The energy levels of a quantum harmonic oscillator are (n + ½)ħω, so the spacing between adjacent levels is always ħω, a constant.

quiz.q: Isothermal work for ideal gas uses:
quiz.why: For an isothermal process W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁), the natural log of the volume ratio, since U is constant.

lessons.title: Mock paper A — solved mixed problems

scenes.text: Set a 25-minute timer. Attempt each question before reading the explanation.
Mark yourself honestly; revisit the unit of any question you miss.

steps.title: Paper strategy
steps.body:
- Read the whole paper first; start with the question you are surest of
- For derivations, state assumptions, draw the diagram, then derive
- For numericals: write formula → substitute with units → box answer with unit
- Leave 10 minutes to check units and significant figures

steps.title: Solved: mixed problem 1
steps.body:
A 2 kg disc (R = 0.2 m) rolls without slipping at 3 m/s. Total KE?

- K_trans = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J
- K_rot = ½ × (½ × 2 × 0.04) × (3/0.2)² = ½ × 0.04 × 225 = 4.5 J
- Total = **13.5 J** (= ¾Mv²)

steps.title: Solved: mixed problem 2
steps.body:
A gas engine takes heat at 527 °C and rejects at 127 °C. Maximum work from 10 kJ?

- T₁ = 800 K, T₂ = 400 K, η = 0.5
- W_max = **5 kJ**

steps.title: Solved: mixed problem 3
steps.body:
Light 300 nm on a metal of φ = 2.3 eV. Speed of fastest electrons?

- E = 4.13 eV; K = 1.83 eV = 2.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
- v = √(2K/m) = √(6.4 × 10¹¹) ≈ **8.0 × 10⁵ m/s**

quiz.q: KE of a rolling ring of mass M, speed v:
quiz.why: For a rolling ring, translational ½Mv² plus rotational ½(MR²)(v/R)² = ½Mv² gives a total of Mv².

quiz.q: A 5 μF capacitor at 100 V; charge:
quiz.why: Q = CV = 5 μF × 100 V = 500 μC.

quiz.q: Grating 4000 lines/cm, λ = 625 nm: first-order sinθ:
quiz.why: 4000 lines/cm gives d = 1/4000 cm = 2.5 μm. First order d sin θ = λ, so sin θ = 0.625/2.5 = 0.25.

quiz.q: Adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas causes:
quiz.why: In an adiabatic expansion there is no heat flow in, so the work done by the gas comes from its internal energy and the temperature falls: cooling.

quiz.q: Electron in a 2 nm box, E₁ ≈ (0.376 eV for 1 nm):
Field at 2 cm from a long wire with 4 A:

questions.q: Unit of magnetic field B:
questions.why: The SI unit of magnetic field is the tesla (T). The henry is for inductance and the weber for flux.

questions.q: Entropy is measured in:
questions.why: Entropy change is dS = dQ/T, which has units of joule per kelvin (J/K).

questions.q: Photon momentum:
questions.why: The momentum of a photon is p = h/λ = E/c.

questions.q: Total energy of SHM is constant because:
questions.why: Ideal SHM has only conservative restoring forces, so the total energy stays constant while it moves between kinetic and potential forms.

questions.q: Moment of inertia of a disc about a diameter:
questions.why: For a disc I_z = MR²/2 about the perpendicular axis. By the perpendicular axis theorem I_x + I_y = I_z and by symmetry I_x = I_y, so about a diameter I = MR²/4.

questions.q: Grating of 6000 lines/cm, λ = 500 nm: highest order:
questions.why: 6000 lines/cm gives d = 1/6000 cm = 1.667 μm. Maximum order n ≤ d/λ = 1667/500 = 3.33, so the highest order is 3.

questions.q: If T doubles (K), v_rms changes by factor:
questions.why: v_rms ∝ √T. Doubling T multiplies v_rms by √2.

questions.q: Induced emf in a 200-turn coil when flux per turn changes by 0.01 Wb in 0.05 s:
Assertion: Displacement current makes Ampère's law consistent with charge conservation. Reason: The divergence of a curl is zero.
questions.why: Both true: without displacement current, ∇ × B = μ₀J would imply ∇·J = 0 (the divergence of a curl is zero), contradicting charge conservation. Maxwell's added term fixes this, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Two springs (k each) in series hold mass m. Period:
questions.why: Two springs of constant k in series give k_eff = k/2, so T = 2π√(m/k_eff) = 2π√(2m/k).

questions.q: Monatomic ideal gas: heat needed to raise 2 mol by 10 K at constant pressure:
questions.why: For a monatomic gas Cp = 5R/2 = 20.785 J/mol·K. Q = nCpΔT = 2 × 20.785 × 10 ≈ 415.7 J.

questions.q: de Broglie λ of a 54 eV electron (Davisson–Germer):
questions.why: λ = 1.227/√V nm with V = 54: 1.227/7.35 ≈ 0.167 nm, which matches the Ni lattice diffraction.

questions.q: Case: Satellite at height R above Earth's surface. g there equals:
questions.why: A height of R above the surface puts the satellite at distance r = 2R from the centre. g ∝ 1/r², so g′ = g/4.

questions.q: Spherical shell of radius R holds Q. Potential at its centre:
questions.why: Inside a conducting or charged shell the field is zero, so the potential is constant and equals the surface value kQ/R.

questions.q: Thin film μ = 1.5 in air, normal incidence, reflected bright for λ = 600 nm at minimum thickness:
questions.why: In air, reflection off the film's top surface has a λ/2 shift but the bottom does not. Brightness needs 2μt = λ/2, so t = 600/(4 × 1.5) = 100 nm.

questions.q: An inductor (L = 2 H) current rises 0 → 3 A. Energy stored:
questions.why: U = ½LI² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

questions.q: A Carnot engine has η = 1/6. Lowering the sink by 62 K doubles η to 1/3. Source temperature:
questions.why: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1/6 gives T₂/T₁ = 5/6. With the sink at T₂ − 62: 1 − (T₂ − 62)/T₁ = 1/3, so (T₂ − 62)/T₁ = 2/3. Subtracting, 62/T₁ = 1/6, so T₁ = 372 K.

questions.q: Electron in an infinite well of width L: wavelength emitted in 3 → 1 vs 2 → 1 transition, ratio λ₃₁/λ₂₁:
questions.why: Eₙ ∝ n². The 3 → 1 gap is 9 − 1 = 8 units and the 2 → 1 gap is 4 − 1 = 3. λ ∝ 1/ΔE, so λ₃₁/λ₂₁ = 3/8.

questions.q: A uniform rod of length L pivoted at one end is released horizontal. Angular speed at the vertical:
questions.why: Energy conservation: loss of PE for the centre of mass drop L/2 is MgL/2 = ½Iω² with I = ML²/3. So ω² = 3g/L and ω = √(3g/L).

questions.q: Coaxial cable: inner wire current I, outer shell −I. B outside the cable:
questions.why: Ampère's law on a circle outside the cable encloses I − I = 0 net current, so B = 0 there. The two magnetic fields cancel.
